#3554. 10 Hacks Every Google Messages User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Messages is Google's official texting app, and while it hasn't always been first to roll out useful features, it has caught up to what other messaging services offer and has a handful of hidden hacks to make communicating and coordinating with contacts easier and safer. Here are the best tips and tricks that every Google Messages user should know.

Google Messages recently got a Google Keep integration, which allows group chat participants to collaborate on notes and checklists directly in the message thread without having to click over to a separate app. This also centralizes ideas in one place rather than spread across a thread with dozens of separate text messages. Changes to Keep Notes sync automatically for all users. Tap the plus icon in the message compose bar in Google Messages, select Keep Notes, and either choose an existing note or tap to create a new one to be shared in the chat.

Over the last few years, Google has rolled out a number of security features for identifying and defending against scams and fraud spread via calls and text messages. These work by detecting suspected spam and either preventing it from being delivered or hiding it in a separate folder, as well as flagging suspicious links. A newer opt-in enhanced protection mode for Google Messages uses AI to catch more complex threats and alert you if a conversation or unfamiliar link that looks legit might put you at risk. Standard protection is on by default, but you can turn on enhanced protection under Messages settings > Protection & Safety > Spam and scam protection.

If you have an idea you want to write down but not send immediately—because it's outside of work hours or late at night—you can draft it in Google Messages and schedule it for later. "Send later" features in messaging and chat apps are useful for maintaining good boundaries without having to remember to type and send at a different time. Once you've entered your message in the text field, touch and hold Send, choose from the suggested actions, then tap Send again.

Swiping left or right on your conversations in Google Messages will either archive or delete them. You can customize which swipe maps onto which action for quick inbox triaging or disable one or both to prevent accidentally triggering an unwanted action. Tap your profile photo > Message settings > Swipe actions > Customize to select your preferences.

Google Messages has a pinning feature that will anchor conversations at the top of your message history, but you can also star important messages you want to save and return to later. Starring makes it easy to keep track of data like flight information, contacts, or dates that might otherwise get lost in a thread or be difficult to pull up in a basic search—starred messages have their own search filter. Simply tap and hold the message and tap Star at the top, then go to Search conversations > Starred > More options > Starred to see your list of saved messages.

We've all been in the overactive group chat that we don't want to see notifications from in real time but also don't want to leave. You can snooze threads semi-permanently, but you can also turn on a temporary snooze that will lift so notifications restart after a short period of time. This can be useful for threads discussing live events or games you will be catching up on later or if you need silence during a focused work period. Touch and hold the conversation, tap Snooze, then select your duration and tap Snooze to confirm. You can choose from 1 hour, 8 hours, 24 hours, or always.

Google Messages has two group chat modes. Group MMS is your typical group text—it sends a single message to all recipients, and everyone receives replies in the thread. Mass Text, by contrast, is like BCC. This sends your message to each user individually, and replies come only to the original sender. Using this mode allows you to share information with a bunch of people at once without creating the dreaded reply-all thread. You can change your default group messaging settings via profile > Message settings > Advanced > Group messaging.

Google Messages finally launched integrated real-time location sharing earlier this year, which allows you to send your live whereabouts to trusted contacts directly in a message thread. Location sharing makes it easier to coordinate meeting up or let someone know where you are if there are any safety concerns. You can set a limited duration or leave location sharing on indefinitely for specific contacts. Open a conversation and tap Attachment > Real-time location

You don't have to live with the embarrassment of sending a text in error with Google Messages—at least not if you catch the mistake quickly. Google Messages has a "Delete for everyone" function that can remove sent messages from the devices of users who are running the latest version of the app. Conversations must be using RCS for this to work, and you have only a limited window—anywhere from 15 to 40 minutes, according to support documentation—to use the feature before your messages are permanent. Long-press a message to pull up available delete options.

If you want to stay on top of your text threads but get distracted by other things every time you pick up your phone, you can log into the Google Messages web interface on your browser. This also makes it easier to send photos and files from your computer via Google Messages without having to transfer them to your phone first.

#3553. Inside LA’s Election Night Parties as DSA-Backed Nithya Raman Threatens to Unseat Karen Bass

Ta-Nehisi Coates (Vanity Fair senior staff writer) recently said that if he reads “another scene from a DSA party in Brooklyn where people are drinking beer and doing whatever, I’m going to scream.”

But I can report that there were a lot of ecstatic and tipsy socialists in oversized vintage jackets at the DSA election party on the edge of Skid Row in Los Angeles Tuesday night. And, boy, did these socialists have a lot to celebrate.

Democrats were trouncing Republicans nationally. Democratic socialists were projected to take at least seven seats in the House, up from two. And in Los Angeles, the DSA’s preferred mayoral candidate, Nithya Raman, appeared poised to unseat Karen Bass. The incumbent Democratic mayor held a less than 1% lead in early returns, but ballots are expected to skew toward the more progressive candidate, Raman.

“Karen Bass said that she would need to be up 10 points on election night to be comfortable,” one DSA-LA leader told the crowd. He gestured at a graphic showing Bass’s narrow lead and said, “I’m not good at math because I’m gay. Is that 10 points? I don’t think so.” (Bass didn’t actually say that, but a pundit on KTLA did say something to that effect.)

Karen Bass during an election night event in Los Angeles, November 3, 2026.

At the DSA party, people cheered victories elsewhere in the country by socialists and establishment Democrats alike, but they booed when Bass appeared on television, and laughed when a Fox News commentator suggested the economy was doing well. At one point, organizers put on Hasan Piker’s livestream, and at another they played an AI-generated video showing Raman dancing while wearing a traditional Russian fur hat with ear flaps and a red star. When local TV station KTLA suggested Raman would likely win and Mayor Bass’s face appeared onscreen, someone shouted, “Whoa, get fucked, Karen.” It kind of encapsulated the strongest force animating the DSA members I talked to in this mayoral race: their dislike for Mayor Bass. They even called her the C-word onstage: “conservative.”

The DSA and Raman have had something of an on-again, off-again relationship. The organization helped propel her to an upset City Council victory in 2020, only to reprimand her over disagreements about Israel, housing policy, and the city’s mansion tax. The local DSA chapter endorsed her candidacy late in the campaign, but the national organization almost stripped it from her at the eleventh hour. The national DSA voted last week to preserve its Los Angeles chapter’s endorsement of Raman by a single vote, after a dispute over her refusal to embrace the movement to boycott Israel.

“I think people here have varying levels of begrudgingness about supporting Raman, but I think everyone here voted for her,” said one DSA-LA member at the party who worked on the chapter’s video team and declined to give her name.

Still, the DSA members at the party seemed to think this mayoral race offered another encouraging sign for their organization, even if Raman isn’t quite New York mayor Zohran Mamdani. She was attacked consistently by her opponents—mainly Spencer Pratt—as a dangerous extremist, but with the help of the DSA (it said members knocked on more than 110,000 doors this election cycle) she might be the first LA mayoral candidate to defeat an incumbent in over 20 years.

Meanwhile, at the Raman campaign’s official election night party at the Greek Theatre in Los Feliz, there weren’t any signs calling to “Tax the Rich” or to implement “Medicare for All,” as there were at the DSA party, but comedian Guy Branum from Apple TV’s Platonic sounded pretty similar to those socialists. He argued that Raman’s coalition reflected a class divide within Hollywood.

“Nithya has way more of entertainment’s middle class,” Branum said, describing workers worried about their next job. And Raman’s husband, television writer Vali Chandrasekaran, understands the industry’s problems firsthand, he argued.

Branum, who hangs with the couple socially, also wanted voters to appreciate one of her lessdiscussed qualifications. “They lead with the master’s in urban planning, and the Harvard, and the MIT,” he said. “But what you really need to see is that [she can dance]. You really need to see that hair let loose.” (Vanity Fair did not stick around at the party long enough to verify Raman’s dancing skills.)

Raman held her election night party at the Greek Theatre in Los Angeles, November 3, 2026.

Raman’s campaign manager, Ian Manheimer, was pretty psyched when he took the stage outside the Greek. “Holy shit! What is good, Los Angeles?” he shouted. Nearly three quarters of his campaign staff had never worked on a political campaign before, he told the crowd. Regardless, they managed to knock on over 100,000 doors, according to Manheimer.

The campaign’s grassroots operation had apparently become a bit of a competition. Volunteer Leo Blain, 25, told VF he’d knocked on more than 300 doors, putting him near the top of the campaign leaderboard. But the person to beat was Raman’s father, whom volunteers said had knocked on more than 1,000. All of that knocking was crucial, especially since Raman didn’t have a lot of institutional support or name recognition. Many of California’s most prominent Democrats stayed on the sidelines, because most of them would do anything to avoid the choice between an establishment incumbent and a rising DSA-endorsed challenger. But their neutrality didn’t necessarily mean indifference. A high-ranking official in Sacramento told me that plenty of state legislators were privately rooting for Bass, who had served as Speaker of the California Assembly before heading to Congress.

John, a DSA member who volunteered for Raman after having worked on Tom Steyer’s gubernatorial campaign, expected strong support for Raman among the local socialists, arguing that her independent thinking was a positive.

Raman’s party also included some unlikely converts. Kathleen Jensen, a Toluca Lake resident who previously supported Republican Rick Caruso, told me she considered Raman brilliant and wanted a “doer” in City Hall. Although she said some of her Democrat friends remained uneasy about Raman’s DSA association.

By 10:30 p.m., Bass’s election night party at the Loews Hotel in Hollywood had grown considerably quiet as her supporters began to digest the initial results. But the people who remained were still getting down to Snoop Dogg. The demographic differences between the parties were striking. Raman’s crowd skewed whiter, and more Asian, and the music was more alternative and disco. Bass’s crowd was notably more Black, reflecting the mayor’s decades of relationships in the city’s African American community.

Vaval Victor, 28, a member of Alpha Phi Alpha, the historically Black fraternity with which Bass has worked, remained confident that she would pull through. “She started the LA Black Dems Club in her kitchen,” he said, invoking her long history of organizing. “People are thirsty for hope.”

Bass had spent the campaign defending her record on homelessness, city finances, and last year’s catastrophic fires. Caruso, whom she defeated four years earlier, had swooped in at the end to say that he was voting for her, giving some of the city’s more conservative voters permission to support the incumbent. But early election-night returns were not the decisive advantage her campaign hoped for.

For all the divisions this mayoral race exposed, the three parties shared something that had been in short supply among Democrats lately: liberal joy.

#3552. Skydance Inherited Massive Flops From Warner Bros. Deal - And Things Could Get Worse

There's a new mega-studio in Hollywood, and it's got a lot to prove. The Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount merger was recently made official, with the new company named Skydance. This $111 billion deal has been met with intense scrutiny, in no small part because Skydance is now saddled with billions of dollars in debt. So, to make all this look even remotely tenable for the foreseeable future, that means Warner Bros. has to deliver at the box office.

Unfortunately, the new owners at Skydance inherited a string of massive flops ... and it may get worse before it gets better.

Indeed, a report from Page Six has examined Warner Bros.' ex-film bosses Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy's "free spending" ways. Recall that Warner Bros. set a huge box office record in 2025, with six movies in a row earning at least $40 million on opening weekend. But this year has not been kind to the studio, with this report stating that Warner Bros.' 2026 slate will lose around $800 million. Can it really be that bad? Yes, it can.

Here's a full breakdown of Warner Bros.' 2026 at the box office, movie by movie:

"Wuthering Heights" — $80 million budget/$241 million worldwide

"The Bride!" — $90 million budget/$24 million worldwide

"They Will Kill You" — $10 million budget/$19 million worldwide

"Lee Cronin's The Mummy" — $22 million budget/$90 million worldwide

"Mortal Kombat II" — $80 million budget/$129 million worldwide

"Supergirl" — $170 million budget/$126 million worldwide

"Evil Dead Burn" — $20 million budget/$72 million worldwide

"The End of Oak Street" — $90 million budget/$121 million worldwide

"Practical Magic 2" — $75 million budget/$106 million worldwide

"Digger" — $180 million budget/$49 million worldwide

"Clayface" — $44 million budget/$84 million worldwide (still in theaters)

I previously broke down how movie box office actually works. Basically, without getting too far into the weeds, theaters keep around half of all money from ticket sales, and budget figures don't include marketing expenses. Taking that into account, we can see that only "Wuthering Heights," "Lee Cronin's The Mummy," "Evil Dead Rise," and "Clayface" will go down as hits for Warner Bros. this year, when all's said and done. And some of those are rather modest successes at best.

The rest of the slate is either filled with big disappointments or crushing flops. Tom Cruise's "Digger" will lose a lot of money at the box office, potentially as much as $250 million. That's just the tip of the iceberg, too. "The Bride!" also lost a fortune, while "Supergirl" flopped in a rather terrible fashion. Movies that were expected to be blockbuster hits instead became shipwrecks, with the debris washing up on the rocks. It's been bad.

The validity of that $800 million figure is somewhat irrelevant. It's crystal clear that WB's 2026 slate, overall, is going to lose a lot of money. Even if movies like "They Will Kill You" eventually made money on VOD/streaming, Skydance needs big hits. What it's gotten is a string of disastrous flops.

Even "One Battle After Another" was still a box office bomb ($213 million worldwide/$170 million budget) despite winning Best Picture at the Oscars. This Page Six report estimates it lost around $75 million. The Oscar helps, but probably not quite that much. Hence, Skydance needs Warner Bros. to deliver at the box office more than ever, and the hope is that 2027 will deliver green pastures. But that's far from a sure thing at this juncture.

On paper, there are some surefire bets on Warner Bros.' upcoming slate in 2027. 2024's "Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire" became the highest-grossing "Godzilla" movie ever, so it stands to reason that its sequel, "Godzilla x Kong: Supernova," will be a hit as well. But Warner Bros. will have to split that revenue with Legendary, so that's a somewhat qualified winner.

There's also the studio's much-anticipated return to Middle Earth. Even though Peter Jackson isn't directing "The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum," it has a lot of appeal and revives a multi-billion-dollar global franchise. Optimistically, that should pan out pretty well, too, though how well remains to be seen. On top of that, there's the "Minecraft Movie" sequel, James Gunn's "Superman" follow-up "Man of Tomorrow," and "The Conjuring: First Communion," the latter of which ought to deliver. Remember, only six horror movie franchises have made over $1 billion at the box office, and The Conjuring Universe is one of them.

Outside of that? It gets far more murky. Director J.J. Abrams' "The Great Beyond" was pushed back to 2027, presumably because WB wanted an IMAX release. It's expensive and far from a sure thing. Even riskier is the new Nancy Meyers rom-com tentatively titled "Paris Paramount," which reportedly cost a dizzying $120 million. As for Sam Esmail's $60 million "Panic Carefully" and the CGI/live-action hybrid movie "Animal Friends?" They're big question marks.

For seemingly every sure thing on WB's 2027 slate, then, there's a real risk. Skydance film bosses Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg have a lot of decisions to make. For now, though, It's be less about the movies they want to make and more about how they're going to handle all the dicey prospects they've inherited.

He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the events of WandaVision (and, slightly more tangentially, Agatha All Along), VisionQuest returns to the story of Marvel's favorite synthic being, an artificial creation who fights supervillains and ponders the nature of his own existence, rather than more typical AI pursuits like creating deep fakes.

White Vision (the character, not the political agenda) is a copy of the Vision who died two Avengers movies ago. He's living within his own mind on a fantasy country estate while on the run from bounty hunters and in pursuit of his semi-fictional son. In that spirit, here are 10 more science fiction shows that involve artificial people and/or elaborate constructed realities.

In the near-future world, highly advanced “synths” are commonplace, doing the work that regular humans can’t be bothered with. These beings are treated as entirely disposable sources of cheap labor, despite their apparent burgeoning humanity. The first season introduces the Hawkins family, who buy (on sale) a domestic servant synth named Anita (Gemma Chan); mom Laura is a little uncomfortable with the arrangement, especially when she finds her husband having sex with Anita, who has her own complicated backstory. Humans interrogates the ways humans always seem to find excuses to dehumanize others, which is just the type of thing that sci-fi is pretty great at. Stream Humans on Peacock, Prime Video, and Tubi.

One of the smartest recent shows is a dark comedy based on the Hugo-Award winning book series by Martha Wells. Alexander Skarsgård is the title's hilariously deadpan robot, a private "security construct" who's managed to hack its way through its own programming and gain free will—which it mostly wants to use to binge its favorite streaming shows. It can't just run off for fear of drawing attention, but the self-named Murderbot (it's being ironic, kinda) is content to do the bare minimum when it's assigned to a team of naive hippie researchers who don't see the need for a killer security robot—at least, not until they're enmeshed in a complicated capitalist plot in which they're all just cogs. Stream Murderbot on Apple TV.

From playwright Tearrance Arvelle Chisholm (Hooded: Or Being Black for Dummies), this show stars Okieriete Onaodowan as the title character, an inhabitant of an alternate present who is turning 33 and pursuing therapy for the first time. He's offered the chance to use DIRT (Digital Immersive Reality Therapy), in which he can visit and view other versions of himself, as long as he doesn't interfere. Which, of course, he does, with results that are sometimes poignant and sometimes funny. Hard to believe that this clever show almost wound up in the bin, a victim of that stupid moment a couple of years ago when streamers and studios were shelving otherwise great projects for tax reasons. No robots here, but a human exploring a complex world inside his own head. Stream Demascus on Tubi.

In this more darkly dangerous vision of a virtual world, video-game-obsessed Arisu gets his wish, after a fashion; he finds himself, along with a couple of friends, transported to an alternate, eerily abandoned version of Tokyo—the title’s Borderland—vividly brought to life via clever green screen work. The three are directed to an arena and given the instructions for the game, which they’ll be playing whether they want to or not. The first competition involves a locked-room-style puzzle; if they fail, the room goes up in flames with them in it—think Ready Player One, with deadlier stakes. There are games each night, though the rules allow for winners to get time off. There are a lot of rules, actually, but the games are cleverly and sadistically constructed. Stream Alice in Borderland on Netflix.

Though ostensibly an X-Men spinoff, this phantasmagoric show from Noah Hawley (Fargo, Alien: Earth) stands entirely on its own, taking place largely inside the headspace of a deeply troubled man. Dan Stevens plays David Haller, diagnosed with schizophrenia and possessed of tremendous psychic abilities. In one of the many psychiatric hospitals to which he's been committed, he meets first the free-wheeling Lenny (Aubrey Plaza) and then Syd (Rachel Keller), who can trade bodies with anyone she touches. Veering in and out of trippy astral planes and deeply damaged psyches, David soon comes to realize that he's not crazy—and also that he's probably not the hero of the story, even as he's caught between the authorities who'd like to use him for his power and the Shadow King who's been haunting his mind since childhood. Stream Legion on Hulu.

Just a science fiction action comedy about a nun married to literal Jesus on a quest to save the world from the title's artificial intelligence by finding the Holy Grail alongside her ex-boyfriend. So, yeah, there’s a lot going on in Mrs. Davis—sometimes a little too much, but the show gets major points for ambition. Betty Gilpin holds everything together as Sister Simone, playing it straight in an extremely over-the-top world. It’s refreshing to see a show that’s so unafraid to take big swings, and it works much more often than it should. Though it was cancelled after one season, it ends reasonably well, and, like co-creator Damon Lindelof’s HBO series Watchmen, would probably be best served by remaining a one-and-done. Stream Mrs. Davis on Peacock.

A charming comedy-drama set in a science fiction world, Robbie Amell stars as Nathan Brown, a young computer programmer who's also recently deceased. In the future of 2033, humans have the option of having their consciousnesses uploaded into virtual worlds post-mortem and Nathan's is chosen for him by his rich and rather possessive girlfriend. The exclusive afterlife setting of Lakeview is stifling, as is the fact that said girlfriend has a say in his perpetual existence. He's on the brink of despair until he strikes up a friendship with Nora (Andy Allo), his very-much-alive customer service rep. Stream Upload on Prime Video and Hulu.

Tricky to recommend, given that the show's four seasons saw a period of decline followed by a cancellation just when it was getting really good again—however, when Westworld was cooking (as in its addictive first season), there was nothing else like it on television. Set, initially, in a high-tech, near-future amusement park designed to appeal to wealthy clientele, the show finds the lifelike androids created to service the guests gradually waking up to their disposability. In the best tradition of sci-fi, this one's less about AI than it is about a world of disposable beings existing purely at the whim, and for the amusement of, the ultra-wealthy. Which is definitely not a 100% relatable metaphor. Buy Westworld from Prime Video.

You've likely seen this one if you're watching VisionQuest, but it's worth mentioning as not only a fairly essential preface, but also one of the best (and most distinctive) bits of Marvel media...ever? (Agatha All Along is also great, but less essential to Vision's narrative). At least initially, WandaVision confused dedicated Marvel fans as much as noobs, making it a unique on-ramp, even if it does have many threads connected to the broader superhero universe. Its story of a grieving witch living out her sitcom fantasies is an impressive swing into the surreal, well worth it if you’re content to go along for a weird and surprisingly emotional ride. Stream WandaVision on Disney+.

It can be tricky for co-stars who have great chemistry to get away from the shipping culture online, particularly when it’s already got a massive book following. So it makes sense that their love lives are going to come up more the bigger the fandom is, and right now, thanks to Sunrise on the Reaping, one of the actors can’t seem to stop talking about her relationship… and she’s not complaining. Mckenna Grace invoked District 12 when talking about her love life and I get it, considering who Hunger Games fans ship her with.

When Sunrise on the Reaping hit the 2026 movie schedule, I knew it wouldn’t be long before ships started sailing, especially after getting the first reactions to the movie. Grace plays District 12 tribute Maysilee Donner (along with her twin Merrilee). So naturally, she spends a lot of time with Joseph Zada who plays young Haymitch, and even though she’s happily dating a different co-star, Mason Thames, fans are still shipping them. The actor made sure to shout out her partner in an interview discussing all things Hunger Games with Cosmopolitan.

While dishing about manifesting her Hunger Games role and being "Team Peeta," she assured fans that she’s never been happier. She has been dating Thames since the two took their Regretting You romance from the screen into real-life. The couple went public earlier in the year on Valentine’s Day, and have been going strong ever since. Grace shares:

Your girl is happy. I’m feeling very lovey-dovey. I have somebody I can be a complete nerd with. I got my best friend, and so I don’t see the point in not loving loudly.

Grace is going all in on "loving loudly," and I’m loving how similar it is to her dedication as a fangirl. After all she dressed like Jennifer Lawrence for the prequel’s press tour. According to Grace, she doesn’t see the point in keeping her feelings to herself:

There are moments that are just for you and your person. But I don’t see the point in not celebrating who you’re in love with. A lot of people’s hesitation around this stems from the idea that if you post about someone a bunch and then you break up, that’s embarrassing. But why would I even think about that? I’m just going to focus on the present.

It can be stressful having a relationship in the public eye, but the actor seems to be handling with grace. Though I didn’t expect her to invoke District 12 when bringing up her dedication to Thames. In hindsight, given how much of a fan girl she is of Peeta Mellark, I should have. Additionally, in what can only be described as a Tom Holland move, Thames was often hanging out around the cornucopia with her while filming:

It’s a terrifying thing in a relationship to surrender yourself to that thought of, I’m just going to be at my most vulnerable and trust you, and this part of my life is fully in your hands. But I don’t see the point in building a relationship based on fear. I am the biggest fan of the person I’m with, so why wouldn’t I be like, ‘This is my person. I am so stoked I have this’? We’re always on each other’s sets anyway. He’s like an honorary member of District 12 at this point.

The shout out to Thames’ visits could have to do with die hard fans shipping her IRL with co-star Zada. It definitely feels like her polite way of reminding people, because she's well aware of what the fans want to see. During the press tour, the co-stars were asked what they thought.

The two quickly laughed it off and described it as “pretty weird.” For them, it goes beyond the two already dating other people. While Grace is outright about her relationship with Thames, Zada goes a more private route with his non-actor girlfriend. Truthfully, it has to do with the fact that they view each other like family thanks to long hours on the Hunger Games prequel. Check out this exchange between them during an interview with Refinery29 Australia:

However, this hasn’t stopped the two from calling out their own favorite ships amongst their castmates. From Zada and Ben Wang to Grace and Laura Marcus, there’s plenty to choose from, but for Grace she’s team ‘Maydove.’ In fact, she informed Zada that she’s “coming for [his] girl.” (Though I’m surprised Grace didn’t shout out Peeta and Katnis, especially since they reprised their roles in the movie. We all know about Grace's fan edits.)

Regardless of ship preference, it’s nice to see the co-stars having fun with the shipping culture, and not taking anything to heart. Besides, Grace is clearly thriving in her "lovey dovey" era with her very own Peeta and I love that for her.

#3549. Project Hail Mary Author Andy Weir's Sci-Fi Recommendations For Capturing His 'Vibe' [Exclusive]

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

If you're an aspiring science fiction novelist, you would do well to take the advice of author Andy Weir, who's red hot in publication and Hollywood thanks to the runaway successes of "The Martian" and "Project Hail Mary." That the former was self-published before getting turned into a bestseller and a blockbuster film directed by Ridley Scott — one that starred Matt Damon and earned seven Academy Award nominations, including a nod for Best Picture — is the dream of every up-and-coming writer.

So, genre authors have good reason to hang on Weir's every word, especially when it comes to capturing his profitable vibe. And while I'm a firm believer in finding your own vibe, there's a time-honored tradition in this industry of proving you can write comfortably within established formulae. With Weir, it's about straddling the line between hard science and uplifting, humanistic engagement with a vast universe that needn't be as harsh as we've been led to think. We can always, as Damon's character in "The Martian" says, "science the s*** out of" our various predicaments. I think that's naively hopeful in an age where the United States government is vehemently anti-science (unless it lines the pockets of AI-shilling tech billionaires), but Weir's got that storytelling magic that makes you want to believe we're not too far gone.

Weir is but one man, though, so if you're wondering where you can find his vibe in other work, he shared some suggestions with /Film's Jeremy Mathai, starting with his go-to recommendation:

"Well, if you consider an Andy Weir vibe to be just hard science fiction, with accurate science in there, then you got to go for [James S.A. Corey's] 'The Expanse.' That's really, really good hard sci-fi. That's really solid."

"The Expanse," for those not familiar, deals with a relatively realistic colonization of our solar system that does not initially involve interstellar travel. There's literally a lot of space to fill, but it's subject to the kinds of territorial disputes that have sparked wars on Earth. Ultimately, the narrative expands, bringing in aliens and the like, but, in its television incarnation, Mark Fergus and Hawk Ostby (who brilliantly adapted P.D. James' "The Children of Men" in 2006) approach the scenario with intellectual rigor.

Andy Weir also voiced enthusiasm for Blake Crouch's "Dark Matter," a frantically paced sci-fi novel that's been successfully adapted into an Apple TV series via the author himself. The small screen version of Crouch's parallel universe thriller stars Joel Edgerton and Jennifer Connelly, and it finds the former's character struggling to skip back to his reality (where his family is being appropriated by an alternate universe version of himself).

Finally, Weir is a proponent of Ben Bova's "The Grand Tour" novels, most notably the fourth entry in the book series titled "Mars." As Weir explained:

"That's a fairly hard sci-fi approach to a mission to Mars. It's about the first mission to Mars. It's got some pretty interesting twists in there that turn out to be ... at first, they look a little bit woo-woo, aliens, oh no. Then you find out the twist reveal of what's going wrong, and the thing is absolutely scientific and completely sensible and you're like, 'Ah, nice one.'"

Again, I'd advise you to find your own vibe, but if you want to catch the eye of publishers or studio execs, maybe check these works out and find your way forward the Weir way.

#3548. Forest Temple dungeon walkthrough in Ocarina of Time

The Forest Temple is the first dungeon you'll encounter after you travel into the future in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake.

After you grab the Hookshot from the graveyard in Kakariko Village, you'll make your way over to the Sacred Grove. You'll learn that Saria has gone inside the temple, and cannot be found. Additionally, you find out that she's meant to become one of the Sages. It's up to you to head inside, and save her from the twisty dungeon that is the Forest Temple.

Here's how to complete the Forest Temple dungeon in Ocarina of Time remake.

As soon as you walk into the Forest Temple, two Wolfos will appear and attack you. Remember that they're only vulnerable when they're attacking or if they miss their own attacks. Then, look up the large tree, and you'll find a Gold Skulltula all the way at the top. To get it, climb onto the branch, and then use your Hookshot to hit it and pull the token back to you. Then, open the chest on the other tree to get a small key, which you can use to open the locked door below.

Unlock the door and head inside, but watch out for the Skulltula that will drop from the ceiling. In the main room, you'll encounter four colored Poes, who seem to snatch away the fire from the torches at the center of the room. Before you venture off, go up the staircase directly opposite of you. Then, look to the right to find a Gold Skulltula. Use your Hookshot to get its token.

Go inside the door at the top of the stairs, and you'll encounter a Blue Bubble, which isn't a bubble, but actually a flying skull. Block it with your shield and then hit it with your sword to defeat it. Continue into the next room, where you'll find two Stalfos, which look like skeleton warriors. Wait for them to swing their sword, and then go in for the attack. After you defeat them, a chest containing a small key will spawn.

Grab the key and return to the main room. This time, head northwest and you'll find a large cube. If you interact with it, Navi will tell you that the cube has the same design as the door in the Temple of Time. Play the Song of Time (A - L - R - A - L - R) and the box will disappear.

Head inside the next room, and be careful as there are Deku Babas scattered about. First, turn right to see a wall covered in vines. Use your Hookshot to defeat the Skullwalltulas and climb up to the balcony. Turn around to spot another balcony that has a point that you can Hookshot to, but be careful as there's a Blue Bubble waiting for you.

Hookshot over and defeat the flying skull. Then, step on the button, which will lower the water in the well below you. Jump inside and follow the path to a chest that contains another small key. Climb up the ladder, and you'll end up in the northeast room. Hookshot to the target ahead of you, but be weary of the Octorok in the water. Open the chest to get the dungeon map. Exit through the door and step on the button to return to the main room.

Unlock the door on the west side of the main room and head inside. In this room, a spotlight will shine down on you. Make sure to roll out of it. A Wallmaster, which looks like a severed hand, will drop down shortly after. Wait for them to fall, and then take them out. Defeat the Wallmaster and the Blue Bubble, and then climb the ladder.

In this room, you'll find a large cube and arrows on the floor. Your goal is to move the cube along the arrows, so that it falls into a small ditch in the southwest corner of the area. First, pull the cube until it's resting just on top of the arrows. Then, push it to the end of the hallway. From here, you'll need to go around and push the cube from the other side, but you'll find a ladder where the cube once was. Finish pushing the cube into the corner, and then go up the ladder.

In this area, you'll find another cube. Push it to the end of the hallway. Then, go back to the initial cube that you pushed. Climb onto it and go to the next floor. You'll find a cube in your path, which is the cube that you just moved. Push it to the end of the hallway, and climb up to the next floor.

Follow the path to the third floor until you reach a room with two Blue Bubbles. Defeat them, and step on the button in the hallway. This will make an elevator appear, but don't step on it just yet. It'll take you back down to the entrance, but there's still more to explore here.

Open the door with your small key, which will lead to a twisty hallway. Walk into the next room, and another spotlight will appear. Either defeat the Wallmaster or quickly hop across the platforms to the next room. Ignore the chest for now, as we'll be back for that later. Follow the path to the bottom of the staircase, and go inside the room ahead.

In this room, you'll need to beat three Stalfos, but as a reward, you'll get the Fairy Bow!

As the way forward and backwards are blocked, you'll need to find a way to unlock one of the doors. Look above the door behind you to see a familiar eye on the wall. With the Fairy Bow in hand, you can now hit the eye with an arrow.

Return to the room just before the twisty hallway, and look above the door to see another eye on the wall. Shoot it, and then go back to the red room at the end of the now-normal hallway. Open the chest on the ground to get the boss key.

Before you climb back up the ladder, look to your left to find a hole that drops into a room full of water. Drop into it and quickly defeat the Blue Bubbles inside. Go through the door, which will take you to a balcony in the northwest room.

Go into the first door on your right, where you'll encounter a Floormaster, which is another hand monster. You need to wait for it to stop glowing to deal damage to it. However, it'll split into three smaller hands once defeated, so be ready to keep slashing away! Once defeated, a chest with a small key will spawn.

Get the key and head back outside. Don't go into the room to the south just yet. Instead, follow the path to the left of the door to find a Gold Skulltula on the southern wall. Hit it with your Hookshot to retrieve it, and then go into the southern door. This will take you back to the beginning of the west room. Don't ride the elevator to the top. Instead, climb up the ladder to the area with the blocks.

Climb up the second ladder and take the second right turn to find an eye on the wall. Shoot it, and a chest with a purple rupee (50 rupees) will fall onto the ground. Collect it, and make your way back up to the room just before the twisty hallway. Shoot the eye to make the hallway twisty again.

Make your way back to the staircase with the paintings of the moving Poe. Don't get too close to the painting, but instead, shoot the Poe in the painting with your Fairy Bow. Repeat this process with every painting until the Poe comes out of the painting and heads downstairs.

Follow after her and take her on as you would any other Poe. Avoid looking at her until she gets close and then hit her with your sword. If she does catch you looking at her, she'll spin in your direction. Because she was spinning so fast, she'll stun herself, leaving her vulnerable to attacks. After you defeat her, open the chest to get a small key.

Go through the door, and unlock the door in the next room with a small key. You'll find yourself in a familiar staircase room, only this time it's blue. Hunt down Beth, the Poe hiding in the paintings, just like you did before. After you defeat her, open the chest to get the compass, and then head upstairs to the newly unlocked door.

In the next room, go up the ladder to find Green Bubbles, which are just like their blue counterparts, just green. Defeat them and unlock the door at the end of the hallway.

Step on the button, which will light a stone torch. Go past the torch and turn around to see a frozen eye on the wall. Your goal is to shoot an arrow through the fire and into the eye. If successful, the ice will melt, and you'll need to shoot the eye again to twist the hallway.

Go back through the previous hallway and drop into the hole on the floor. You'll enter a long checkered room that has a collapsing ceiling. There is a hallway on your right that leads to a Gold Skulltula, but you can't reach it at the moment. You'll have to come back after you learn the Scarecrow Song to get it.

For this room, you need to move onto the tiles that have spotlights on them, but avoid the lit-up tiles with shadows. Skulltulas will drop from the ceiling on those tiles. Make your way over to the door at the end of the room, but make sure to step on the button and open the chest along the way.

In the next room, shoot the Poe in the painting on the wall, and they'll go into a block that will shortly break into a bunch of pieces. You'll need to put the pieces back together to recreate the painting. However, you'll notice that there's a duplicate piece. The piece in the center isn't moving like all the other pieces, so move that piece over to the side.

Then, find the pieces that contain the Poe's head, and place them next to each other. Then look for the Poe's lower body. The square with the arm pointing to the left will go on the left, while the square with the arm pointing to the right will go on the right. Place these two squares below the squares with the head, and Amy, the fourth-born Poe sister, will come out of the painting. Defeat her as you did the previous two Poes by avoiding their gaze.

Go through the door, and you'll immediately be greeted by another painting. Shoot the Poe in the painting, and they'll run back to the main room. Chase after her, which will lead to a fight against Meg, the firstborn Poe sister.

Meg is a bit different compared to her other sisters. She'll split into four copies of herself, but only one is real. For the first two splits, look for the Poe with a purple torch. Shoot that one with your Fairy Bow and attack her. For the third and final split, three out of four Poes will be squinting. Shoot the Poe with wide-open eyes and attack her. After you've defeated her, an elevator will rise from the floor in the middle of the room.

Ride the elevator down, and head toward the south room. A Skulltula will drop from the ceiling, but you'll find a Gold Skulltula inside.

In this room, there are two bars that stick out from the walls. To reach the boss, you'll need to push the bars and press a few buttons to unlock the boss room's door.

First, rotate the room clockwise three times. Open the chest to get some arrows and then step on the button in the other room. Then, rotate the room clockwise one more time. Look through the window to the east to see that a stone torch is in front of a frozen eye. Shoot an arrow through the window at the eye to melt it. Then, shoot the eye again, and the door to the boss' room will unlock. Use the boss key to unlock the boss' room.

Before you go up the stairs, we recommend using headphones or increasing the volume on your device, as you'll need it for the first part of this fight.

When you're ready, head up the stairs to face off against the Evil Spirit from Beyond, Phantom Ganon.

For the first part of this fight, Phantom Ganon will ride his horse in and out of the paintings. Multiple Phantom Ganons will appear in the paintings, but you can hear the real Phantom Ganon's horse sounds as he's exiting the painting. Aim your Fairy Bow at the real one, and shoot it just as it's coming out of the painting. Repeat this two more times, and Phantom Ganon will start flying around the room.

For the second part of this fight, Phantom Ganon will float around the room and throw projectiles at you. You need to hit the orbs back at Phantom Ganon until he misses. He'll fall to the ground in a vulnerable state, so run at him and swing your sword as many times as you can.

Occasionally, Phantom Ganon will charge at you instead. He'll swing his spear in a circle, and the tip of the spear will shine just before he's about to charge at you. Try your best to avoid him here, but he'll lose his invulnerable glow, so you can shoot a few arrows at him if you're quick enough.

Continue to dodge his charge and reflect the orb at them until you defeat them. Grab the Heart Container and exit the dungeon through the ring of light when you're ready.

#3547. Tim Burton Partners With Loewe for a ‘Nightmare Before Christmas’ Capsule Collection

“Things in life are the best as surprises,” says Tim Burton, the iconoclast filmmaker, calling from London. More than 40 years after making his directorial debut with Pee-wee’s Big Adventure (1985), and penning the poem that would eventually inspire The Nightmare Before Christmas, Burton is expanding his artistic remit once more. The director has partnered with Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez, the designers of Loewe, for a new capsule collection featuring memorable vignettes and characters from the latter film. “When they came to me and were talking about it,” Burton tells Vanity Fair, “I just got very excited, because I’m a frustrated designer myself.”

The capsule, available starting November 12, includes a range of handbags with whimsical recreations of the film’s most beloved characters. Zero, Jack Skellington’s dog, floats on the side of a handbag; the Harlequin Demon is rendered with feathers and leather scales; and Skellington himself is painted as a peekaboo surprise inside a carryall.

“They took something that means a lot to me and they put their own spin on it,” he says of working with Loewe. “The way they make things, the textures and the elements involved are just beautiful,” he continues. “It’s exciting for me to see it happen.”

Jack Skellington peekaboos from the inside of a handbag.

Snakes pop out of a woven leather bucket bag.

In the more than three decades since the film was released, Jack Skellington and The Nightmare Before Christmas have become synonymous with a certain brand of Halloween-like spookiness, a soft spot for Christmas and the holidays, and a wondrous gothic style and sensibility. The film originated from a poem Burton wrote in 1982 while working as an animator at Walt Disney Productions. “It was something that came not so much from a thought, but was just more slightly from the subconscious,” Burton says in a documentary short accompanying the Loewe collection.

But just as film and animation have changed over the years, the meaning of the film and its legacy have too. The Nightmare Before Christmas has become arguably one of the most renowned stop-motion-animation films. The painstaking process of making the film required the creation of 227 puppets and the shooting of 109,440 frames to bring the story to life. “I love [stop motion] because it’s all handmade,” Burton says. “When you see the puppets and the sets, you wish everybody could experience the tactile nature of what goes into making a stop-motion film, or any film.”

In the age of artificial intelligence, the movie has become a symbol of human craft and ingenuity. “The more it keeps going that way,” Burton says of the proliferation of AI, “the more I appreciate [the human] side of it. I think it’s something that’s very important to keep in the world, the tactile, not being on a screen all the time and doing all that sort of thing. To me, [humanity] is very important to life and art and anything, really.”

A still from a documentary short featuring Burton that accompanies the collection.

Rather than be overly protective about some of his most famous intellectual property, Burton wanted to let the legacy leather-goods house and its designers follow their own instincts. “They consulted me, and we talked about this and that, but I respect them and I respect what they do,” he says. “It’s more fun for me to see things beautifully done.” Fashion, after all, he says, is a medium different from film. “I mean, I’ve seen Nightmare merchandise, and some of it’s good and some of it’s really bad,” he says with a laugh. “And even the bad ones are kind of good sometimes.” One example? A “big fat Jack Skellington.” “Well, no, he’s not a big fat Jack Skellington, but as a stuffed little toy, he’s kind of cute,” Burton adds with a laugh. “Things change and mutate, and you just [need to] keep the spirit of something, but then do something [with] your own interpretation of it.”

Many members of The Nightmare Before Christmas’s original 1993 audience are now adults atop creative industries. Burton’s work, in a way, is part of their own imagination. “The things that inspired you from the very beginning, they just stay with you,” Burton says. “Whether it’s conscious or not, it’s just part of your DNA.”

Revisiting past work, Burton says, “can be a beautiful experience, but not always.” Though he says he “had no real desire” to make a sequel to Nightmare, Burton did direct 2024’s Beetlejuice Beetlejuice, a sequel to the 1988 film Beetlejuice, starring Winona Ryder and Catherine O’Hara. Returning to the film 35 years later “made sense” for him “emotionally.” “It was like, nobody’s getting any younger and blah, blah, blah,” Burton says. “I really did that movie not to make a sequel, but it was something that I enjoyed, and we tried to do it in the style of the first movie, shot it quickly, did live effects. So it was an experience that meant a lot to me. And I think for me, it’s always important to make something that I really, really feel.”

Burton illustrating some of his characters.

There’s plenty of interest in Burton revisiting other parts of his oeuvre too. Since the release of Corpse Bride in 2005, fans have been clamoring for a live-action remake of the film. Burton laughs when asked if he’d ever honor the request, and while he doesn’t deliver a straight answer, he doesn’t exactly say no. “I’ve got thoughts swirling around and all sorts of things going on, but I’ve been through too much to go, Okay,” he says, noting that he’s had projects mutate and change over the years. “I keep it open, and I’m just finishing something, so I’m in an open spot now, and I’m really excited to look for what the next thing is.”

Away from the big screen, Burton has experienced somewhat of a resurgence with the success of Netflix’s Wednesday, and he’s enjoyed ventures outside of the film industry. This capsule with Loewe is one of those projects, and the director also collaborated with A$AP Rocky, whom he describes as “a real artist,” for the visual rollout of his album released earlier this year, Don’t Be Dumb, creating characters for its cover and a music video. “I love this stuff because film has [become] such a business. It’s gotten so big,” he says. “That’s why I enjoyed doing stuff with Rocky. It’s what I love doing, and it’s just a different form of doing it.”

Burton hasn’t been on the lookout for new opportunities, but he likes being surprised by them. “It’s always just this nice, beautiful, strange surprise when somebody asks to do something or collaborate,” he says. “I mean, that’s what film’s all about. You’re working with different artists and you’re working with different people with one [goal] in mind. So it’s not that much different. I like those kinds of surprises.”

You know, I’ve come to expect the unexpected on Dancing with the Stars. However, sometimes it really gets me with its song choices. That happened again when the songs for Grammy Night were revealed, and we learned that Maura Higgins will dance to “Thong Song.” Now, while this made me chuckle as I pictured what a dance to this track will look like, I am also excited to see Higgins and Mark Ballas “shaking that thing” on the 2026 TV schedule after a week of tough scores and criticism.

Yes, you read all of that right: Maura Higgins and her partner Mark Ballas will be dancing to “Thong Song” by Sisqó on Grammy Night. According to EW, they’ll be doing an Argentine tango to it.

For a bit of a history lesson, in 2001, Sisqó's “Thong Song” was nominated for Best Male R&B Vocal Performance and Best R&B Song. That year, Sisqó was also nominated for Best New Artist, and the album Unleash the Dragon was nominated for Best R&B Album. It did not win any Grammys, as “Say My Name” by Destiny’s Child won Best R&B Song, D’Angelo won Best Male R&B Vocal Performance for “Untitled (How Does It Feel)” and Best R&B Album for Voodoo, and Shelby Lynne won Best New Artist.

Other songs that will be featured on Grammy Night are “Boom Boom Pow” by the Black Eyed Peas, “All for You” by Janet Jackson, “Die With a Smile” by Lady Gaga and Bruno Mars, “Crazy in Love” by Beyoncé, “SexyBack” by Justin Timberlake and “Bring Me to Life” by Evanescence. So, it’ll be an episode full of bangers and lots of nostalgia, and I cannot wait to specifically see Ballas and Higgins "when the beat goes (da na da na)."

On Disney Night, Higgins and Ballas ended up at the bottom of the leaderboard with 68 points, putting them one point behind Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik and Julia Stiles and Ezra Sosa (who ultimately were eliminated). Mark and Maura's performance and scores were a bit shocking considering they were the leaders early on. It was also clear The Traitors vet was having a tough week.

After all that, she took to Instagram to address what happened and explain the reality of working on this show. The Love Island star, who came on DWTS with no dance experience, wrote, in part:

This week was definitely one of the toughest I’ve had so far. I was really unwell, running on very little energy and trying to learn two dances, but I gave it absolutely everything I had❤️

She also explained that she’s continuing to try her best, and as she’s learning, mistakes and hard weeks happen:

I came into this experience knowing I wasn’t a dancer, a performer or an athlete, but I wanted to challenge myself, step outside my comfort zone and give something completely new my absolute best & that’s exactly what I’m trying to do every single week. I’m learning, I’m making mistakes, I’m pushing myself and I’m growing along the way!! Some weeks will be better than others, and that’s okay. I’m only human🥹

She said that she wasn’t writing about this “for sympathy or to make excuses.” All she wanted to do was share “the reality behind the scenes.” The reality star also gave a lovely shoutout to her partner, and she promised to “keep giving it everything [she’s] got!!”

Well, this week, that will include her dancing to “Thong Song,” and I cannot wait to see how she and Ballas pull off an Argentine tango to the iconic track. To see this pair "Livin' la Vida Loca," you can catch Grammy Night of Dancing with the Stars on Tuesday, November 10, at 8 p.m. ET on ABC or with a Disney+ subscription.

#3545. DC Studios Officially Casts Mason Thames As Robin — Will He Play Him In Live-Action?

We might not know when the DC Universe will unveil its version of Batman, but we just got news that the franchise has cast its Robin. Well, at least we know who'll be voicing one of the Robins in the upcoming "Dynamic Duo" movie. In an interview with Collider, DC Studios co-head Peter Safran confirmed that Mason Thames has been cast as the voice of Dick Grayson in the upcoming film.

Thames is best known for starring in "The Black Phone" and its sequel, as well as playing Hiccup Horrendous Haddock III in the live-action "How to Train Your Dragon" movie. But it seems he's been gunning for a DC role. "We always talk about wanting volunteers and not recruits to be part of the DCU, to be part of DC Studios," said Safran, "and Mason always wanted to be Dick Grayson. He just did."

According to the producer, Thames came in to read for Grayson and "auditioned the s*** out of it." "He's a wonderful young actor," he continued. "But boy, did he want this. He was just obsessed. When he came over to the DC offices, he came over with his dad at the time, and we've got tons of great archives and stuff in there, and wanted to take a picture of everything and with everything. He's a fan."

That certainly bodes well for a committed performance from the 19-year-old, who most recently appeared alongside Dave Franco and O'Shea Jackson Jr. in the most startling comedy of 2026, "Idiots." The question is, will Thames actually play Dick Grayson in live-action? According to past comments from Safran's DC Studios co-head James Gunn, that's exactly what will happen. But there's no confirmation as of yet.

"Dynamic Duo" is an animated film that's being developed by DC Studios in collaboration with Swaybox Studios. The latter's unique animation style combines puppetry and CGI to create a stop-motion-like effect that will be used to tell Jason Todd and Dick Grayson's origin stories. Mason Thames' casting as the latter had previously been rumored, with scooper Jeff Sneider reporting it in September 2026. But now it's official, meaning Thames will join Logan Kim, who's playing Jason Todd, in "Dynamic Duo" — much to the dismay of "Titans" star Curran Walters, who reacted to the news of the Jason Todd recasting with disappointment.

The movie is set for a September 22, 2028 release, with Arthur Mintz, who co-founded Swaybox with Theresa Andersson in 2013, directing. For now, further details about the film are scarce, but Lee Pace and Steve Buscemi have reportedly been cast as members of the Red Hood Gang.

As it stands, we at least know who will be voicing two of the most significant versions of Robin in the DC Universe. The question is, will Thames and Kim portray their characters in live-action? They certainly should, given James Gunn's prior comments.

When he and Peter Safran became co-heads of DC Studios in 2022, they promised this latest on-screen superhero franchise would not simply be more of the same. Gunn touted a shared universe without a house style and confirmed that DC Universe actors would portray their character across film, TV, animation, and even video games, streamlining the franchise in a way that sounded as though it could be bad news for animation voice actors. But it remains to be seen whether he will stick to that claim moving forward, especially since much has changed since 2022.

James Gunn has repeated his claim about actors portraying their DC Universe characters across mediums on several occasions. In 2023, he told DC.com "Television, movies and games all intertwine within the same universe. We're going to cast actors that are going to be able to play the characters in this, as well as in other things, some of which we've already cast." Thus far, Frank Grillo has played Rick Flag Sr. on the big screen in "Superman," on TV in "Peacemaker," and voiced the character for animation in "Creature Commandos." As such, it would make sense for Logan Kim and Mason Thames to follow a similar path.

But as we've seen in recent years, nothing is set in stone. Leaving aside the Warner Bros. Discovery/Paramount merger becoming official in October 2026, James Gunn and Peter Safran announced a slate of movies back in 2022, some of which have now been scrapped. Gunn confirmed that DC had cancelled the planned "The Authority" movie, for instance, and he has spoken openly about how plans for the DC Universe otherwise shifted following Warner Bros.' initial announcement. All of which raises the question of whether he's sticking to his plan for actor continuity across mediums.

It would certainly make a lot of sense given his previous explanations. In 2023, Gunn spoke to The Hollywood Reporter about how Aaron Pierre would be playing Green Lantern John Stewart in both the HBO series "Lanterns" and on the big screen in the upcoming "Man of Tomorrow." "We don't want the series to feel in any way like step-children or lesser-than," he told the outlet. "[The show is] just another way to tell a story." Time will tell if the same holds for Kim and Thames.

#3544. Elon Musk Spent $474 Million on the 2026 Midterm Elections. On Election Day, He Fell Silent.

Elon Musk, the Tesla CEO and former intimate of President Donald Trump’s, may have ever so slightly eroded his 14 (that we know of) children’s inheritances during the 2026 midterm elections, spending $474 million (of his estimated $901.7 billion bankroll) on Republican campaigns across the US. But as Election Day continued across the country, the prolific user of his own social media platform, X, remained relatively restrained.

“Vote red today,” was an early tweet, interspersed between abundant promotions of his company’s AI agent, Grok Bot. A shared tweet featuring Michigan Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed was simply captioned with the raised eyebrow emoji.

And that was the most Musk had to say about the midterms on Tuesday, despite what The New York Times reports is the most that “any donor has ever spent in a single election cycle,” barring former New York City mayor Michael R. Bloomberg’s spend on his own 2020 presidential campaign, which cost him more than $1 billion.

And as the blue wave continued, Musk started removing tweets instead of adding them. Early Wednesday morning, around the time James Talarico took the stage to celebrate his win in Texas, Musk removed the missive he had pinned to the top of his account, an October 29 post in which he said his “biggest concern…if there is a clean sweep by Democrats of the House, Senate and Presidency in 2028,” is that they will open the borders, create a larger Supreme Court, and grant statehood to DC and Puerto Rico. “That is why you should vote for Republican senators this election,” he concluded. "Other reasons are irrelevant compared to this one.”

Per the Times, Musk’s spend is likely to exceed the $474 million currently reported, as any donations made after October 14 have yet to be counted. Of that current figure, $216 million went to his own super PAC (America PAC), with $212 of that going to support US Senate hopeful Ken Paxton. An additional $168 million went to the pro-Republican Senate Leadership Fund, and $30 million went to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the primary super PAC for House Republicans. An additional $16 million went to state-focused political efforts in Michigan, Texas, and Wisconsin, while $44 million went to federal Republican groups or candidates.

That’s a lot of money to most of us, but by early Wednesday morning, Musk appeared to be taking the expenditure in stride. “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” he tweeted at 1:12 a.m. ET, followed almost immediately by “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time,” punctuated by the shrug emoji.

#3543. Why Is John Malkovich’s New Movie Called Wild Horse Nine? The Answer Is Not What I Expected

Well, I didn't expect this answer from Martin McDonagh.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Before I walked into my screening of Wild Horse Nine, a big question I had was: Why on Earth is it called Wild Horse Nine? When I walked out of the film starring John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell, I was still pondering that question. So, when I had the chance to interview Martin McDonagh, the writer/director of the project on the 2026 movie schedule, I asked him about the meaning behind his film’s title. I have to say, his answer is not what I expected.

Knowing that Wild Horse Nine follows two CIA agents, Malkovich’s Chris and Rockwell’s Lee, as they travel to Easter Island in the ‘70s, I figured the movie’s title could be related to their mission. I thought Wild Horse Nine could be a code for something. However, that was totally wrong, because when I asked Martin McDonagh why he gave his film this title, he told me:

Yeah, I've got no idea. I like numbers, and I like horses.

Well, there you have it, there’s really no rhyme or reason to the name. McDonagh just likes numbers and horses, and that’s all there is to it, according to him. That's certainly not what I expected to hear when I asked the question.

However, the title is by no means completely meaningless. Wild horses are important to the film, and they come up often, especially in relation to Chris’s journey. So, that part makes sense. However, the number nine is totally random…as far as I and McDonagh can tell.

This is also quite funny because many of his movies have straightforward names. Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri, which Sam Rockwell won his Oscar for, is about just that: three billboards outside Ebbing, Missouri. The beloved Seven Psychopaths is about a man writing a screenplay with the same name, and it’s also about psychopaths literally. In Bruges takes place in Bruges, Belgium. And the great 2022 comedy The Banshees of Inisherin is set in the fictional Inisherin, banshees and their existence are discussed, and there is a song of the same name that’s talked about too.

At no point in Wild Horse Nine are the words said together, it’s for sure not a CIA thing, and it left me very curious about why McDonagh named it that. Personally, I love that he just did it for no big reason; he simply liked numbers and horses. From my point of view, it also just sounds really cool.

The movie is very cool, slick, funny and deeply tragic too. To me, John Malkovich gives a performance so incredible that Wild Horse Nine is bound to go down as one of his best movies. Rockwell beautifully balances him out, too, and further proves why he’s such a great fit for McDonagh’s writing – seeing as this is the third movie they’ve worked on together. Parker Posey, Steve Buscemi and Mariana di Girolamo round out the cast of this dark comedy, and like the leads, they also play out the laugh-out-loud comedy brilliantly.

So, if you are looking to see Wild Horse Nine, you can catch it in theaters on November 6. It’s one wild, funny and thought-provoking ride. However, don’t think too hard about its name, because that really doesn’t mean anything.

#3542. Jurassic Park's Lost Animated Series Pitch Has Finally Surfaced In Video Form

It's been over 30 years since "Jurassic Park" changed movies forever, with Steven Spielberg's 1993 adaptation of Michael Crichton's sci-fi thriller novel delivering not only a perfect film, but a production that brought a systemic change to how Hollywood made movies. It also marked the last time a dinosaur franchise would become a bonafide hit, as Hollywood continues to try and fail to make audiences care about dinosaurs unless the title includes the word "Jurassic." (David Robert Mitchell's "The End of Oak Street" is the latest example of audiences largely avoiding non-"Jurassic" dino movies.)

Given how incredibly successful the "Jurassic Park" franchise has been, it's no wonder it's expanded to include spin-offs, including video games, cartoons, and more. But what is surprising is just how slow this franchise has been to grow. After all, the first film came out in 1993, at a time when practically every big movie somehow got turned into a cartoon, regardless of whether the original was for kids or not.

"Jurassic Park" did almost get an animated series back then, but it never made it to production. Still, we've heard about this show on and off over the years, and now, we finally have the very first bit of footage, reportedly titled "Escape From Jurassic Park." The trailer surfaced on Twitter/X, and it quickly spread. Watch for yourself right below.

After all of these years, it has finally been found!

Fans of Jurassic Park, I humbly present to you, the animated Pitch Trailers for the canceled Jurassic Park Animated Show!

More info coming soon! pic.twitter.com/UGT5lOvvd5

— Jurassic Library (@JurassicLibrary) October 31, 2026

The trailer for the "Jurassic Park" animated film, thought lost forever, doesn't show much, but it does perfectly capture the look and tone of the Spielberg classic and mixes it with that recognizable '90s Amblin animated look we saw in "Animaniacs" and other shows of the time.

There's not a whole lot of information about the lost "Jurassic Park" animated series. We do have old pitch decks and story treatments that give an idea of what the series could have been about, as well as old concept art from cartoon veterans Will Meugniot and artist William Stout, who were meant to spearhead the show.

Perhaps most importantly, the "Jurassic Park" TV series was meant to be a direct sequel to the first film, with the first season reportedly focusing on BioSyn creating its own rival dinosaur theme park, leading to — you guessed it — another dino outbreak.

According to William Stout, this "was not going to be a kiddy show (although kids of all ages, including myself, could enjoy it)," he said in his blog back in 2014. "They wanted the show to be a mature prime time series with top writers and state-of-the-art television animation augmented with quite a bit of CG animation."

That much is clear from the leaked trailer for the "Jurassic Park" animated series. Though it still features kids, a big sense of adventure and wonder, and a visual style reminiscent of Don Bluth, the trailer also makes it clear this is a show about man-eating dinosaurs, and seems to hint at an appropriate amount of violence.

We also know from reports about the series bible and its proposed episodes that the "Jurassic Park" cartoon would have been serialized, with each episode building up to the next and the first season ending with the rival park opening. That's a quite approach surprising for 1993, when serialization was virtually unheard of in animation.

Though the series never made it to production, we eventually did get a "Jurassic Park" cartoon (seen in the photo above), and it remains the best sequel to that original movie.
