#3526. Harriet Phillips Says Raising Her Daughter Solo Was “Painful.” But Now She Can Ask Kate Middleton for Advice

Harriet Phillips, the wife of Peter Phillips, son of Princess Anne, sat down with Hello! for an exclusive interview five months after her royal wedding, which took place at All Saints’ Church in Kemble, Gloucestershire, the village where she grew up. The ceremony was attended by King Charles III and Queen Camilla, as well as many other members of the royal family.

For Harriet, who until then led a life far removed from high society, her official entry into one of the world’s most famous royal families inevitably brought about some big changes.

Harriet and Peter Phillips at Royal Ascot

She and her daughter, Georgina, now live at Gatcombe, Princess Anne’s estate. Peter’s sister, Zara Tindall, also lives there with her husband, Mike, and their three children. After 24 years with the British National Health Service (NHS), where she specialized in child mental health and caring for the most vulnerable children, Harriet left the NHS to embark on a new professional venture at a private foundation, continuing to focus on early-childhood development.

She has also taken on her first official role as patron of Home-Start Cotswolds, an organization that supports families with young children. “Becoming a parent can be one of the most wonderful experiences in life, but it can also feel overwhelming and isolating,” Phillips told Hello! “We often assume that parenting comes naturally, but the reality is that everyone needs support at different points. Home-Start offers vital, practical, and nonjudgmental support. Just having someone to listen can make an enormous difference.”

For Harriet, the decision to leave the health service does not represent a break with the past: “It’s been an enormous privilege to spend 24 years working in the NHS, and I’ve loved my career. It has taught me so much, professionally and personally. Over time, I’ve become increasingly passionate about the importance of promoting healthy brain development. If we can support parents during this critical early period, we have an opportunity to make a lasting difference for children.”

The Phillips couple at the 2026 DMMI Royal Charity Polo Cup

Harriet then looked back on her love story with Peter, which began in an entirely unexpected way. The two first met properly in early 2022, when their three daughters were on the same hockey team. At first there was just some casual small talk between them, then walks with their dogs, followed by dinners at pubs away from prying eyes and, finally, evenings spent cooking together. A low-key courtship, away from the spotlight, blossomed into a love story.

When she met Peter, there wasn’t a “thunderbolt moment”; Harriet said she simply felt comfortable with him, enjoying an unspoken sense of calm. “I just felt incredibly at ease with him and experienced a lovely, peaceful, safe feeling when talking to him—like being with a really good friend,” she told Hello!

He was the one who made the first move: “Peter was the brave one in recognizing that there was something between us and acting on it. This time, I thought, If I’m lucky enough to meet someone again, I want things to move slowly and ensure that everything is entirely right.” Then she added, unable to hide her happiness: “He is very romantic, loving, kind, loyal, amazing, and my best friend.” Their early dates were simple and low-key. “He’s a great cook and I love cooking. He’s great at barbecues. It was wholesome and suited to who we both are as people,” she said.

On July 25, 2025, during a weekend in the south of England, Peter proposed on a beach. “We were on a weekend getaway in the south of England on a hot day during the heat wave. He asked me to marry him on the beach; I was completely overcome,” she said. “He had the ring made at Pragnell beforehand—it’s absolutely beautiful.” Neither of their families had been told about the surprise: “It was the best-kept secret ever.”

During the interview, Harriet also reflected on her childhood in Gloucestershire and fondly remembered her parents and their long marriage. “I was brought up in a village in the middle of fields. My parents celebrated an incredible 51 years of marriage, and sadly, my father died just before Peter and I got together.” It was an experience that left a deep mark on her life, and today, as she said in reflecting on her own love story, Harriet also sees it in the context of meeting the Princess Royal’s son: “I often think maybe that’s why Peter came along.”

The loss of her father, and the difficulties she faced in the years that followed, helped shape her outlook on life. Harriet explained: “There is a beauty that comes out of difficult situations. A beautiful jewel is formed under pressure. Difficulties in life enable you to relate to people and build empathy.”

Harriet and Peter with Princess Royal Anne

Harriet then talked about her first meeting with Princess Anne, her eventual mother-in-law, which was much more informal than she had imagined it would be. They met in the garden at Gatcombe, sitting on benches and drinking cups of tea. “There was always going to be initial nerves about meeting anyone’s family members, but I am quite a calm person,” she said. “It was really relaxed…It couldn’t have been nicer.”

Harriet has come to appreciate, above all, the princess’s dedication to her work and local charities: “She sets an amazing example with her work ethic. What I’ve seen is her tireless attention to local charities and her genuine interests. It’s important to do things that match who you are, where you live, and what your passions are.”

And their relationship already seems very strong. “She’s brilliant, really good fun, and straight-talking,” Harriet said. “She’s incredibly generous—we had our wedding reception at Gatcombe, and it was amazing and special for Peter and I to have our wedding where he grew up.”

Charles and Camilla also welcomed her warmly right from the start, as seen in the various photos taken at public events. Her first meeting with the king and the queen consort took place at Royal Ascot: “It was so lovely and relaxed and there was lots of laughter. You feel as though you’re meeting family, but at the same time, it feels otherworldly. Both the king and the queen have been so welcoming to me and Georgina. I can’t thank them both enough.”

The couple with the king and queen at Royal Ascot

After their wedding, Harriet and Peter attended several public events, including Wimbledon. In September, they were together at Somerset House in London for the opening of the exhibition “Reviving Craft: Reflection of the Mind,” dedicated to traditional Chinese craftsmanship and featuring over 70 artists.

Harriet also spoke with Hello! about Kate Middleton, including the admiration she feels for her and the bond they’ve formed. “I can look to Catherine for advice and guidance,” she said. She recalled a special moment during a vacation on the Isles of Scilly: The children (Georgina, George, Charlotte, and Louis) found themselves playing in the water together, in a spontaneous and informal atmosphere. “I’ve had an incredible experience being welcomed in. We happened to be on holiday in the same place. It was great because the children were all jumping into the water at the same time,” she shared. “It was very casual, but there is a clear level of respect there.” And speaking of the Princess of Wales, she added: “She’s very openhearted, and I would always feel comfortable asking her if I needed advice about something.”

Her first stay at Balmoral with her daughter was also a special experience. Scotland is one of Harriet’s favorite destinations, and vacations with the royal family have remained surprisingly simple: “It’s the loveliest family holiday with an extraordinary layer…. We go walking and running, play football with the children, cycle in the hills, and go wild swimming, which is fantastic.”

Then, inevitably, her memories turned to the wedding, an event marked by emotional moments. Harriet got ready with her mother and the three girls in the family: Georgina, Savannah, and Isla. Then her brother, Nicholas, arrived to drive her to the church. “It was quite wet and it had rained that morning, but the girls kept my train completely white and immaculate,” said said. “They did a really good job.”

In the church, decorated with floral arrangements that seemed to bring nature indoors, Harriet carried a bouquet with myrtle and lily of the valley: “All my family members have had myrtle in their wedding flowers, so I continued that tradition.”

Before going in, the couple prayed together with the vicar. “Then [we] walked into the fragrance of the flowers in the church. It was incredible,” she said. “It’s such a beautiful church, and I grew up going to it. It’s tiny—we were all squished in!” The presence of the king, the queen, and other members of the royal family didn’t distract her: “I was so focused on being in the moment. Of course, you’re aware that people are around you, but I really wanted to enjoy it and be present. I was so happy. That’s very natural for me. I was peaceful. I prayed. Maybe the peace of God came over me.”

The reception took place in the garden at Gatcombe. The sun came out at one point; there was live music, Champagne, and a casual menu featuring lamb raised on the estate. Instead of the traditional wedding cake, there was a huge tiramisu. “There was lots of laughter and it was an amazing family day. It finished at midnight, but everyone wanted it to carry on,” she said.

Before meeting Peter, Harriet was a single mother raising her preteen daughter, Georgina. It wasn’t always an easy journey, which made her particularly sensitive to the challenges that parents face and the importance of having a support network.

“Although at times it was a painful experience, I did have the support of people who loved us. Any time in life when you’re under pressure or facing adversity, something good always comes from it,” she said. “Lean in; don’t be scared.” Her Christian faith played an important role—“It’s definitely the foundation of how I live; it’s like a golden thread that has woven through my life. I was brought up in a Christian family, but this is a little bit different because it’s like making a decision for yourself: It is a personal relationship and a conscious choice, rather than just being religious.”

Harriet is very proud of her daughter and the relationship they’ve built. “Becoming a mother gives you an inner strength to protect your loved one and face whatever comes,” she said. “Everyone has challenges in life that are dressed up differently. Maybe this has been my challenge—the experience of bringing up a child on my own. I’ve been able to see the good things that have come out of it.”

Harriet and Peter with their three daughters on their wedding day

Today her family has grown, and Harriet looks to the future with enthusiasm, but without rushing: “Peter and I are so fortunate to have such wonderful girls between us. I’m excited about what’s to come with our family and always mindful that going gently is so important.”

Her new life with Peter doesn’t mean setting aside her own identity. “I will continue as I am. I’m a professional and will continue working in the area I’m passionate about,” she said. “I’ve got a wealth of knowledge that I don’t want to waste, so I will continue to use that.” When asked what she’d like to accomplish in the next 12 months, she gave an answer that once again came back to children and families: raising greater awareness of the work of Home-Start Cotswolds. As she explained, “We don’t just support babies by caring for them directly—we support babies by supporting the people who care for them.”

It’s a philosophy that also seems to capture her new sense of balance in her life. She has joined the royal family without ceasing to be Harriet, the woman who for 24 years worked alongside children and their parents, and who today has found in Peter a life partner and, above all, a best friend.

Her mission at Home-Start brings her even closer to the Princess of Wales, who has also been committed for years to supporting the well-being of children in their early years, a crucial period that shapes their personalities and determines the adults they will become. Who knows if the two women, now close friends, might one day form a professional partnership as well.

Harriet with Peter, Zara, and Mike Tindall.

Warning! Spoilers for Season 15, Episode 5 of Chicago Fire, “Three Hundred,” lie ahead.

Chicago Fire has had a revolving door of cast members over the 14 years it has been on the air. And unfortunately, that door is still spinning amid Season 15 on the 2026 TV schedule. Fans have already had to say goodbye to Dermot Mulroney’s Dom Pascal, but and that's not all. This week marked the NBC hit's 300th episode as well as the departure of Joe Cruz, played by OG cast member Joe Miñoso. While I was a mess watching Cruz’s farewell to 51, there were apparently “a lot of tears” on set, too, as Miñoso told me.

Following Season 14's cliffhanger, the Season 15 premiere revealed that no one at 51 died. However, Cruz broke his spine as a result of a collapse at the warehouse, and despite him doing extensive rehab, it would basically take a miracle for him to be a firefighter again. Wednesday’s episode, “Three Hundred,” saw Cruz getting the news that if he continued to do rehab and work hard, he could go back to work in a matter of months.

That being said, following the birth of his and Chloe’s twin girls, Cruz decided to take a step back and go to a great rehab facility in Minnesota close to Chloe’s parents. He had a very vulnerable chat with Severide about his decision, and his goodbyes with Hermann, Mouch, Tony, and Capp were equally emotional and funny. I definitely couldn’t stop crying while watching it, especially when Cruz stopped by Otis’ memorial and talked with his late friend. Unsurprisingly, Miñoso got emotional while filming his character's sendoff, and he spoke to CinemaBlend about the final scene he shot:

A lot of tears. The last scene that we did was with me and Taylor [Kinney], and it was where I'm explaining why I'm leaving. And so much of it felt really, kind of like true-to-life. It felt like a lot of things that Joe and Taylor would have said to each other, and it was such a, I think, you know, probably the most human and intimate scene that Taylor and I have ever had the opportunity to do.

Given Miñoso had been part of the cast since the very beginning, it's honestly got be hard to imagine Chicago Fire without him, and 51 without Cruz. It’s great, however, that he was able to have that opportunity with Taylor Kinney not only for their characters, who are basically brothers, but for themselves, too. That’s not the only reason it was emotional, though, as Miñoso will also have a core memory that lasts a lifetime:

It was, first and foremost, such a gift to be able to have that scene with him just because we've never really sat face-to-face as equals like that in a scene. It felt really special. The fact that it was the very last scene on the stage with my wife there, who I met on the show as a makeup artist 10 years ago, and we just celebrated our 10th anniversary. It'll be an implanted memory forever. It's like one of those core memories. It's definitely going to be one of the shining bright ones in my mind for a long time.

It was announced over the past summer that Miñoso would be leaving Chicago Fire, and many fans were not happy about it. That being said, the fact that Miñoso was able to be ushered out with five episodes to wrap up Cruz’s story makes it just a little bit more bearable.

Following the Season 14 cliffhanger, though, there was no telling what the result would be, and how it could figure into Cruz’s departure. Chicago Fire has killed off a handful of characters following season-ending cliffhangers. Luckily, when it came to how Cruz would bow out, there was only one way to handle it, per Miñoso:

There were a lot of discussions between the writers and producers and myself in terms of how we wanted to say goodbye to the character. But [showrunner] Victor [Teran] was pretty adamant from the very beginning that he wanted to be able to explore a different type of trauma on this show. We haven't really been able to play this storyline in terms of our firefighters getting so hurt that they can no longer be the person they think they are.

Cruz has been such a staple at 51, and his passion for the firehouse and his job trumped just about everything, aside from his family. With Miñoso leaving, it really only made sense for him to decide to leave 51 because of his family. And Miñoso loved the way it all came together:

But at some point, they overcome it and then ultimately make the decision to walk away on their own terms. So, it was really an honor, a joy, a privilege. I feel very lucky that they gave me the material and thought and believed in me to be able to bring it to life.

Character exits are always tough in the One Chicago franchise, especially when it’s someone who has been around since the start of a show. But since Cruz, Chloe, the boys, and now their baby twin girls are only a couple of states away, it’s possible that this won’t be the last we see of them. Nevertheless, I'll probably continue to be an absolute mess whenever I revisit this episode of the show.

If anything, all episodes of Chicago Fire are streaming with a Peacock subscription, so there is plenty of Cruz to still enjoy. As for new episodes, those air on Wednesdays at 9 p.m. ET on NBC.

Passionate writer. Obsessed with anything and everything entertainment, specifically movies and television. Can get easily attached to fictional characters.

#3524. Dune: Part Three's Official Runtime Confirms It's The Shortest Movie In The Series

I don't know if you've heard the news, but there's been a sea change in cinema lately. A three-hour documentary about Elizabeth Holmes is currently the talk around town and, despite one notable setback, will likely make a major play for the Oscars. The stop-motion Laika fantasy film "Wildwood" just tied a record for the longest American animated film ever made. And, of course, "Dunesday" is set for later this year as "Dune: Part Three" and "Avengers: Doomsday" will arrive on the exact same weekend in December (for some reason). Clearly, audiences have spoken and the message has been received loud and clear: Movies with longer runtimes are in, baby.

But that's also what makes this latest news liable to catch some fans by surprise. While "Doomsday" is already confirmed to reach a whopping 165 minutes, director Denis Villeneuve's "Dune" threequel is about to make history in a very different way. According to the Irish Film Classification Office (via World of Reel), the ratings body has logged the final cut of "Dune: Part Three" and it clocks in at a runtime of 151 minutes, or 2 hours and 31 minutes for those who've yet to consume their daily allotment of spice. On the face of it, that's an interesting outcome for a trilogy-capper whose predecessors amounted to 155 minutes for the 2021 original and 166 minutes for "Part Two" in 2024. Instead of following in the same footsteps as "The Return of the King" and end things on as extravagant a note as possible, it's instead going to be the shortest of the trilogy?

But, for those who've done their homework and are familiar with author Frank Herbert's source material, this begins to makes a lot more sense ... while raising a host of other questions at the same time.

I hope you remember to bring your stillsuits to the theaters this December, because it's not likely that "Dune: Part Three" will have many built-in moments to take a bathroom break. Still, it could've been worse. The threequel is now reported to be the shortest film in the entire trilogy, which might seem somewhat confusing to those conditioned to think of this saga as a "The Lord of the Rings"-sized epic. While that's not entirely off-base, the truth is this makes perfect sense for those who've read "Dune: Messiah."

Frank Herbert's famous sequel novel strikes a very different tone from the original story in more ways than one. The author goes out of his way to make it more overt that Paul Atreides (portrayed by Timothée Chalamet in the adaptations), uh, isn't exactly a good guy. More shocking still, however, "Messiah" actually doesn't have that much plot to get through by comparison. Where "Dune" more than earned its reputation as quite the formidable tome, the second book is very different story — literally. This comparison posted on social media by critic Darren Mooney paints a stark picture, while serving as a handy visual reminder that Denis Villeneuve's first two movies split the first book in half.

https://t.co/2ldN7xcmW1 pic.twitter.com/kDtJqjXThK

— Darren Mooney (@Darren_Mooney) November 3, 2026

Now, "Dune: Part Three" should have plenty of room to tell the events of "Dune: Messiah" to completion ... and, perhaps, pad the narrative even further. 151 minutes is still a very hefty runtime, to state the obvious, and Villeneuve has already shown a tendency to expand beyond the pages of Herbert's books. Might he encroach on the events of "Children of Dune," perhaps?

We'll find out when "Dune: Part Three" hits theaters on December 18, 2026.

#3523. Water Temple dungeon walkthrough in Ocarina of Time

The Water Temple is a dungeon located at the bottom of Lake Hylia in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, and it's only reachable after Link has traveled into the future.

This infamous dungeon is fairly complicated, as you need to constantly adjust the water level inside to unlock more rooms and items. However, as the water level changes, you'll need to constantly adjust your depth to find more rooms. It's a surprise Link doesn't suffer from decompression sickness.

To save Link from a headache, here's how to complete the Water Temple in Ocarina of Time remake.

To get inside the Water Temple, you'll first need to get the Iron Boots from the Ice Cavern and the Zora Tunic from King Zora. Then, approach the island with the large tree on it from the northeast. You'll find the remaining water in Lake Hylia and an underwater door. Equip the Iron Boots and walk into the water. Look above the door to see a target, and Hookshot it to open the door to the Water Temple.

Walk inside the Water Temple, and take off your Iron Boots to float to the surface. Walk into the main room ahead, and defeat the Blue Tektite on the middle platform. Then, put the Iron Boots back on and descend to the floor. There will be Spikes roaming around, and they're only vulnerable when their spikes are retracted. You can't use your sword underwater, so use your Hookshot to hit them. Go into the doorway on the east side of the room, where you'll find Princess Ruto.

After you talk to Ruto, take off the Iron Boots to float to the surface. Open the chest to receive the dungeon map. Then, stand in front of the crest, and play Zelda's Lullaby (Y - X - A - Y - X - A). This will lower the water level in the hole behind you.

Drop into the hole and make sure to land in the water. With the water gone, the torch near the entrance is now lit. Stand in the doorway, and look toward the lit torch. Then, aim your Fairy Bow, so that your arrow will go through the fire, and hit one of the unlit torches along the wall. Alternatively, if you unlocked the Great Fairy Fountain at the top of Death Mountain, you can use Din's Fire. Light both torches to unlock the door, and head inside.

There will be three Spikes in this room. Roll away from them, and then hit them when their spikes are retracted. After you defeat them, a chest with a small key will appear. Open it and return to the main room.

Break the rock wall to the south, and use your Iron Boots to sink to the bottom of the water. A Shell Blade will be waiting for you at the end of the hall. Quickly hit the inside of their mouth with your Hookshot to defeat them. If you miss, make sure to roll out of the way and try again.

Walk to the end of the hall, and take off your Iron Boots to float to the surface. Climb onto the platform, and step on the button on the second tier. A statue with a target will rise from the ground. Hookshot over to it, and defeat the Blue Tektites up ahead. There's also a Like Like on the higher platform. Rather than Hookshotting to the target, Hookshot to the Like Like to stun them. Then, you can unload a ton of attacks on them before they try to suck you up. Avoid their attack and then go in for the final few swings. Then, open the chest to get the compass.

Return to the main room, and this time, head to the east. Push the block until it drops into water. Then, put on your Iron Boots and drop in. A Shell Blade will be waiting for you in the water, so be ready to hit the inside of their mouth with your Hookshot. After you defeat them, walk to the north and take off your Iron Boots to float to the top.

In the next room, there will be a whirlpool. If you look in the water, you'll see a platform about halfway down. Put on your Iron Boots and float to the platform. Then, hit the object in the statue's mouth with your Hookshot. This will open a gate underwater. Take off your Iron Boots, dash through the gate, and quickly dash to the surface. There are two Shell Blades, but you can avoid them if you quickly get out of the water. Open the chest to get a small key.

Return to the main room, and use a small key to open the door on the pillar in front of you. Once inside, turn around and look up to see a target that you can Hookshot too. You'll find the royal crest, so you know what that means. Play Zelda's Lullaby (Y - X - A - Y - X - A) in front of it, which will raise the water level.

You can't reach the Hookshot target on the ceiling just yet, so instead, put on the Iron Boots and sink into the hole that the cube was blocking. Down here, you'll encounter three Spikes. Defeat them with your Hookshot, and then Hookshot the object on the wall. A hole in the ceiling will open up, but a Shell Blade will also come with it. Wait for it to open its mouth, and then Hookshot its insides.

Float into the hole in the ceiling. In this room, you'll find a red rupee and a Gold Skulltula on the west wall. Return to the area with the crest, and go through the door beside the floating cube. This will spit you out in the main room, but now the water level should be at the second floor.

Head to the east and break the rock wall. In this next area, there are Stingers in the water, so be ready to hit them with your Hookshot! After you defeat them, walk to the end of the path and Hookshot to the target above. In this room, there will be a pillar of water and a diamond-shaped object submerged in a pool next to it. Hit the diamond-shaped object, and the pillar of water will lower. Stand on the platform, and hit the diamond-shaped object again to ride the water up. Jump over to the hallway, and open the chest inside to get a small key.

Return to the main room, but this time, put on your Iron Boots and sink to the lowest level. Go into the east room again, and float to the top to find a rock wall. Break it, and you'll enter a room with three Shell Blades and a Gold Skulltula. Defeat the enemies, get the Gold Skulltula token, and then head back to the main room.

Unlock the west door, and hit the diamond-shaped object inside. A Blue Tektite will ride the water down. Defeat it, stand on the platform, and then hit the diamond-shaped object with a ranged weapon like your Hookshot or Fairy Bow. You'll rise to find another royal crest. Play Zelda's Lullaby (Y - X - A - Y - X - A) on the platform, and the water level will rise again.

Return to the main room, but don't walk off the balcony. Play the Scarecrow Song, which will summon Pierre onto the balcony. Pierre will speed up the process later on, so now you're free to unlock the west door. In this room, you need to quickly Hookshot from platform to platform until you reach the top. Walk to the edge in front of you, and drop onto the platform below. Then, look up and Hookshot to the moving platform in front of you. Then, keep Hookshotting to the higher platforms until you make it to the top.

Head through the door and hit the diamond-shaped object. Statues with targets around the room will rise, and so will the water level, bringing a few Blue Tektites with it. Defeat the enemies, and then Hookshot over to the statue to your east. Hit the diamond-shaped object to lower the statues, and then Hookshot to the target on the wall to the north.

Climb over the statue's head, and hit the diamond-shaped object. Then, jump onto the platform on the statue's head, and hit the diamond-shaped object again. After you ride the platform up, go through the door to the north.

The next room is full of fog. Head straight ahead and go past the tree. Walk up to the door, but it'll lock itself. If you turn around, you'll see a shadowy figure standing beside the tree. If you walk up to it, you'll realize it's actually Dark Link!

There's one important thing to note when fighting Dark Link: don't attack him while his shield is up. He'll jump onto your sword and absolutely mog you. Early on in the fight, he'll just jump off, but later on he'll hit you. It's also just one of the coolest things you'll see in all of Ocarina of Time, so if you do want to see it, do it early on in the fight.

There are two phases to the Dark Link fight. For the first part, he'll slash his sword three times, with the third being the most powerful. Make sure to side jump or flip away a couple of times to avoid the third attack, and then get in a few swings of your own. Repeat this a few times until Dark Link submerges himself in the water.

When he resurfaces, he'll incorporate two new attacks: a jump attack and a spin attack. For the jump attack, Dark Link will swing twice and then do a side jump. Wait for him to jump, flip away, and then go in for your own attack. Later on in the fight, Dark Link will start to jump attack without any warning, so be ready to dodge as soon as he jumps. For the spin attack, he'll swing twice, stand in place, and then charge up his sword before unleashing the spin attack. Back away, wait for the spin attack to finish, and then go in for an attack. Like the jump attack, Dark Link will just go straight into the spin attack later on in the fight, so get ready to back away.

After you defeat Dark Link, the door to the north will open. Head on through and open the chest to get the Longshot. This will upgrade your Hookshot, letting you reach targets twice as far away.

Longshot to one of the targets above, and drop into the water below. Follow the water current, but avoid the whirlpools. You can either dash away from them or equip your Iron Boots and walk by them if you want to be safe.

After the first corner, there will be a short turn coming up, but there is a Gold Skulltula on the wall nearby. Equip the Iron Boots after the first corner, and walk to the turn. Look up to the north wall, and you'll see the Gold Skulltula. Longshot it to retrieve its token.

Climb onto the ground just before the final whirlpool, and hit the eye on the wall above the gate. Quickly Longshot to the target before the gate closes, and head through the door to the south. Drop into the water, which will put you in the east room on the lowest floor. Follow the path to return to the main room.

Put on your Iron Boots and go back to the east room on the lowest floor. Float to the top and use Zelda's Lullaby (Y - X - A - Y - X - A) to lower the water level. Then, go into the central pillar, and Longshot to the second floor. Play Zelda's Lullaby at the crest to raise the water level, and then Longshot to the ceiling to get the Gold Skulltula.

Exit the door, and go to the floating cube on the north side of the pillar. Longshot the eye on the wall, and then Longshot the target to pull yourself in. Go to the northeast corner and Longshot the target above the waterfall.

Equip your Iron Boots and follow the path until you find a stone cube on your right. Pull the cube out until you can't pull it anymore, and then Longshot onto the target again. This time, push the cube until you can't anymore. Go into the opening in the wall and float to the surface. Open the chest at the top of the stairs to get a small key.

Return to the main room, and sink to the lowest level. Go into the northern doorway, and Longshot to the target at the end of the hall. Open the door, and you'll enter a room with a whirpool that is full of Blue Tektites. Get rid of the Blue Tektites with your Fairy Bow, as they'll be pretty annoying if you don't.

Additionally, there are two holes in the wall: one in the northwest corner and one in the southeast corner. Rolling boulders will fall out of these holes. Wait for the one in the southeast to pass, and then drop into the water. Swim over to the north side of the room, and then put on your Iron Boots. Wait for the northeastern boulder to roll by, walk up to the wall, and float to the top. You should grab the ledge and pull yourself up.

Go into the next room, which has three rock walls and a pool full of Stingers. There's also a button at the bottom of the pool that will raise the water level as long as it's being pressed. For now, break the middle rock wall, and pull the cube out. Then, break either the left or right rock wall, go behind the cube, and push it into the water.

After the water level rises, swim over to the doorway and follow the path. Take out the two Blue Tektites with your bow and then step onto the button. Jump across the three platforms and go through the door on the other side. This will bring you to the southeastern corner with the rolling boulders.

Wait for a boulder to pass, walk through the waterfall, and jump into the opening on your left. A Shell Blade will be waiting for you, so take them out or just run into the door behind them. Inside the next room, you'll find a chest with the boss key.

Before you sprint back to the main room, exit the room and look through the waterfall on your right. There will be a Gold Skulltula hiding near the ceiling. Use your Longshot to retrieve its token.

Return to the main room, and Longshot to the scarecrow in the southwest corner. Then, raise the water level at the crest. Go back to the main room and Longshot to the target in the north. Go through the door, and put on your Iron Boots to fight against the current. Wait for the Blade Traps to go by, and then walk to the top to find the boss room door leading to the Giant Aquatic Amoeba, Morpha.

Before you start the fight, it's important to note that Morpha is actually the orb floating around in the water. To damage them, you'll need to pull them out of the water with your Longshot. Additionally, Morpha will go back into the water after every attack. Some of their attacks will sprout multiple tentacles out of the water, but only one of them will be real. Look in the water and watch them as they swim around. Where they end up will be where their real tentacle appears.

When you're ready to take on Giant Aquatic Amoeba Morpha, hop onto the floating platforms in the middle of the room. For the first part of the fight, Morpha will sprout out of the water, slam the ground three times, and then rest for a bit. Use your Longshot to pull them out of the water while they're resting, and unload as many attacks as you can.

Then, Morpha will come out of the water and do a spin attack. We recommend running around the outskirts of the arena during this part. Once they stop spinning, pull them with your Longshot and attack them.

Morpha will go back into the water, and a bunch of water tentacles will appear. Only one of them will contain Morpha's body. Find the correct tentacle and move over to it, but if you get near a tentacle, it will slam onto the ground. This is a great time to Longshot to the targets on the wall to get to Morpha as quickly as possible. Approach the real tentacle, and wait for it to slam the ground. Pull them out, and hit them as many times as you can.

For the next attack, three tentacles will come out of the water, and you guessed it, only one will contain Morpha's real body. However, this time, you won't have to chase it down, as it'll do the spin attack again and come for you. Like always, pull them out with Longshot and attack them. If you've been spam attacking Morpha, there's a good chance that the fight will end here.

If the fight didn't end, Morpha has one more attack up its sleeve. A wall of tentacles will come out of the water, and they'll all slam the ground at once. Look for Morpha's body, and attack it until you defeat them.

After you defeat them, collect the Heart Container and exit the dungeon through the ring of light.

#3522. Jon Ossoff and Abdul El-Sayed Cinched a Blue Wave With Snug Tailoring

On Monday night, the eve of the 2026 midterm elections, the fashion crowd celebrated at the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards, colloquially referred to as the Oscars of American fashion. Tory Burch was honored with the Positive Change Award, which was presented to her by Anna Wintour, the global editorial director of Vogue and chief content officer of Condé Nast. In her remarks, Wintour made the evening’s only direct reference to the midterms, reminiscing about attending a fundraising event for James Talarico, who successfully flipped Texas in the race for the Senate last night, alongside Burch. After applause from the audience, Wintour, a prolific Democratic fundraiser herself, looked up and addressed the room: “Let’s hope all of Texas feels the way you do,” she said.

The American fashion crowd has largely distanced itself from politics since the 2024 election. During their time in the White House as first ladies, Michelle Obama and Jill Biden were staunch supporters of the American fashion industry, often wearing American designers for public appearances. Melania Trump, in contrast, has more often preferred European labels. It’s an MO that trickles down into the political parties they represent.

There were many headlines that came out of last night’s midterms: Talarico flipped Texas, Annie Andrews flipped South Carolina, New Hampshire’s Chris Pappas became the first out gay man to be elected to the Senate, and Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia and Deb Haaland of New Mexico became the first Black and Native American women, respectively, to be elected governor in the history of the US.

And yet it wasn’t just good news (and many great memes) that circulated in my group chats last night; there were also some fashion choices worth noting. First, the most pressing: Where were Steve Kornacki’s khakis? And what was the reasoning behind Haley Stevens’s ludicrously capacious hat? Some questions in life simply go unanswered.

Kornacki, a national political correspondent for NBC News, does not make his political affiliations public. But men in his age range (he is 47) and in the generations that follow—millennials and Gen Z—have been contending with what formalwear means and signals today.

Democratic men have been hard at work on their public image since the 2024 election, largely distancing themselves from the MAGA look and its too-large suits and extra-wide ties. In separating themselves from the manosphere, men like Abdul El-Sayed, who won the Senate race in Michigan, and Jon Ossoff, who was reelected to the Senate in Georgia, have been dressing more like the less buttoned up, progressive men they represent and less like the old establishment politicians on both the right and the left.

On the campaign trail, El-Sayed often sported tees and sweaters rather than button-downs and ties, frequently wearing taut sweaters and henleys under his suit jacket, while Ossoff largely opted for rolled cuffs and no jacket. As the two delivered victory speeches last night, they each wore a tailored suit—a little too tight in the arms; these are men who seem to eat their fair share of protein—and ditched their tie.

It’s a familiar image of a more laid-back look, but one in stark contrast to that of the faces of the right: Donald Trump, JD Vance, et al. Ossoff and El-Sayed, similarly to Kamala Harris during her presidential bid, also leaned into what was happening on the internet. These days, netizens are happy to objectify men and christen a new internet boyfriend every week. Ossoff’s and El-Sayed’s campaigns seemed to understand the power of thirst—that their suits were too tight was most likely not completely intentional, but it did help underscore a simple fact: that they are fit, and that their virility can be both attractive and nonthreatening all at once.

Zohran Mamdani speaking at an event on election night. Mamdani also ditched his tie on Tuesday, in line with some of his fellow Democrats.

It is worth noting, however, that there are some men further to the left, both in politics and around it, who have reembraced the suit: Zohran Mamdani and Hasan Piker. On one hand, this has served a similar purpose as Ossoff’s and El-Sayed’s choices: It has distanced them from looksmaxxers and other conservative-leaning young men. On the other hand, a suit for Mamdani and Piker signifies what suits have always represented: that these are grown men doing important things.

The men are not the full story, however. Bottoms and Haaland came as they are, nodding to the communities they represent. The former wore a bright fuchsia suit and matching blouse, a callback to the lively and monochromatic dressing that is a deeply embedded and celebrated tradition in Black church culture. Haaland’s jewelry—firefly earrings and a beaded necklace—nodded at the style of accessories that is representative of Native style and fashion. If there is something that fashion clearly signifies, it’s community and belonging.

It is a running punch line that the left is more closely connected to fashion—it’s the wine-and-cheese crowd, the elites. (Hillary Clinton, during her bid for the presidency in 2016, was dragged online and by the press for wearing an Armani jacket that reportedly retailed for some $12,000 while delivering a speech that touched on income inequality.) While it’s true that fashion designers are often more enthusiastic about dressing progressives than they are about dressing conservatives, in the era of Trump and the MAGA look, this has become a half-baked story.

Olivia Reingold, a staff writer at The Free Press, made a post on X last night while reporting from an event for the Michigan Democratic Party. “So far at Abdul El-Sayed’s election night event I’ve spotted, Valentino heels, a Chanel bag, a Moncler jacket, Rolex watches, and a YSL bag among other designer items,” Reingold wrote, captioning an image of a woman holding a gold quilted Chanel handbag and a pair of Valentino Rockstud leather pumps.

Read Fit Check: Your front row seat to the power players, peacocks, and deep pockets of fashion—and how they influence the rest of the world.

When one takes a closer look, however, the image has several discrepancies. The style and make of the Chanel Flap bag is inconsistent with others the brand has sold, and the Valentino shoes in question appear askew in proportion; their straps have several punched holes that the authentic Valentino style does not. This could mean that the products in the image are not authentic, but there is another suggestive tell: The bottom strap on the left shoe appears to cut through its connecting strap rather than around, a classic mistake made when artificial intelligence is used to create or alter an image. A run of the image through several AI detectors, including SynthID, a digital watermarking approach created by Google DeepMind that detects media generated by OpenAI, Google, Nvidia, and Kakao, suggests the use of AI. SynthID detected that “this media was made or edited with OpenAI.” (Vanity Fair has reached out to Chanel and Valentino to advise on the authenticity of the products and to Reingold regarding the potential use of AI in the image.)

It’s become too easy to try to make a point about the left’s fashion choices: that Rama Duwaji, wife of Mamdani, should not wear pricey shoes, even if borrowed, because of her political beliefs; or that Democratic women should not carry Valentino or Chanel and vote for a candidate seeking to tax the wealthy. Therein lies the crux of the argument: Does this mean that luxury shoppers should align themselves with MAGA because it’s a party associated with billionaires like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos and logo-clad celebs like Nicki Minaj, who wore Chanel to the polls in New Hampshire? The answer is simple: no.

Our fashion choices say much about our values, identity, and aspirations. And while politicians have oftentimes utilized fashion to align themselves with specific groups or appear friendly to voters, they, in broad strokes, do not define our political affiliations. A Chanel bag does not make a Democrat, just as a red tie does not make a Republican.

#3521. New Dunkin' Donuts Commercial Explains The Biggest Threat The Avengers Face In Doomsday

Marvel Cinematic Universe die-hards might have a more complete understanding of what awaits in "Avengers: Doomsday," but the average viewer just knows the Avengers are going up against Robert Downey Jr.'s Victor Von Doom. Now, however, a wise sage has arrived to explain the plot of the upcoming superhero team up: Dunkin' Donuts. A new commercial for the company's Marvel Studios collab, available on YouTube, sees Channing Tatum's Gambit laying out the premise of "Doomsday" with the help of the Fantastic Four's H.E.R.B.I.E. in the most straightforward way possible.

"Doomsday" takes place fourteen months after the events of "Thunderbolts*," and sees three groups of heroes team up to take on Doctor Doom. Just what Doom is up to in the movie remains somewhat unclear at this point. Thus far, the "Doomsday" trailers have mainly focused on hyping up Doom's arrival and the return of beloved characters from MCU history. We do know the Avengers, New Avengers, Wakandans, Fantastic Four, and the 20th Century Fox-era X-Men will be putting up a united front against RDJ's villain, but otherwise we're eagerly awaiting the film's December 18, 2026 release to find out just how he fits into the story.

In the meantime, Channing's Gambit and H.E.R.B.I.E. (Humanoid Experimental Robot, B-Type, Integrated Electronics) are here to offer a simplified explanation of the existential threat facing the MCU. Marvel has teamed up with Dunkin' to deliver a new range of treats that look at once delicious and capable of dissolving your insides in a matter of seconds. Turns out, these new menu items are also pretty handy for explaining the impending collapse of the multiverse.

In the Dunkin' promo clip, entitled "Incoming Munchkins Incursion!" H.E.R.B.I.E. and Gambit are seen in Avengers Tower. The robot points out the window at a planet seemingly on a collision course with the one on which he and Gambit sit. He then uses two donut hole Munchkin treats to represent worlds colliding with one another, in what's known as an incursion, thus explaining the core problem at the heart of "Avengers: Doomsday" more clearly and succinctly than any of the trailers so far.

We first learned about incursions in the sort of fun Sam Raimi movie "Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness," wherein John Krasinski's Reed Richards explained how "an incursion occurs when the boundary between two universes erodes, destroying one or both entirely." In "Doomsday," it seems multiple incursions are happening at the same time, threatening the existence of the entire multiverse. As various universes collide with one another, characters from different timelines (i.e. different eras of Marvel's cinematic history) come into contact, hence why "Doomsday" features characters from so many different films. We sort of knew "Doomsday" would feature multiple incursions, given the events of films leading up to the movie. But the Dunkin' commercial makes it about as clear as possible.

That said, in the commercial, Gambit appears to be in Avengers tower, which means he's almost certainly on Earth 616 in the main MCU timeline. But when H.E.R.B.I.E. points to the planet in the sky, Gambit says "That's our world, there?" Channing Tatum has confirmed his Gambit is from the same world as the Fox-era X-Men. So when Gambit says, "That's our world there," is he talking about the Fox-era universe? Or H.E.R.B.I.E. and the Fantastic Four's universe? Likely the former, but it isn't entirely clear.

Channing Tatum was originally supposed to lead a Gambit movie during the 20th Century Fox X-Men era. But Tatum's Gambit movie failed after the studio tried to make it a comedy and once Disney bought the studio, it seemed that was the end of the whole thing. Tatum thought he'd lost Gambit forever before "Deadpool & Wolverine" came along and gave him a chance to finally debut as Remy Etienne LeBeau, the New Orleans native with the power to manipulate kinetic energy.

But Tatum's Gambit accent created a hilarious problem on "Deadpool & Wolverine." Because the movie was infused with the irreverent comedy of Ryan Reynolds' previous Deadpool outings, Gambit was made to use a heavy Cajun accent that essentially made him unintelligible — a joke that caused his co-stars to crack up on-set. But it seems he'll be toning down the accent for "Doomsday," as evidenced by the Dunkin' commercial.

The actor previously told Variety, "I'm not gonna go full Cajun. [Directors Anthony and Joe Russo] want things to be funny, but they don't want to go full 'Deadpool.' They want to keep the drama and keep it tight." This Dunkin' commercial is the first time we've been able to hear just how Tatum's new Gambit accent will sound, and it's certainly more intelligible than in "Deadpool & Wolverine."

Otherwise, "Avengers: Doomsday" is shaping up to be a tumultuous moment for the MCU, both on and off-screen, with Marvel Studios attempting to bring audiences back on board following a less than impressive Multiverse Saga. We'll have to see how it all pans out when the movie hits theaters on December 18, 2026.

#3520. Bottom of the Well dungeon walkthrough in Ocarina of Time

The Bottom of the Well is a mini dungeon in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake. It's found in Kakariko Village, and it's home to the Lenses of Truth, a key item that will show what's real and what's an illusion.

However, getting to the Bottom of the Well is a bit tricky, as you'll need to manipulate time a bit to find its entrance. It can also get a little creepy inside, as there are ReDead, Gibdo, and even a Dead Hand, living in the well.

Here's how to complete the Bottom of the Well in Ocarina of Time remake.

To get into the Bottom of the Well dungeon, you need to drain it first. Make sure you've learned the Song of Storms from Music Man inside the windmill in Kakariko Village. You need to travel into the future and interact with him to learn it. Then, return to the past, and head inside the windmill in Kakariko Village. Play the Song of Storms (L - R - X - L - R - X) for Music Man, and the well water will drain.

Only young Link can enter the Bottom of the Well, so hop into the well and climb through the tunnel.

Open the door and head down the ladder. Defeat the Skulltula ahead, and read the plaque on the floor, which states: "A wall is not merely a wall. Do not accept only what you see as truth." So, just walk through the wall ahead of you.

Follow the water to the northern side of this area. Stick close to the water, and avoid wandering off, as there are invisible holes in the floor that will send you straight to the basement. You'll eventually find a Triforce on the ground in front of a frog statue protruding out of the wall. Play Zelda's Lullaby (Y - X - A - Y - X - A), and the water level will lower. Walk straight off the ledge and crawl through the hole in the wall.

Follow the path, but be careful of the Skulltula that'll drop from the ceiling. Defeat it and go through the door ahead. There will be a chest in front of you, but there's actually an invisible hole in the floor. Drop into it anyway, and you'll end up in a foggy room. Walk closer to the mound of dirt, and a Dead Hand will pop out of the ground. To beat it, get close to it so that it lunges, but quickly back away before it grabs you. Then, unleash a flurry of attacks. If it does grab you, spam all your buttons until it lets you go.

After you defeat it, a whole body will pop out of the ground! As it turns out, this is actually the Dead Hand. The limb was just its arm. Hold up your shield, and let it approach you. Wait for it to lower its head and attack its face. After you deal enough damage, its body will go back underground. Then, the limbs will pop out again. Hit them until they disappear, and the main body will come back out of the ground. Repeat the whole process, attacking Dead Hand's face and destroying the limbs, until you defeat Dead Hand. Open the chest that spawns to get the Lenses of Truth.

If you're trying to finish the game as fast as possible, you can technically leave and go straight to the Shadow Temple now that you have the Lenses of Truth. There isn't a boss waiting for you at the end of this dungeon, nor is there another key item for you to find. However, if you'd like to finish the Bottom of the Well, continue on to the section below.

Equip the Lenses of Truth in the Equipment menu. Now, you can press Up on the D-Pad to equip the Lenses of Truth or take it off. The Lenses of Truth will show you what is real and what isn't, but it'll also consume magic power while it's active. If you look to the south, you'll see that there's actually a hole in the wall that leads to a ladder.

Go up the ladder, and feel free to break the pots behind the fake walls. Go up the next ladder, and go through the wall at the top of the stairs. Open the invisible chest on your right to get a purple rupee. Then, drop to the area below, but don't crawl through the hole just yet. If you want a Business Scrub Seed, turn around and go through the door that took you to Dead Hand. Put on the Lenses of Truth, and jump over the hole in the ground to the chest. If not, feel free to crawl through the hole, which will take you back to the Triforce on the floor.

Now that you're back in the main room, you need to find a way to the basement to get the dungeon map, which means you'll have to walk over some fake flooring. Luckily, there's a pit nearby. Put on the Lenses of Truth, and take the path to the left. Just in front of the door, there is a pit that'll take you to the basement. Drop into the hole to get to the basement.

In this basement, there are a bunch of ReDead, which are the zombie-like monsters that will stun you with their gaze. We recommend just running by them, but you can defeat them if you'd like. As you walk into the central room, five crystals, like the crystals from the Ice Cavern, will appear. To get out of the basement, you'll need to collect five of them. For now, pick up the crystal ahead of you and run over to the pool of green liquid. Throw a bomb at the rocks in the corner, and grab the crystals on top of the green liquid while you're here. Once the rocks blow up, grab the crystal and open the chest at the end of the path to get the dungeon map.

Grab the last crystal floating on top of the water, and go through the unlocked door. Climb up the ladder and exit the room.

Look to your left to find a pool of water. Drop into it, and dive to the other side. Climb up the wall and go into the door at the top. In this room, you'll find a bunch of coffins and a Gibdo, which looks like a mummy. An easy way to defeat it is to play the Sun's Song (A - R - X - A - R - X) to stun them, and then attack them.

Light a Deku Stick on fire, and hit the western coffin to open it. Inside, you'll find a small key. Collect it and return to the main room.

Use your Lenses of Truth and look into the hallway. You'll see that there's a hole in the wall that leads to a room in the center of the area. Jump into it, and a spotlight will onto you from the ceiling. A Wallmaster will shortly drop, so get out of the spotlight and defeat it.

Inside this room, you'll see that there are two barred rooms. One of them has a small chest with a blue rupee, while the other has a large chest. If you use your Lenses of Truth, you'll see that there's actually a huge pit in front of the large chest, but there's an opening in the wall behind it. Exit the room through the west opening, and use the Lenses of Truth to find the opening behind the chest. Jump through the hole, and open the chest to get the compass.

Make your way over to the southeastern corner of the area, and look to the central wall with the Lenses of Truth. Jump through the hole in the wall and open the chest to get a small key.

Then, head through the door in the northeast corner, but make sure not to fall into the pit that takes you to the basement. In this room, you'll find three Fire Keese and a Beamos. Be careful though, as there's a hole in the ground just in front of the Beamos. Use your Boomerang to take out the Keese, and throw a bomb at the Beamos. If you're running out of bombs, navigate your way to the chest to get five more. Then, go through the door in the corner.

You'll quickly find yourself in a locked room with a Like Like. Luckily there are no invisible holes on the floor, so take them out like normal. Then, hit the Gold Skulltula on the eastern wall, and then use your Boomerang to collect its token. Climb up the ladder, and head back to the hidden room in the center of the area.

Unlock the east door and head inside. There will be a bunch of Keese just sitting on the walls. Take them out, and then equip the Lenses of Truth to see that there is a secret path along the wall. Follow it to find a Gold Skulltula. Use your Boomerang to collect its token.

Then, unlock the west door and head inside. There will be a Deku Baba, and a Gold Skulltula. Defeat Deku Baba, and collect the Gold Skulltula token.

Aaaand that's everything in the Bottom of the Well. There isn't a final boss, but you can collect the remaining chests for a few extra rupees. On the brightside, now you can go back to Hyrule Castle Town and use the Lenses of Truth to win the chest game!

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3519. Meet Colleen Allen, the Future of American Fashion

This is the November 4, 2026 edition of Fit Check, your front row seat to the power players, peacocks, and deep pockets of fashion—and how they influence the rest of the world.

The United States has been overtaken by a blue wave following last night’s midterm elections. James Talarico flipped Texas to make it to the Senate, Chris Pappas of New Hampshire became the first out gay man to be elected to the Senate, and Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia is now the first Black woman to be elected governor in the history of the US. There were great memes about what this could mean for the country—largely, the comeback of woke—and some fashion moments worth discussing. Scroll down for a midterm-fashion verdict, including notes on the curious case of a seemingly AI-generated picture featuring Chanel and Valentino products supposedly spotted at a Michigan Democratic Party election night event in support of Abdul El-Sayed.

In other news, Ye is staging a comeback Yeezy show in Los Angeles tonight at the brand’s flagship—keep an eye out tomorrow for a report from my Angeleno colleague Maxwell Adler. Congratulations are in order for Schiaparelli’s Daniel Roseberry, who is having a great week after running the New York City Marathon on Sunday, posting a much-discussed thirst trap on Monday morning, and receiving the Leader in the Arts Award at the Smithsonian’s annual Hirshhorn New York Gala on Monday night. Congratulations as well to the winners and honorees at the 2026 CFDA Awards. More on that very curious evening below, including an interview with Colleen Allen, certified fashion darling and Emerging Designer of the Year winner.

Mentioned in this issue: Jon Ossoff and his tight suit, Colleen Allen, Ralph Lauren, Jill Biden, Melania Trump, Hasan Piker, Zohran Mamdani and Rama Duwaji, and Tim Burton and his new Loewe collaboration.

The CFDA Fashion Awards on Monday night brought some star power to the American Museum of Natural History: Keke Palmer hosted, and presenters included Matt Damon, Cole Escola, Lupita Nyong’o, Laufey, and Demi Moore. And yet the mood of the evening was somewhat tentative. The Council of Fashion Designers of America is under something of a renovation: Steven Kolb, its former CEO, resigned in September following an altercation with PETA protesters at New York Fashion Week. Serving in his stead is Hildy Kuryk, a comms expert who spent four years at Vogue as its executive director of communications following a career in politics. Kuryk is serving as interim CEO and heading up the search for Kolb’s permanent replacement. On Monday night, she stayed out of the spotlight, leaving most of the audience wondering—and gossiping about—who the new face of the CFDA could and should be.

Rachel Scott of Diotima took the main award of the night as womenswear designer of the year, and Anthony Vaccarello, who just left Saint Laurent, was presented with the International Designer of the Year Award by muses Zoë Kravitz, Hailey Bieber, and Rosé. Ralph Lauren was named menswear designer of the year, securing his place as the most awarded designer in CFDA history. Mr. Lauren himself made an appearance—a crowd-pleaser that also left me wondering if the American industry often puts too much emphasis on its past and not enough on its future. In that spirit, I called up Colleen Allen, who took the prize for emerging designer of the year, and asked her to introduce herself to those of you who haven’t met her yet.

Colleen Allen received her award from designer Gabriela Hearst and actor and writer Cole Escola.

José Criales-Unzueta: What would you say is the most important thing for people to know about your background?

Colleen Allen: I often lead with that I always was a menswear designer and was never intending on doing womenswear. That point of view has really guided my work and who I’ve become. I just love the process of making. I did menswear because there wasn’t an identity of women that I saw that I connected with, really, with brands when I was first going to school. And I just loved the craft of tailoring and learning the physical process of cutting a pattern. I think there’s such an ephemerality in making womenswear, in a way. Draping on a mannequin is quite abstract to me. A huge part of my identity is thinking like a tailor.

Where did you go to school, and where did you work before starting your brand?

I did half at Parsons, half at Central Saint Martins. I consider Parsons to be quite technical, and Saint Martins sort of opened up the world conceptually for me and gave me a lot of freedom and thinking about world-building. I was at The Row doing menswear for three years, and then I also interned at Vogue for a minute [and] Calvin Klein 205W39NYC was a very formative experience. When I was an intern there, I was full-time. I was there for eight months, but it was just so cool because it was all in the same room with Raf [Simons, now at Prada], Pieter [Mulier, now at Versace], Matthieu Blazy [now at Chanel]. You knew at that moment how special it was and how crazy it was. I think the world didn’t process it, but when you were in the room, you knew these people were all so important. And so I think being around that every day and absorbing the way that they worked together and they’re such world-builders, all three of them are very conceptual. I think that was a huge informative experience for me.

I think that people know me for color. The feedback that I get from people who buy the clothes is that when you’re wearing a big velvet coat in a color, or even just a dress or a top, people get stopped on the street just because it’s so visually impactful. Velvet is also a signature. That duality of color and texture, and also a bit of a historical Victorian sensibility.

Where do you think that interest in Victorian garments comes from?

There’s an emotional, aesthetic love for it. There’s a bit of a groundedness and a weight to it, and a bit of that period of time was quite spiritual thinking about the afterlife and death, but there was a sense of romance around that that I think really seeped into the clothes in a way that I don’t know if other periods of time really reflect. On the other side of it, it isn’t Victorian specifically, but a lot of historical dress for women is incredible tailoring—thinking about those bodice jackets that have a lot of tiny little panels with lots of little grosgrain finishing on the seams on the inside—and it’s all about molding to the female body. As a menswear designer, I love wearing men’s clothes and wearing a tailored jacket, but I think that the idea of having that sensibility and also reflecting femininity is the perfect storm for me. A lot of that just got lost in a certain period of time once women were able to wear pants, and in the transition of women being able to access menswear, women’s tailoring never got back to that sort of technical level of fitting the body or the female form.

You’ve never done a runway show, which is something that many young designers feel signals their arrival. Why is that?

I love fashion and wanted to work in fashion because I loved watching fashion shows. And specifically, I loved shows that were immersive. I always go back to [Alexander] McQueen [that signaled] fashion is more than product. It is this world-building, cinematic performance art, and you can take it just so much further emotionally. If I’m going to do a show, I want it to carry that level of weight. For me, at my scale, it just feels like the most manageable way to encapsulate a sense of emotion is to do it through a [photo] shoot and showroom appointments for now, just in truly a practical sense. But it is my dream, and I’m working towards having a show. But when I do it, I want it to feel special.

It’s a bit surreal, in a way. It’s especially cool that it’s voted by the industry, and it sounds maybe kind of cheesy, but I do just feel like that is the best reward. That all these people that I’ve worked with are acknowledging [me]. It feels solidifying, grounding. It feels like I’ve been doing this forever, and it’s also going by so fast at the same exact time. It lets me be present and acknowledge myself for how much work has been put into it and that I did it and it’s real and it’s something I dreamed about for so long.

Do you feel like a fashion-industry darling?

[Laugh] Oh my God, how does one answer that question? Gosh, I think that three years ago I was entering these rooms knowing absolutely no one... I think the showroom has actually really fostered real relationships and friendships in the industry, and a sense of community that just feels really good. I work as hard as I can to support whatever the stylists are doing or the editors, I’m always physically running around to make sure that they get the clothes because I love what they do. I love that I know the photographer and the stylist and all the people, and know that if my clothes are in it, it will be amazing for me and they made the effort to reach out to me, to include me in it. The word darling is such an ick word [laugh]. I feel like the word I want to say is camaraderie, because everyone just works so hard. Nobody is flouncing around being a darling. We are all hustling together, and if I can support your hustle and you support mine, that’s the best thing. And when it works, it’s just so satisfying.

Tim Burton, iconoclast filmmaker extraordinaire, has a new capsule with Loewe, which has recreated characters and vignettes from The Nightmare Before Christmas as bags and charms. These kinds of collabs were a staple when Jonathan Anderson was at the brand, and Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez seem to be game to keep them coming with the same endearing whimsy.

In the age of artificial intelligence, the film has become a symbol of human craft and ingenuity. “The more it keeps going that way,” Burton told me yesterday, calling from London and answering a question about the proliferation of AI in film, “the more I appreciate [the human] side of it. I think it’s something that’s very important to keep in the world, the tactile, not being on a screen all the time and doing all that sort of thing. To me, [humanity] is very important to life and art and anything, really.” We also spoke about his collaboration with A$AP Rocky and whether he’d ever do a live-action remake of 2005’s Corpse Bride.

#3518. Star Trek Cast A Real-Life American Hero In The Perfect Role

In the image above, you'll see real-life Georgian politician Stacey Abrams, the minority leader of the state's House of Representatives from 2011 through 2017. She played the president of a united Earth in a notable 2022 episode of "Star Trek: Discovery."

The final episode of the fourth season of "Discovery" was called "Coming Home," and it wrapped up a story arc involving the mysterious Species 10-C, an alien species so cognitively and physiologically different from average humanoids that communication proved near-impossible. The species was so different, in fact, it took months of research to get them right.

Species 10-C was responsible for unleashing a widespread gravitational cataclysm called the Dark Matter Anomaly, which was unwittingly poised to do untold destruction on Earth and other worlds. A lot of diplomacy and panic were involved in trying to contact Species 10-C and explain to them what they were doing. /Film reviewed the season, and found it to be a tricky balance between the cosmic and the personal.

Throughout the season, there is chatter about evacuating Earth, and mention of the planet's president. In the 32nd century, when "Discovery" takes place, Earth will still be united, and will have a singular presidential figure overseeing its government. The president appears at the end of "Coming Home" to put a button on the whole season, reiterating that communication and diplomacy are very, very good indeed. It's wholly fitting that a real-life politician like Stacey Abrams should be willing to appear as that character.

Abrams famously ran for governor of Georgia in 2018, but narrowly lost to Republican Brian Kemp. She ran again in 2022, but lost to Kemp a second time. She has long been an outspoken advocate for voting rights, and founded the organization Fair Fight Action, which aims to fight against voter suppression. She's quite well-suited to appear in the futuristic utopia of "Star Trek."

The end of "Coming Home" involves Earth rejoining the United Federation of Planets, an organization that had fallen by the wayside in the previous few centuries. Stacey Abrams has a scene with Captain Michael Burnham (Sonequa Martin-Green), the show's lead character in which the President of United Earth is presented as somewhat regal, although Abrams, not an actress, brings a grounded officiousness to the role as well. When she says, "United Earth is ready right now to rejoin the Federation, and nothing could make me happier than to say those words," it sounds like a speech that a 21st-century Earth politician might say.

Martin-Green was blown away to be working with Abrams, something she gushed about in an interview with Deadline. She said:

"I'm still floored when I think about Stacey gracing us with her presence in our Season 4 finale. [...] We spent so much of our time fanning out and pretending to be cool in her midst. [...] She's a legend in the making and a civil hero, and she was an absolute delight to work with. [...] She wowed us with her charm, humility, and generosity, and she whipped out some acting chops too! [...] It was an honor for me as a Black woman to stand with her in the story. It's an experience I'll cherish for the rest of my life."

Abrams is cherished throughout the American political landscape. In 2019, she was selected to deliver the response to the President's State of the Union address, and she was even buzzed about as a potential running mate for presidential candidate Joe Biden. The New York Times cited Abrams as a major influence on boosting voter turnout in her state.

Stacey Abrams seems to believe that everyone should have a voice in American elections, which is a philosophy that falls very neatly in line with the overall egalitarian thinking behind "Star Trek." If anyone was to be present for Earth to rejoin the Federation, Abrams certainly fit the bill.

According to The Hollywood Reporter, Abrams has long been a fan of "Star Trek," and was well aware of the rise of Captain Michael Burnham. Abrams wanted to be involved in "Star Trek: Discovery" no matter what plotline was being explored. She posted a video to her Twitter/X account, and was quoted as saying:

"Whatever the story was, I wanted to be a part of it because watching Michael Burnham come into her power as captain, watching this party-crew reclaim itself — not only in a new era but in a new space that is so reminiscent of what they remembered but so different — that, to me, speaks of why we do the work we do in politics. [...] It's about giving people hope and giving them a better life and creating this vision of what is possible."

Abrams has long stood up for justice, fairness, and equality. One can find ample evidence online tracing her stances on issues like criminal justice reform, her belief in the power of public education, and her need to address her state's maternal health crisis. She possesses a progressive standpoint politically, which is fitting for the overall progressive attitudes of "Star Trek, so this was smart casting. As we mentioned in our own article ranking the best "Star Trek" guest stars, Abrams and "Star Trek" both remind us that the future can be better.

#3517. This Cult Sci-Fi Horror Series With Stephen King Vibes Has Become A Major Netflix Hit

There are so many problems with streaming media, but a big one is that each of these companies is hellbent on creating new movies and shows to fill out their library of licensable titles. There's a lot that's worth watching, but there's nowhere near enough time to watch these worthy works. As a result, great films and series fall between the cracks or get unceremoniously cancelled before they can complete their run.

So it's something of a miracle that "From," a science fiction horror series created by John Griffin that flew under the radar for several years, survived for five seasons. The final season was greenlit by MGM+ last April, thanks in large part to the show's enthusiastic cult following, but the company might consider lobbying Griffin for another season. Because this cult favorite has become a bona fide hit on Netflix.

Netflix began streaming the first three seasons of "From" last month, and it's currently the fourth most popular series on the service. It's not hard to understand why. Griffin's show is basically "Lost" with major Stephen King vibes, and it even features one of the show's stars, Harold Perrineau.

"From" opens with a family of four being forced to re-route their road trip when their chosen path is blocked by a fallen tree. They wind up in a small town where they receive directions out of the area from Sheriff Boyd Stevens (Perrineau), but they soon find themselves back in the town again. Gradually, they discover that there is no escaping this unnamed town.

"From" quickly makes "Lost" look like a lovely tropical vacation when it's revealed that the town turns decidedly lethal at night, due to the presence of vicious, human-looking monsters. And the show is unsparing in depicting these creatures' savagery. It's a gorehound's delight.

A major reason why "From" never caught on with mainstream viewers is that the first season streamed on Epix, which would eventually be acquired by MGM+. So Netflix is essentially doing a huge favor for MGM+, because "From" is every bit as addictive as "Lost."

Given the series' uptick in visibility, perhaps the critically acclaimed show (all four seasons rate over 90% on Rotten Tomatoes) will finally earn some Primetime Emmy nominations. It won the Saturn Award for Best Horror Television Series last year, and Perrineau is well overdue for Emmy consideration. The only impediment here is that voters will have to binge four seasons of a show that was off their radar.

If voters do take the plunge, they'll find a smart, terrifying series that flirts with the bleakness of Stephen King's legendary horror bummer "The Mist." A lot of people may not have the stomach for that, but Griffin and his writers adroitly plumb the darkness of our era, where days often feel like a purgatorial drag. But "From" keeps us watching because we need to believe there's a way out of this.
