#3515. Chicago Fire’s 300th Episode Fasttracks Its Death By A Thousand Cuts | Review

NBC celebrates a rare milestone as Chicago Fire hits 300th episode. Unfortunately, the hour fails to be match the importance of the moment.

Ana Dumaraog is a Writer and Editor at Screen Rant, where she expertly covers Network TV offerings, among other things She has spearheaded the effort to make the site an authority on broadcast shows, initially starting with The Big Bang Theory franchise, NCIS, and One Chicago before taking on the specialization in general. Ana has also covered a wide-spread of topics in the past — from franchises like, the MCU and Star Wars, to classic TV favorites, such as Frasier and MASH.

Ana brings clarity and enthusiasm to every story she tackles—whether reporting on new releases or offering deep dives into fan-favorite franchises. Her coverage translates complex entertainment developments into engaging, audience-focused content.

For a milestone as rare as hitting 300 episodes, Chicago Fire fails to deliver a memorable celebratory episode. As NBC's fall 2026 slate continues to rely on fully-established projects led by the Law & Order franchise, One Chicago's inaugural series continues to build its own legacy as the third-longest-running procedural on the network. Premiering in 2012, Chicago Fire is arguably the most popular first-responder show on TV right now. Aside from paving the way for spinoffs, such as Chicago PD and Chicago Med, it also inspired a string of shows in the same sandbox, with both ABC and CBS trying to replicate its success.

After 14 years on the air, Chicago Fire celebrates its 300th episode with "Three Hundred." Considering the ongoing trend of TV seasons getting fewer and shorter, this feat is becoming increasingly rare, which is a reminder of the show's longevity. Throughout the last decade and a half of its run, Chicago Fire has had its fair share of celebratory episodes. 2016's "One Hundred," 2019's "The Plunge," 2021's "Two Hundred," and 2024's "Inside Man" all delivered bigger and more consequential narratives that either honored the show's past or set up its future. For "Three Hundred," the focus is on the latter, as the outing marks a major shift in Firehouse 51.

NBC and Wolf Entertainment use Chicago Fire season 15, episode 5, as the send-off for Joe Minoso's Joe Cruz — one of the very few cast members who have been in the series since season 1. Given that, there was an expectation that "Three Hundred" would deliver a highly-emotional swan song for the character, despite the fact that the project has been gradually building towards his exit ever since his paralysis narrative started. Unfortunately, the lack of focus, the sheer number of plots simultaneously happening, and other head scratchers result in an ultimate letdown.

As Cruz's final outing, there was an expectation going into the episode that the hour would put an effort into highlighting his legacy with Firehouse 51 while also laying out a justified reason for his departure. Over the years, Chicago Fire has seen its fair share of character exits, and while some are done better than others, NBC and Wolf Entertainment have done decently when it comes to sending off characters who were on the show for a considerable amount of time. Sadly, that isn't the case for Cruz. "Three Hundred" starts with the character doing considerably better, with Chicago Med's Dean Archer even telling him that he would be back at Firehouse 51 soon enough. Everyone is on board with the idea, except for Chloe, who gives birth to their twins early due to overall stress about doing everything for the family. Apparently, she had been against her husband going back to work, afraid that he would be hurt again and she would be left alone.

While it makes sense for her to be worried, the way Chicago Fire establishes this reveal is so poorly-executed. It makes Chloe look unreasonable, considering how much Cruz has been working hard to get back to work. On top of that, her husband giving up his career and means of living at this point in their family life seems impractical in terms of their economic standing. Now, Cruz doesn't have any path towards going back to work. The fact that this whole plot happens separate from anyone over at Firehouse 51 makes it worse. Firehouse 51 has always differentiated itself by being a tightly-knit team, and yet, it's odd that there's no effort to help Cruz's family beyond making sure that he can return to Squad 3 — even then, Kelly Severide's attempt to convince him to stay sounds self-serving.

Granted that it still has to move on beyond Cruz's stint with Firehouse 51, the least Chicago Fire could have done is give him a compelling and solid swan song, not something that makes it seem like an afterthought.

Instead of focusing on Cruz's struggle for a more emotional send-off, Chicago Fire season 15, episode 5 tackles several more stories separate from its main plot. Stella Kidd deals with a probationary struggling after a call, Christopher Herrmann has an odd arc regarding his new professional headshot, while Violet Mikami and Lyla Novak deal with personal stories. "Three Hundred" even opens with Severide working on an arson case. Granted that it still has to move on beyond Cruz's stint with Firehouse 51, the least Chicago Fire could have done is give him a compelling and solid swan song, not something that makes it seem like an afterthought. Even the poignant tribute to Otis Zvonecek at the end of the hour doesn't have the emotional impact that it should have.

To better understand the failures of Chicago Fire's 300th episode, it's important to remember that the outing doesn't exist in a bubble. It's a culmination of all the small but detrimental issues that the project has been facing in the last few years. Now, the pile has gotten so big that it's nearly impossible to ignore. For starters, Minoso's exit is primarily motivated by NBC's yearly cost-cutting measures. While some actors left on their own, a handful of them, especially in more recent years, were written out of Chicago Fire and One Chicago in general to cut costs. This has resulted in sudden story shifts, as the writers scramble to find a way to write out a character in the quickest way possible.

Secondly, and still tied to the first point, the constant changing of the ensemble makes it difficult for Chicago Fire to properly establish a new overall dynamic. On a smaller scale, one-on-one relationships are also scarce outside the long-standing ones, such as Herrmann and Randall "Mouch" McHolland's friendship, as well as Severide and Kidd's romance. These types of pairings were the backbone of the Chicago Fire during its earliest years, as effectively emphasized by the bittersweet moment between Cruz and Otis. Now, since no new character stays long enough, any kind of personal and relationship build-up goes out of the window.

One fan-favorite series on NBC will officially make tv history by breaking an industry record that has been established over two decades ago.

As Chicago Fire season 15 continues, hopefully, it is able to find the balance that it needs to be able to sustain another 300-episode run. The show has one of the most engaged fan communities, and it would be a shame if these problems continue to plague it until it's eventually canceled.

#3514. Shadow Temple dungeon walkthrough in Ocarina of Time

The Shadow Temple is one of the many dungeons in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake that you take on after you've traveled into the future.

In this dungeon, you'll need to question what is real and what is fake, as your eyes will deceive you. There are hidden traps, fake walls, and invisible enemies lurking about. However, they might be the least of your worries, as even the floor isn't safe. Luckily, you'll find the Hover Boots to keep your mind at ease.

Here's how to complete the Shadow Temple dungeon in Ocarina of Time remake.

Before you start, you'll need to get the Lenses of Truth from the Bottom of the Well and Din's Fire from the Great Fairy Fountain at the top of Death Mountain. If you're trying to grab every Gold Skulltula, you'll also need the Scarecrow Song from Lake Hylia.

Use the Lenses of Truth at the entrance to see a ring of unlit torches. Stand on the platform in the middle, and use Din's Fire to light every torch.

Head inside the Shadow Temple, but be careful of the Flying Pots in the first hallway. Longshot to the target, and walk through the fake wall in front of you.

Just inside the next room, you'll find a vulture statue that is surrounded by podiums with skulls on them. The plaque on the statue reads, "The tip of my beak seeks the skull of truth. Should it find falsehood, darkness shall fall." So, you need to use the Lenses of Truth to find the skull of truth, and rotate the vulture statue so that its beak is pointing at it. When you use the Lenses of Truth, only one podium will have a skull. Rotate the beak so it's pointing at the statue, and a door on the other side of the room will open.

Now, if you look at the door, you'll notice that there's a huge pit in front of it, and it's real. Instead of trying to jump across, head to the northwest corner of the room, and go through the fake wall. Open the door and interact with the skull on the ceiling, who will essentially tell you that you need the Lenses of Truth.

Equip the Lenses of Truth, and take the hidden path to the north, just below the large skull on the wall. Head inside the door, and you'll enter a room with a ReDead and two Keese. Play the Sun's Song (A - R - X - A - R - X) to stun the ReDead and defeat all the enemies. A chest containing the dungeon map will spawn shortly after.

Return to the previous room, and use the Lenses of Truth to reveal a path to the west. Then, in the next room, there will be another hidden path in the northwest corner. Go down the hall. One of the floor tiles will sink, but don't worry as you won't fall to your death.

Go through the door, and you'll face off against a Dead Hand. A bunch of limbs will pop out of the ground first. If you have a lot of magic power, you can stand on the platform in the center and use Din's Fire to get rid of all the arms at once. Then, the main body will come out. Wait for them to approach you. Once they lower their head, quickly attack their face until they retreat. The arms will pop back out of the ground, so you'll need to repeat this process until you beat the Dead Hand and a chest spawns. Open the chest to get the Hover Boots. These boots will let you float and walk on air.

To use them, you need to have them equipped, and simply walk off a ledge. You'll only float for a short period of time, so don't try to walk too far! Exit the room and use the Hover Boots to walk over the floor tile that fell. Then, return to the room with the vulture statue.

Now that you have the Hover Boots, you can cross the gap to the door. (Just make sure they're equipped first). In the next room, there will be a Beamos, so throw a bomb at it to destroy it. There's a fake wall to your north and south, and there's also a rock wall to the east. First, take the path to the south. You'll enter a room with two ReDead. Play the Sun's Song (A - R - X - A - R - X) to stun them and take them out. A chest containing the compass will spawn.

Go back to the previous room and take the path to the north. In this room, you'll need to collect five crystals to unlock a door to a chest. The only problem is that there are two scythe-wielding statues that are rotating in the middle of the room. The scythes cover the majority of the room, so you'll need to jump on top of platforms to avoid them. After you collect the five crystals, open the chest to get a small key. There is a hole in the northeast corner of this room, but you can't do anything there at the moment.

Head back to the previous room and destroy the rock wall. Use your small key to open the door and follow the path, but be careful of the Skulltulas and guillotines along the way. Wait for the guillotines to start rising and then walk past them. At the end of the path, you'll find an elevator. Ride it down and you'll find even more guillotines.

The first guillotine drops a bit fast. Instead of walking under it, use your Hover Boots to walk around it. You can use your Hover Boots for the second guillotine, but be careful as a Red Bubble will be waiting for you on the next platform. Walk around the third guillotine, and you'll find a Stalfos on the last platform. Remember to take off your Hover Boots so you can freely move around while fighting.

After you defeat the Stalfos, turn to the east and put on your Lenses of Truth. Use your Hover Boots to walk to the platform and then the door. There will be a Business Scrub on your left, where you can buy a green potion if you're low on magic power. Go through the door, and you'll see a Like Like in the far room. However, there's actually another one of those rotating scythe statues in the center of the room. Avoid the scythe, and defeat the Fire Keese and the Like Like to unlock the door to the next room. Use the Lenses of Truth to open both chests, and collect the Gold Skulltula token.

Return to the previous room. Get onto the moving platforms, but stop on the last one just before the Beamos. There are five crystals you have to collect to unlock the door to the next room. Wait on the last platform until it rises. You'll find one crystal in the air at the top. Collect it, and blow up the Beamos with a bomb. Then, grab the two crystals in the middle, but make sure to avoid the Blade Traps.

The crystal to the north is on an invisible floating platform. Use your Hover Boots to grab it. Then, climb the wooden platforms in the south, and use the Hover Boots to get to the last crystal.

In the next room, there are spike traps that fall from the ceiling, but if you use the Lenses of Truth, you'll see a stone cube hidden in the wall. Pull it into the groove on the floor, and push it under the first spike trap. Then, head through the hole in the northern wall and find the fairy's thoughts on the opposite side. Play the Song of Storms (L - R - X - L - R - X) to restore your health and magic power.

Then, push the cube under the second spike trap, but make sure that your body isn't under the first trap. Walk into the cell and open the chest inside to get 20 rupees. Push the cube the rest of the way and climb up to the next floor. Climb up again and step onto the top of the spike traps. Ride it to the top and step onto the platform in the northeast to find a Gold Skulltula. Use your Longshot to grab its token, and then open the chest in the southwest corner of the room to get a small key.

Exit the room and go back to the invisible floating platform where you collected the crystal. If you use your Lenses of Truth, you'll see that there's actually a moving platform just below you. Drop onto it and head through the door.

You'll enter another room where you have to collect five crystals. The room may look empty, but there are actually a bunch of spikes scattered around the room. Also, there are two ReDead, but you can take care of them using the Sun's Song (A - R - X - A - R - X). Use your Lenses of Truth to avoid the traps, and use the Longshot to grab the crystals floating in the air. After you collect every crystal, go through the unlocked door.

In the next room, you need to cast a dark orb into the black skull. Go up the stairs, take out the Keese, and throw a bomb into the skull. The skull will blow up, revealing a small key. Pick it up and go back to the previous room. Longshot to the target in the northwest corner, and use the Hover Boots to walk over to the locked door.

In this next room, you'll need your Iron Boots to fight against a strong fan. Equip the Iron Boots in the Equipment menu, and walk through the hallway. Watch out for the Skulltula, and then Longshot to the target on the ceiling. Before you drop down, turn around to see a Gold Skulltula on the wall. Use your Longshot to retrieve its token.

Head into the next room, which is a long hallway with a bunch of fans on each wall. For the first two fans, there will be a small alcove on the opposite wall that contains a few pots. Feel free to swap to your Hover Boots when the fans aren't blowing, and then use the wind to reach the alcove. However, keep in mind that you'll need to constantly swap between your Iron Boots and Hover Boots as you progress down the platform. The wall on the opposite side of the third wall is actually fake. Before you head inside, you can grab a Business Scrub seed in an invisible chest in the room at the end of the hall, but feel free to skip it.

Put on your Lenses of Truth and Hover Boots, and use the wind to reach the door behind the fake wall in the northeast corner. Defeat the two ReDead inside, avoid the Blade Traps, and destroy the rock wall to find a chest containing a small key. Unlock the door and go to the next room.

Ride the elevator down, and you'll find a stone cube on your left. Pull it out and push it to the end of the track. Climb up to the top of the wooden scaffolding, and look at the top of the metal cage to spot some spiraling leaves, which means you can summon a scarecrow. Play the Scarecrow Song, Longshot to it, and you'll find a Gold Skulltula on the wall.

Drop back down and make your way over to the large boat. Step onto the Triforce and play Zelda's Lullaby (Y - X - A - Y - X - A). The ship will start to move, but two Stalfos will spawn as you ride the boat. Avoid their attacks (especially the jump attack), and defeat them. The boat will eventually crash and sink into the abyss, so make sure to jump off before it disappears!

Head over to the spider web on the west side of the platform, and light it on fire with a Fire Arrow or Din's Fire. Go inside and you'll spot a few Floormasters. If you try to walk over to them, you'll realize that there are actually invisible walls everywhere in this room. Equip the Lenses of Truth, defeat the Floormasters, and make your way to the southern room.

Inside, there will be an invisible Floormaster. Defeat it and open the chest to get a small key. Then, make your way to the west room. Go up the stairs and throw a bomb into every skull. A Gold Skulltula and some rupees will pop out of the last one.

Return to the previous room and head to the locked door in the north. When you step inside, the walls will start to close in on you, so make sure to equip Din's Fire or your Fire Arrows before you go inside. Set the walls on fire, and they'll disappear. Then, defeat the ReDead and open the chests to get a large magic jar and the boss key.

Return to the area where you jumped off the boat, and head to the east side of the platform. You'll see a bird statue, but if you look at its base, you'll see that it looks like a rock wall. Break the base, and the statue will fall over, creating a bridge to the other side. Cross it and enter the door to the south.

Put on your Lenses of Truth and your Hover Boots. Take the path to your right, and follow it until you reach the door to the boss room.

Before you jump into the hole and take on the Phantom Shadow Beast, Bongo Bongo, there are a few things you should know about the fight:

When you're ready, jump into the hole. For the first part of the fight, Bongo Bongo will play the bongo like normal: three hits with their left hand and one hit with their right hand. Then, they'll stop, and one hand will come toward the center of the arena. You'll only be able to see their shadow above you. Move away from the shadow, and wait for the shadow to twitch, as that means it'll slam onto the bongo in just a moment. Quickly equip the Hover Boots or jump to avoid being launched into the air, and attack the hand. If you missed the timing, take out your Fairy Bow and shoot the hand instead. The other hand will move right above you and do the same thing, Dodge its slam and attack it.

After you attack both hands, Bongo Bongo's eye will light up. Put on your Lenses of Truth to see their body. In just a moment, Bongo Bongo will charge at you with their whole body. Shoot their eye with your Fairy Bow or Longshot to stun them, and then run in and attack them with everything you've got. It's best to hit their eye a bit late, so you don't have to run toward them. But, it's better to be safe, so shoot them whenever you can. They'll repeat this attack every time you take out both hands, so be ready to shoot their eye after you do so.

For the remainder of the fight, Bongo Bongo will start incorporating new attacks:

After you hit one of the hands, the other hand will either perform the first attack or any of the attacks listed above. When in doubt, wait for the hand to stop glowing and then hit them with an arrow. Then, shoot Bongo Bongo's eye and attack them as many times as you can.

Repeat this process until you beat them, and you'll earn a Heart Container. Then, you're free to exit the dungeon via the ring of light.

#3513. Anne Hathaway's 2026 Thriller Sets Surprise Return With New Alternate Ending

Colleen Hoover adaptations have proven to be profitable undertakings. Four have now been made so far, and at this rate, the odds are high that more will follow. The latest adaptation of Hoover's work, starring Anne Hathaway in the titular role, extends the impressive hot streak. Despite being panned by critics and having a relatively short theatrical run, the movie still turned a tidy profit, grossing over 4X its production budget. Fast losing screens across the country, the movie received an early digital release and is now set for wider access with an upcoming release.

Verity was adapted for the screen by Nick Antosca, whose strong track record in the psychological thriller genre includes NBC's Hannibal and the Apple TV series Cape Fear. Antosca took huge liberties with his screenplay, which seems to have disappointed the critics as well as the portion of the audience who had already read Hoover's book. The critics essentially faulted the execution of the story's plot twists. The audience, especially those who went in blind, deemed it a decent movie, as reflected in its 72% Popcornmeter score, with words like "hooked," "sexy," and "nailbiting" contained in the audience consensus.

Verity's ending, though it closely resembles the book's, has been the most debated aspect of the movie among the fans. For those who thought it failed to stick the landing, an upcoming release could explain the gaps. Amazon MGM Studios, in association with Alliances Entertainment, has prepared a Blu-ray, 4 K release of Verity. The release will reportedly come loaded with bonus content including two alternate endings and deleted, never-before-seen scenes that could help demystify that ending. The two-disc combo-pack release, which will hit shelves on December 15, will also include an audio commentary by the director, Michael Showalter.

Four criminal masterminds. One of them was always going to be yours. Here is who comes for you, why they picked you out of everyone available, and what they want from the encounter.

Your nemesis does not want to beat you. He wants to know you completely, and he is patient enough to wait for it. The frightening part is how good the conversation is.

Your nemesis is not after money, territory or revenge. He is after a demonstration, and you are the person he has chosen to prove his point on.

Your nemesis respects you, which sounds flattering until you work out what it means. He chose you because nobody else was worth his time.

Your nemesis has no personal interest in you whatsoever, and that is precisely what makes him unsurvivable. You are not a rival. You are a stop on the way.

Given that Verity rapidly lost screens across the country due to lower turnouts, many missed the chance to watch it on the big screen. The next reliable way to catch up on the movie is either via digital, DVD purchase, or on subscription-based streaming. As Amazon MGM handles Verity's distribution, it will eventually stream on Prime Video.

The timing of a streaming release is often predicated on its commercial performance, where a strong showing, as in Project Hail Mary, forces a delay in favor of a longer theatrical run. However, should Verity face a delay in its arrival on Prime Video, it would be due to a different reason — an extended time for PVOD sales. Regardless, a release on Prime Video before the end of the year is likely. Stay tuned for updates.

#3512. Aaron Eckhart's 83-Minute Gritty Neo-Western Becomes A Global Streaming Hit

Thanks to "Yellowstone" and its various offshoots, Paramount+ has become the primary purveyor of neo-Western entertainment in Hollywood. But the streamer isn't just home to wildly popular Taylor Sheridan dramas. It also has a few great neo-Western movies worth a look, and Aaron Eckhart's latest has just topped the streamer's charts worldwide. Unfortunately, "Thieves Highway" isn't available on Paramount+ in the United States. But if you happen to live stateside and have a Hulu subscription, take this as a sign to check out the movie on Hulu/Disney+.

A department of agriculture agent might not seem like the most badass designation for a B-movie hero, but Eckhart is here to surprise you with a film that proves cattle rustling didn't disappear along with the Old West and that livestock agents can hand out some brutal beatdowns. "Thieves Highway" sees Eckhart play a lonely lawman who single-handedly takes on a modern cattle rustling operation and winds up in a fight for his life. It's silly, over-the-top action that's well worth a weekend watch.

"Theives Highway" isn't one of the greatest Westerns of the 2020s, but it deserves more attention than it got upon its initial release. The film stars Aaron Eckhart as widowed Oklahoma livestock agent Frank Bennett, who encounters Devon Sawa's Jones and his gang of livestock thieves while driving home. He decides to try to apprehend them alone, but is quickly overwhelmed and thrust into a fight for his life. Alone and outnumbered, Bennett has to find a way to thwart the cattle rustlers before they can reach the border, while also making it back home in one piece.

The film doesn't have enough reviews on Rotten Tomatoes for a critic score, and its 18% audience score isn't the best advertisement for its quality. Still, Paramount+ viewers seem to be enjoying it. Per streaming viewership tracker FlixPatrol, "Thieves Highway" is sitting at number one on the streamer's movie charts in 18 countries. Even more impressive, the film hit Paramount+ internationally in early November and debuted in the top spot in all 18 of those markets. It's also sitting at number nine in Canada. All of that has made "Thieves Highway" the number one movie on Paramount+ worldwide.

That's not bad for a film nobody had heard of. While "Thieves Highway" is certainly a low-budget actioner of the B-movie variety, Jessie V. Johnson is one of the better directors working in that area, and the film has a compelling premise with its focus on cattle rustling in modern-day Oklahoma. If you're in the United States and intrigued to see what all the fuss is about, the movie is available to stream on Hulu and Disney+ right now.

#3511. Every Robin in Order From The First Boy Wonder to DC’s New Heir, Explained

The caped crusader patrolling Gotham by night may always cast a massive shadow over Batman's fellow defenders, but that hasn't made the Robins of the DC Universe any less significant. In fact, many have splintered to chart impressive paths of their own, forging key bonds and iconic teams.

Naturally, every reader, viewer, or general consumer of DC media will encounter an instance in which they learn just how many Robins there are. In certain limited instances, untold legions of those bearing the title have existed either in reality or in detailed visions of an alternate future. But many have indeed lived as the primary character bearing the Robin title as Batman's sidekick, and more than one has even died doing the same.

Robins throughout DC continuity have emerged from all walks of life, shouldering trauma, obsession, or general issues of their own. They're often the product of their era, with their fates occasionally decided by committee, in the case of Jason Todd. But every named Robin deserves the spotlight if even briefly, to showcase how far each of them have come.

Robin, Nightwing, Batman, Agent 37, Renegade, Talon, Deadman, Ric Grayson

Like Bruce Wayne, Dick witnessed his parents' murder. Feeling a kinship with the boy, Bruce took him in as his ward and eventually trained him as his crime-fighting partner. After his tenure as Robin, Dick assumed the identity of Nightwing, carving out his path as a hero independent of Batman.

Since then, he has taken on diverse roles, such as a super spy, police officer, and leader of the Titans. Notably, he even filled in as Batman, with Bruce's son Damian serving as his Robin, during a time when Bruce was believed to be dead. There have been plenty of variants on Dick across decades of comics, with cases like Earth 2 where he functioned both as an attorney and as Robin well into adulthood, affiliated with the JSA of his world, too. Despite his many later identities, Dick is easily still the most iconic Robin, a label he'll never fully leave behind.

According to Detective Comics #226, Bruce Wayne was the original Robin, though this was later retconned in Post-Crisis canon. Before this change, Bruce trained under Detective Harvey Harris, who taught him the basics of detective work in the guise of the future Robin identity.

What’s particularly intriguing is that despite not knowing Dick Grayson, Bruce still adopted the classic Boy Wonder costume in the exact form it would later take. It was also Harris who coined the sidekick's nickname, noting Bruce's skills: "Since you're brilliant as a robin redbreast in that costume, I'll call you-- Robin!"

In one of the least known chapters of Robin's history in DC Comics, Bruce Wayne didn't just see the Robin uniform worn by another teen after Dick Grayson, but actually adopted another "son" named Lance Bruner. An orphan, entrusted to Bruce after his parents' death.

Lance was basically the opposite of Dick Grayson, competing with his new brother through deceit, manipulation, and outright lying to Bruce. So when Lance's snooping revealed they were acting as Batman and Robin, he took his opportunity to sell both of them out to Gotham's gangsters for his own payday

Thankfully, in the end, Lance's conscience got the better of him, and he arrived on the scene just in time to witness the death of Robin (or so he thought). Believing Dick dead, Lance donned the same Robin costume and took a bullet intended for Batman. It cost Lance his life, and a legacy as the second Robin... which everyone soon forgot about.

Robin, Red Hood, Red Robin, Batman, Wingman, Arkham Knight

Jason Todd assumed the role of Robin following Dick's departure. However, his tenure as Robin was marked by controversy, and DC Comics famously conducted a poll allowing fans to determine if he'd live or die in the A Death in the Family storyline.

Unsurprisingly, the majority of fans voted for his demise, leading to Jason's death at the hands of the Joker. However, that wasn’t the end of Jason Todd, who eventually came back to life via unknown forces. After a dip in a Lazarus pool and training with the League of Assassins, Jason took up the Red Hood mantle.

Batman: The Dark Knight Returns #1 (June 1986)

Chronologically, Carrie Kelley was the third character to adopt the Robin mantle. However, she exists outside mainstream continuity, residing solely within Frank Miller’s alternate universe of The Dark Knight Returns (1986). Kelley made her debut as half of the Dynamic Duo after an aged Batman, fresh out of retirement, rescued her from would-be muggers.

Inspired by his heroics, she acquired a Robin costume and armed herself with a slingshot loaded with firecrackers, thrusting herself into the Dark Knight’s world. Kelley notably played a pivotal role in defeating the resurfaced Joker and later assumed the mantles of Catgirl, Batgirl, and Batwoman.

Tim Drake inserted himself into Batman’s life, assuming the Robin mantle to assist a grieving Bruce, who was becoming increasingly violent after Jason’s death; recognizing that Batman NEEDED a Robin to function properly.

Tim is renowned as the boy genius within the DC Universe, earning accolades from Batman himself, who acknowledged Tim's exceptional intellect, possibly surpassing his own. He has earned the respect of adversaries like Ra’s al Ghul, who dubbed him "Detective," a title previously reserved solely for Bruce. Tim took up the Red Robin mantle after Robin was given to Damian by Dick.

Initially known as the vigilante Spoiler, Stephanie Brown made waves in the Batman universe when she briefly assumed the mantle of Robin, becoming the first female Robin in Gotham's history. However, her tenure as Robin was short-lived and came to an end when she was nearly killed by Black Mask.

Matt Reeves' returning Batman series sets up the debut of its first Robin, and it will be one of the most iconic bearers of the DC mantle.

Surviving the ordeal, Stephanie's death was faked by Doctor Leslie Thompkins in an attempt to get the girl away from Bruce and his child-endangering crusade. Stephanie eventually returned to Gotham, where she later transitioned into the role of Batgirl, taking on a new identity while continuing her crusade against injustice.

Robin, RedBird, Batman, Nightwing, Damian al Ghul

Damian Wayne, the son of Bruce Wayne and supervillain Talia al Ghul, was raised as a child assassin by his mother before becoming the fifth child to take up the Robin mantle. What sets Damian’s Robin journey apart from others is that he was the Robin to Dick Grayson’s Batman, since Bruce was believed to be dead at the time.

As of 2024, Damian is currently Robin and is partnered with his father. Like Jason Todd, Damian also died while serving as Robin and was later brought back to life; upon his resurrection, Damian possessed surprising superpowers for a short time.

Despite varying fandom opinions, Duke did receive an official Robin badge of honor during the We Are Robin storyline. Following an altercation that leaves Duke unconscious, he wakes up believing he's in police custody and is asked what he's willing to do to locate his parents, to which he replies that it's the duty of the police.

Upon leaving the "interrogation," Duke stumbles upon a biker jacket with a yellow R, a cellphone in the pocket, and a motorcycle, signaling his status as a Robin. Duke's eventual inclusion in the Bat-Family further cements his legitimacy as a true Robin. But he'd carve an exciting new path for himself beyond that, too, with new adventures as the Signal to this day.

Duke, along with the previous four most significant Robin title-bearers, was recently featured in Absolute Batman's "Robin Program" assembled by the Joker to fight Batman. They're a heavily-armed, mechanized force with high mobility thanks to mech suits, motorcycles, and more, led by Captain Dick Grayson and overseen by General Slade Wilson. It quickly led to a dark direction with them already losing one in the heat of battle, and Bruce has hardly seen the last of them.

In 2014's Gotham Academy #1, Mia "Maps" Mizoguchi debuted and quickly became known among fans as an honorary Robin. Her deep admiration for Batman led her to adopt the red, yellow, and green of Robin, and she even collaborated with Batman on a case.

Despite never being officially inducted as a Girl Wonder, Maps has won over fans, particularly through her close friendship with Damian Wayne, Batman’s current Robin. Despite her unofficial status, Maps embodies the spirit, detective skills, and intelligence that make her a strong candidate for DC to fully integrate into the Bat-Family in the future.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3510. James Gunn Approves Fan-Made Timeline Showing How Clayface And Blue Beetle Fit In The DC Universe

"Clayface" just expanded the DC Universe, giving fans their first introduction to the franchise's live-action Gotham City. The street-level story proved this still-fledgling cinematic enterprise can encompass an R-rated body horror just as easily as a charming crowd-pleaser like 2026's "Superman." Meanwhile, there are plenty of upcoming DCU movies that aim to similarly expand James Gunn and Peter Safran's shared universe. While the DC Studios co-heads are aiming to avoid the complexity of the erstwhile Snyderverse, you'd be forgiven for losing track of the new in-universe timeline. Now, we have an unofficial attempt to make sense of that very thing — and it's just been co-signed by Gunn himself.

User comicbookcollide posted a list of DC Universe projects on Threads in an attempt to arrange the various films and TV series into a coherent in-universe timeline. Turns out, they were pretty much on the money. Gunn responded to the post, writing, "Timelines give me anxiety, but I think this is pretty good." That's about as solid an endorsement for a fan-made timeline as you could hope for — though it should be noted that Gunn stopped short of fully endorsing the post as fact.

This particular timeline of events slots "Clayface" in as the second DCU event/project, listing the events therein as having occurred in 2021. Meanwhile, comicbookcollide also included "Blue Beetle," the 2023 film which belonged to the now-shuttered DC Extended Universe. This particular film, which Gunn has confirmed is canon to the DCU, is listed as having occurred in 2023 just prior to the events of "Creature Commandos" Season 1 — the official first DCU project. That also puts "Blue Beetle" before "Superman" and after the events of "Clayface," "The Suicide Squad," and "Peacemaker" Season 1.

James Gunn was never going to confirm a fan-made DC Universe timeline as 100% accurate and official. But there might be more to his reluctance to fully endorse comicbookcollide's post. While Gunn has said "Blue Beetle" is canon to the DCU, he also made clear there are a few retcons required to make it fit. The same is true of "Peacemaker" Season 1, which originally debuted while the DC Extended Universe was still running. The show received a particularly conspicuous retcon when Gunn and his DC Studios cohorts re-edited the Season 1 finale to include the Justice Gang rather than the former Justice League. Perhaps the fact that "Blue Beetle" isn't fully canon (but still sort-of is) accounts for why Gunn hasn't fully endorsed the fan-made timeline.

The Wrap previously reported that Jaime Reyes/Blue Beetle actor Xolo Maridueña is set to appear in Gunn's "Superman" sequel "Man of Tomorrow," which would fully solidify his original film as having been retconned into the DCU. But there's no doubt Gunn's approach is a little confusing.

Rather than rebooting DC's cinematic universe entirely, the director has tried to keep aspects of the former DCEU while charting a new course. Thus far, that hasn't been too much of an issue, but this is exactly the kind of esoteric minutiae that can turn off mass audiences and lead to widespread so-called superhero fatigue. As such, it is at least reassuring to see all the various DCU projects laid out in a timeline that Gunn has mostly co-signed, even if it all seemed a bit unnecessary from the beginning.

While comicbookcollide's timeline is fairly comprehensive, it does leave out some DCU events. For example, "Lanterns" Episode 1 began by clarifying the DC Universe timeline, revealing that Earth's first Lantern, Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler), emerged in 1986 and revealed his identity in 1996. This means he had been operating long before the events of "Superman," which took place in 2025. These small but significant developments aren't included in the list posted to Threads, which otherwise does a solid job of making sense of the DCU timeline and combining former DCEU projects (such as the aforementioned "Peacemaker" Season 1, "The Suicide Squad," and "Blue Beetle") into the new chronology.

Meanwhile, Gunn's comment about timelines giving him "anxiety" seems a little baffling. It's his job to stay on top of this stuff and build a shared cinematic universe that maintains a coherent timeline and structure — otherwise DC would just stick with making the so-called "Elseworlds" projects and not worry about the whole interconnected aspect. He also recently appeared on a special "The Suicide Squad: Is It Canon?" podcast, a show specifically designed to clarify how the 2021 movie slots into the DCU and which parts are officially canon. Clearly, Gunn is thinking about these things and has a good idea of how these earlier films mesh with his new vision, to the extent it seems like he enjoys being the only one who really understands it all. Where the anxiety comes from, I'm not sure.

For now, we at least have a better idea of how "Blue Beetle" and "Clayface" fit into the overall plan, and it will be interesting to see how the DCU continues to expand in the coming years.

#3509. Spirit Temple dungeon walkthrough in Ocarina of Time

Travel through time to get through this dungeon

The Spirit Temple is another dungeon that you take on in the future in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake. You're sent to the Spirit Temple to find for Nabooru, the Gerudo's exalted leader.

However, when you get to the Spirit Temple, you quickly learn that you'll have to literally manage your time properly if you want to solve its puzzles and find Nabooru. The Spirit Temple is the first dungeon that you need to go to in the past and the future to reach its end.

Here's how to complete the Spirit Temple dungeon in Ocarina of Time remake.

Before you make your way to the Spirit Temple, we recommend learning the Scarecrow Song and bringing a magic bean and a bug if you want to collect every Gold Skulltula inside and in the surrounding area.

To get to the Spirit Temple, follow the flags in the Mirage Desert until you reach a building. Before you go up the stairs, go around the stairs and drop into the hole. You'll find a Gold Skulltula on the wall. Go back up to the top and read the plaque, which states, "Those with eyes of truth shall be guided to the Spirit Temple by a welcoming specter." Put on the Lenses of Truth, and you'll see the Phantom Guide. Tell them you're ready to go, and follow them closely. The Phantom Guide is a little annoying as they'll take many useless sharp turns, and they'll run through Leevers, which look like cactus monsters. You'll have to stay as close as you can to the phantom and avoid every incoming enemy until you eventually reach the entrance to the Evil Desert Colossus.

Then, head straight and attempt to go into the Spirit Temple. Sheik will stop you and essentially tell you that you need to go against the flow of time to complete the dungeon. They'll also teach you the Requiem of Spirit (L - R - L - A - R - L), which allows you to warp back to the Spirit Temple. So, play the Prelude of Light (X - A - X - A - Y - X) to go back to the Temple of Time, turn back into young Link, and warp back to the Spirit Temple.

Before you head inside, make sure to place a bug on the soft soil on the left side of the Spirit Temple's entrance to get a Gold Skulltula, and then plant a magic bean into it for when you travel back into the future.

Head up the left staircase, and you'll meet Nabooru just in front of a tunnel. She'll tell you that there's a treasure hidden behind the tunnel that can move the huge stones blocking the way on the other side of the temple.

Crawl through the tunnel, and you'll enter a room with a bunch of Keese, Blade Traps, and an Armos. Defeat all the enemies to unlock the two gates. First, follow the path to the left. In this room, you'll face off against a Stalfos, which will take a bit more to beat as your young self. After you defeat them, look to the north, and you'll see a glowing switch behind a wall. Throw your Boomerang to the left side of the wall, and then look to the right side of the wall to direct the Boomerang into the switch. When you hit it, the wall will fall and turn into a bridge. However, a couple of Green Bubbles will also spawn. After you take them out, head to the chest in the corner, but be careful as the pots are actually Flying Pots. Open the chest to get a red rupee and then crawl through the tunnel into the next room.

In this room, Anubis, a floating statue, will be on the opposite side of the room, and its movements will mirror yours as you walk around and attack. To defeat it, you need to hit the eye switch on the northwest pillar, and then jump onto it so that Anubis is in the fire on the other pillar. Make sure to jump from the center of the room though, or else you'll fall into the abyss. After you defeat Anubis, head through the unlocked door.

For this room, you need to collect the five crystals to unlock the door. However, there will be a Wallmaster and a Fire Keese that try to attack you as soon as you walk in. Take out the Keese first, and get out of the spotlight to attack the Wallmaster. Once they've been defeated, grab the crystals on the ground. Then, climb up the walls to grab the crystals in the air.

The wall will drop, but be careful of the Keese on the other side of the wall. Take a step onto the bridge to make the Keese get off the wall, and then take them out with your Fairy Slingshot or Boomerang. There's also a Gold Skulltula on the left wall. Walk onto the bridge and hit it with your Boomerang to collect its token.

Light a Deku Stick with one of the torches, and use it to light the unlit torches. A chest containing a small key will drop from the ceiling. Collect it and go through the door to the south to end up back in the room you started in. Crawl through the tunnel, and use the small key to unlock the door.

Use your Boomerang to hit the Skullwalltulas and climb up the wall. A couple Lizalfos will spawn in the room at the top. Defeat them, and then look at the western wall to see a breakable rock wall. Use a Bombchu to break the wall. If you don't have any, hit the switch to the south, and a chest containing five Bombchus will drop from the ceiling. Light will beam onto the sun on the floor, and the door to the next room will unlock.

In this room, there is a giant statue of a woman with a snake on her head. You'll find a lit torch and an unlit torch in front of her, and a Gold Skulltula on her right. Light the unlit torch, and a chest containing the dungeon map will spawn. Then, collect the Gold Skulltula token.

Climb to the top of the stairs, where you'll find a button and a statue on the platform above it. Climb up the wall and push the statue onto the button to unlock the door.

Head inside and go up the stairs. You'll enter another room where you must collect five crystals to move on, but this time there are a few Beamos hiding about. Blow up the Beamos with your bombs, and then you'll be free to start collecting crystals. First, climb onto the walls around the room to get four crystals. For the last crystal, climb onto the wall in the center of the room, and jump into it. The door to the next room will unlock, but don't head into it just yet.

Pull the cube with the sun on it into the beam of light, and a chest will spawn in the hole in the wall. Open it to get a small key. Now you're free to go into the next room, but immediately turn around to find a Gold Skulltula above the door. Use your Boomerang to collect its token.

Unlock the next room and head inside. You'll see an Iron Knuckle, which looks like a knight with a greataxe, sitting in a chair at the other end of the room, and yes, you need to defeat them to get to the next room. Get close to them, and they'll stand up. Your shield isn't that effective at blocking their attacks, so instead, you'll need to dodge. Because their attacks are so strong, they're also slow to recover, which is a great time to attack. They'll either slam the ground in front of them or sweep their axe to both sides. Backflip away from their attack, and then do a jump attack of your own to close the distance. If you're low on health, bait their attack into the stone pillars. Three hearts will fall from each one, so you can heal enough hearts to take one of their hits. Repeat this until you defeat them.

Open the door to the next room, and go down the path which will take you outside. Open the chest on your left, and you'll get the Silver Gauntlets, the treasure that Nabooru was looking for. Nabooru will greet you outside, but she'll shortly be attacked by Kotake and Koume. As the Silver Gauntlets can only be used by an adult, you'll now have to warp back to the Temple of Time, and return as an older Link seven years in the future. However, after you teleport, Kaepora Gaebora will greet you outside. They've come to say goodbye, as this is the final time you'll see them.

Travel to the future and return to the Spirit Temple by playing Requiem of Spirit (L - R - L - A - R - L). If you planted the magic bean as young Link, you can ride the plant to get a Gold Skulltula and a Piece of Heart.

Go up the right staircase in the Spirit Temple and push the black stone blocking the doorway on the right. Then, hit the switch on the ceiling to unlock the doors.

Head into the room on the left and a Wolfos will appear. Defeat them, and stand on the Triforce on the floor. Play Zelda's Lullaby (Y - X - A - Y - X - A) and a chest will spawn on the platform ahead of you. Longshot to the target below it, and open the chest to get the compass.

Go back into the previous room, and take the path to the right. In this room, there are a bunch of rolling stones, and you need to collect five crystals to unlock the next room. You'll need to jump for the first crystal, but the other crystals can be found in the small alcoves. Before you play the Song of Time to get rid of the time cube blocking the way to one of the crystals, go into the last alcove on the left to find a Gold Skulltula. Then, play the Song of Time, which will move the time cube into the last alcove, but also reveal the final crystal.

Head into the unlocked room, where you'll find a chest and a Like Like. Defeat the Like Like and open the chest to get a small key. Backtrack into the room with the switch and Blade Trap, and use the small key to unlock the door. Two Flying Pots will charge at you and another Like Like will try to eat you. Defeat them and climb up the wall. At the top, quickly put on your Lenses of Truth to spot the invisible Floormaster. Wait for them to run into your shield or the wall, and then attack them and the hands that they split into.

Turn the light into the sun on the eastern wall, and a chest will fall from the ceiling. Then, skip the next sun, as it'll spawn a Wallmaster, and turn the light toward the sun on the southern wall to unlock the door. You can also skip the last sun, as it'll spawn a fake chest.

Head into the next room, which will be the room with the large statue of a woman who has a snake on her head. First, Longshot onto the statue's left wrist (your right). Step onto the Triforce on the hand, and play Zelda's Lullaby (Y - X - A - Y - X - A), which will spawn a chest onto the statue's right hand.

Before you head over, Longshot to the target in the northeast corner of the room, and hit the button with the Megaton Hammer to unlock the door. Then, drop back down to the floor, but don't immediately go to the door.

This time, Longshot onto the statue's right wrist (your left). Open the chest to get a small key, and then play the Scarecrow Song, which will summon Pierre onto the platform above you. Longshot over, and you'll find a Gold Skulltula on the floor. Collect it and drop back down.

Go through the door in front of the statue, and push the large stone block until it falls. Follow the path and do the same with the next stone block, which will create a path back to the starting room.

Head back to the room with the statue, and Longshot to the target above the door in the southeast corner of the room. Go up the stairs and use the small key to unlock the door, but be careful as there will be a Beamos waiting for you in the next room. Throw a bomb at them and head into the next room, where you'll find three Anubis and a Beamos.

First things first, take out the Beamos with a bomb. Then, go to the far side of the room and play the Song of Time (A - L - R - A - L - R) in front of the symbol on the wall. Next, step on the button in the northeast, which will turn on the fire pit. Direct every Anubis into the fire by jumping over to the time cube and walking to the northwest and southwest corners of the room.

Head into the unlocked room, where you'll find a button on the floor and an Armos on one side, and a beam of light on the other. You can't do anything with the sunlight for now, so stick to the side with the button. The Armos will be a monster, so instead of pulling them onto the button, you need to make them jump onto the button. This will turn them back into a statue and unlock the southern door.

Open the door, and use your Lenses of Truth to open the two chests in the hallway to get some rupees. Then, head into the next room, where you'll find another Iron Knuckle, but this time, you're older and stronger. Take them out like you did before, and remember that you can bait their attacks into the pillars to spawn hearts. However, only one heart will drop from each pillar this time.

After you defeat him, go into the next room and follow the path which will take you outside. Step on the button to spawn a chest, and open it to get the Mirror Shield.

Equip the Mirror Shield and return to the room with the sunlight. Hold ZL to lift your shield and step into the sunlight. Reflect it into the sun on the wall above the door to unlock it. Head inside and open the chest to get a small key. Go back to the room where you defeated the Anubis, and use the key to unlock the door.

Blow up the two Beamos, and head inside. You need to climb up the wall, but it'll be shifting from side to side. Use your Longshot on the highest wall and climb up the rest of the way. Two Lizalfos will appear at the top. Take care of them, and Longshot to the tap of the wall like you did the previous one.

Go into the next room, and play Zelda's Lullaby (Y - X - A - Y - X - A) on the Triforce on the floor to unlock the door. Inside, you'll find a bunch of Torch Slugs and a bunch of fake doors. Use your Megaton Hammer to flip the slugs and defeat them. Then, break the door in the northwest corner with your hammer, and you'll find an eye behind it.

Hit the eye with your Longshot or bow, and a wall will fall over, creating a platform. Longshot to the target on the ceiling, and then step on the button to turn off the fire surrounding the chest. Longshot back over, and open the chest to get the boss key.

Return to the previous room and climb up the wall. Go through the door, but be weary of all the pots in this room as they're all Flying Pots. Drop onto the floor and hit the switch to unlock the door above. Open the door, and you'll find a beam of light and a sun on the wall. If you're low on bombs, reflect the light into the sun to spawn a chest that'll give you five.

Defeat the White Bubbles in the next room, and destroy the rock wall. There will be another reflective mirror and two Dinolfos inside. Jump to the side when the Dinolfos are attacking, and hit them until you defeat them. Rotate the light in the previous room, and aim it at the other light contraption. Then, go to the next room and aim the light at the bars.

Follow the light and drop into the hole. Stand on the platform with the sun on it, and reflect the light into the sun on the wall. The platform will drop and stop just in front of the large statue's head. Reflect the light onto the statue's head. Its face will fall off, but it'll reveal a target and the door to the boss room.

Longshot to the target and unlock the door to enter the boss room. You'll find Kotake, Koume, and another Iron Knuckle. Kotake and Koume will leave, and you'll need to fight against the Iron Knuckle. Defeat them like you did the previous two. The Iron Knuckle's armor will fall off, but this time you'll find out that it's actually Nabooru inside. Kotake and Koume will trap Nabooru again, and unlock the door to the next room.

Go inside, but before you climb onto the platform, there are a few things you should know about the fight against the Sorcerer Sisters, Twinrova:

For the first part of the fight, the sisters will fly around the arena, and take turns shooting a magic beam at you. Don't be afraid of their magic though, as you can reflect it with your Mirror Shield. Wait for them to use their magic, and then reflect the beam toward the other sister. If you miss the beam, there will be a patch of fire or ice (depending on which sister cast magic) on the ground. Avoid it and wait for the next magic cast. Repeat this a few times until the sisters combine into Twinrova.

For the second part of the fight, Twinrova will throw fire and ice magic at you, but you need to reflect three of the same type to counterattack. For example, if you block three ice attacks in a row, you'll reflect the attack back at Twinrova, and she'll become vulnerable. However, Twinrova is not guaranteed to cast the same type of magic three times in a row. If you've already blocked two fire attacks, but the next attack is ice, you need to dodge and wait for a fire attack. If you absorb the opposing spell, your shield will lose every charge, so make sure to dodge if the spell isn't the same type. After you reflect the magic, Twinrova will fall onto a platform. Jump over and attack her as many times as you can.

When Twinrova is casting a different type of magic, we recommend waiting on a platform off to the side of the arena, and waiting until she is just about to cast a spell. If it's the same type, you can stay on the platform and block it. If it's not the same type, jump back to the center right after she casts her spell, and her attack will land on the platform off the side. This way, the main area will be free of any ice and fire magic, and you won't have to worry about finding a safe spot to move to.

From here on out, Twinrova will incorporate a new charge attack. For the charge attack, she'll fly to the edge of the room, and quickly charge at you. Roll to the side as fast as you can to avoid her. She will cast this in between her spells, so make sure to keep the center clean of spells to ensure that you can dodge this attack.

As Twinrova is casting her spells, she'll quickly swap between her wands to trick you. She'll lift her fire wand, but then swap to her ice wand and cast ice magic instead. Sometimes, she'll swap multiple times, and other times, she'll lift the same wand multiple times in a row. It can take a while to block three of the same types of magic, so you'll need to dodge a lot. Remember to stay on a side platform to keep the center clean.

The rest of the fight will just be Twinrova either charging at you or casting a magic spell. Continue to block her attacks until you have three of the same spell type, send it back to her, and then attack as many times you can until you defeat her.

Collect the Heart Container and exit the dungeon via the ring of light as usual.

#3508. The 6 Worst Steamy Thriller Movies of All Time, Ranked

A New York native, Joe graduated from an avant-garde theater school upstate, where he was obsessed with sketch comedy. There, he and his lunatic friends founded The Sketchies — which still lives on at Skidmore College today. Living in New York City, a screenwriter friend of his then taught him how to write for film. This awakened a new passion in Joe. Since then his scripts have garnered over 200 festival selections, nominations, and wins all over the globe (including the BlueCat Best Feature award). Several of his screenplays have been made into feature films — some of them not that bad! Overall, he loves to create unique, hilarious, touching, and bizarre stories.

The steamy thriller had its hot and heavy heyday through the 80s and early 90s, with sultry hits like Body Heat, Fatal Attraction, and Basic Instinct. A few modern takes on this sub-genre succeeded in more recent years as well, like Fifty Shades of Grey, Love, and The Handmaiden. However, as with any trend pervasive in the film world, countless imitators of these sensually stimulating, smoldering flicks have emerged, with limited success (for instance, the 50 Shades sequels…).

Here are the absolute worst steamy romance-thrillers ever made, all proudly produced with little to no redeeming qualities. Some of these films focus on what the filmmakers hoped would be a thrilling plot line imbued with arousing scenes of unbridled bliss — while others opted to forgo any attempt at a compelling story and simply showcased extended sequences of gratuitous carnal desires. No matter how they tried to captivate viewers, all these movies failed in flagrant fashion, delivering far more hot air than steam.

While there are more “older woman has affair with younger guy that turns dangerous” movies in the Lifetime thriller catalog than there are fetching fish in the sea, at least those guilty pleasure Lifetime flicks aren’t trying to pass themselves off as real, intellectually stimulating films. The Jennifer Lopez vehicle, director Rob Cohen’s The Boy Next Door, is a laughably corny attempt at erotically-charged thrills that falls flat in pretty much every way conceivable.

Claire Peterson (Lopez) is a high school lit teacher, and a caring mom to her son, Kevin (Ian Nelson). She’s recently divorced from her cheating husband, Garrett Peterson (John Corbett), and, of course, is in a vulnerable state. When Noah Sandborn (Ryan Guzman), a muscular bad boy who boasts the tender age of 19, moves in next door (get it?), the viewer knows that sparks are about to fly. Yes, Claire jettisons her good judgment and gives in to her primal desire for a good romp. She and Noah share a night of passionate May-December romance. Claire comes to her senses and tries to end things there, but Noah ain’t havin’ it. He turns from charming neighbor to deranged stalker almost overnight. The spurned Noah wants to wreck Claire’s life now, and the movie culminates in a ridiculous sequence involving a barn inferno and the classic trope of Chekov’s EpiPen. With a 12% RT score, this movie is borderline dumb, straining credulity at every turn.

Madonna is a tremendous entertainer, that is not in question. Now, her acting ability? Well, in all fairness, she’s had some moments — comedy seems more up her alley than drama, as evidenced by a decent lead performance in Desperately Seeking Susan. However, her bold attempt at a steamy thriller, is a massive fail. Yet, it absolutely must be noted, the blame doesn’t solely rest on Madge’s shoulders. The direction by Uli Edel is borderline at best, the editing feels rushed, and the worst offender may just be the screenwriter, Brad Mirman. This script feels like it was made with A.I. before A.I. was even a thing (using the keywords: cocaine, Madonna, sex, and “fall out window”).

The story initially does hold water. Rebecca Carlson (Madonna) is an alluring woman who becomes involved with a crusty older dude, Andrew Marsh (Michael Forest). As one may ingeniously predict, her heart isn’t exactly pure, and she’s apparently out for his crusty old loot. Rebecca uses her body as a weapon, and basically sexes the feeble-hearted Andrew to death (the ticker can only take so much BDSM fun). Rebecca doesn’t get off Scott-free, and so she desperately needs the help of her lawyer, Frank Dulaney (Willem Dafoe), to help exonerate her. So, voilà, she sleeps with him. But, just when the viewer thinks they have Rebecca's motivations all figured out, a wild twist is introduced. The problem is, this twist is dumb as dirt, and the film’s finale is immensely unsatisfying — resulting in an 8% RT score.

Director Zalman King was really hoping he could cash in on the buzz of his beloved steamy thriller 9½ Weeks, by casting the then hottie Mickey Rourke again and sticking him into another lust-filled story. Alas, he failed — only now, internationally. Wild Orchid is set in Rio, Brazil, a city with the reputation of being quite a hot place, in all definitions of the word. Unfortunately, this histrionic take on the mismatched love story is a cinematic abomination with a 10% critic score on RT.

Soft-spoken real estate lawyer, Emily Reed (supermodel Carré Otis), has to take a trip to Rio to close a big hotel acquisition deal for her client, along with her co-worker, Claudia Dennis (Jacqueline Bisset). While chilling in the “Cidade Maravilhosa,” Emily encounters a wealthy American, James Wheeler (Rourke). Naturally, James knows all the hot, sexy spots in town, and ushers Emily on a verboten, erotic journey of self-discovery. The self-assured sexual puppet master that is James is eventually revealed to have once been a destitute orphan with a stutter — who grew up to be the callous, handsome money-maker he is today. Through their shared experiences in carnal Carnival intimacy, James finally sheds his hard exterior, and he and Emily find true love. Ok, sure. Unlike 9½ Weeks, Wild Orchid doesn’t have much of a story going for it, and has been mostly viewed as an onion paper-thin excuse for mostly unnecessary, silly soft-core action.

Some steamy thrillers are so widely adored that they inspire a sequel. Such is the case with the dismal cinematic detritus that is Basic Instinct 2. Director Michael Caton-Jones and fellow filmmakers surely believed that Sharon Stone’s Catherine Tramell character would be captivating enough to draw audiences in droves. They. Were. Wrong.

The tale sees Catherine relocate to London to start fresh. Right off the bat, she gets into a drug-fueled car wreck that takes the life of a famous footballer, Kevin Franks (Stan Collymore). The court system in England seems just as favorable to Catherine as that of its U.S. counterpart, and Catherine just has to receive treatment for her “danger addict” lifestyle from a forensic psychiatrist, Dr. Michael Glass (David Morrissey). As Catherine slinks her way into his bed, and blows up his personal and professional life in the process, a bunch of adjacent bodies begin to pile up. Without spoiling the “twist” ending too much, it seems that Catherine has once again used her wiles to compel men to do very bad things for her… With a 6% score on RT (hey, at least it’s not zero), this soggy sequel is a mostly flat, wannabe provocative work of forced drudgery.

Four criminal masterminds. One of them was always going to be yours. Here is who comes for you, why they picked you out of everyone available, and what they want from the encounter.

Your nemesis does not want to beat you. He wants to know you completely, and he is patient enough to wait for it. The frightening part is how good the conversation is.

Your nemesis is not after money, territory or revenge. He is after a demonstration, and you are the person he has chosen to prove his point on.

Your nemesis respects you, which sounds flattering until you work out what it means. He chose you because nobody else was worth his time.

Your nemesis has no personal interest in you whatsoever, and that is precisely what makes him unsurvivable. You are not a rival. You are a stop on the way.

This colorful movie almost doesn’t make this list as it is precipitously close to being a “so bad it’s good” flick…yet, alas, here it is. There are so many confounding things about this movie, really from start to finish (for instance, a car that's blindly sent flying off a building’s roof to try to squish the protagonist), but none may be as convoluted and flat-out baffling as the film’s grand finale of nonsensical, endless twists. Indeed, director Richard Rush’s Color of Night is one long sex scene punctuated with one ludicrous plot point after the next.

The gloriously bizarre plot follows a troubled psychiatrist, Dr. Bill Capa (Bruce Willis, with a rare miss), who, after witnessing one of his patients take their own life, suddenly goes color-blind. He catches a flight across the country to L.A., to hang with his fellow headshrinker bud, Dr. Bob Moore (Scott Bakula). However, Bobby is soon murdered, and the prime suspect is one of his group therapy patients. There is a host of hilariously diverse personalities here, and Dr. Bill opts to take over the group sessions while he’s there. Most notably, there is a troubled boy named “Richie” in the group. Now, a nubile young woman, Rose (Jane March), shows up at Bob’s house and soon “befriends” Bill. Also, she has a romantic relationship with another member of the group, Sondra (Lesley Ann Warren). In any event, Bill has wildly graphic pool intercourse with Rose, and then shower sex, and so on. Finally, (spoiler here, but really, who cares) the film concludes with the big reveal that Rose is also Richie, as she has multiple personality disorder…and is also being controlled by her maniacally manipulative brother, Dale Dexter (Andrew Lowery), forced to be complicit in committing murders…for some reason. It’s all so confusing and melodramatically laid out, that it begs credibility and strains logic at every turn. Naturally, Rose goes to the roof to fling herself off, but after a struggle, Bill saves her. And gets his color sight back. Sure, why not.

Oof. As the title implies, this Blanka Lipińska-penned novel turned Netflix movie covers a year of tortuous action. The issue is that it’s more painful for the audience to endure than the main character. Predicated on the ancient idea that “kidnapping can be sexy,” co-writer/directors Barbara Bialowas and Tomasz Mandes’s exploration of forced “love” is what the kiddos today would call the epitome of cringe.

The story follows a wealthy, striking mafia man, Massimo Torricelli (Michele Morrone), who becomes enraptured with a gorgeous, astute and savvy businesswoman, Laura Biel (Anna-Maria Sieklucka). Instead of talking to her, Massimo takes the only logical course of action: kidnap her and compel her to fall madly in love with him. He has a year to convince her that they are soul mates, and if he fails, he’ll let her go (wow, what a gentleman). Laura initially rebuffs his advances, but through a series of manipulative moves enacted by Massimo, Laura eventually succumbs to Stockholm Syndrome and has passionate sex with the Italian stallion. Critics didn’t love the premise or execution, and 365 Days received a 0% Tomatometer score on RT. Audiences were a bit more forgiving, with the film garnering a 36% Popcornmeter rank. The directors at least knew how to exploit the beautiful backdrops of Warsaw and Sicily, along with their leads’ physiques, but make no mistake, this is an offensively bad movie, in every sense. Widely panned for its overtly anti-feminist themes and machismo-centric motifs, this clunker seemed to undo decades of progress. Yet, somehow, Netflix granted it not one, but two sequels, completing a trilogy in true terribleness.

DJI may be best known for its drones and camera equipment, but the company has also been expanding into portable power, with the Power 2000 being its most capable standalone power station yet. Essentially a large rechargeable battery, it's designed to provide electricity wherever you might need it, whether that's on a camping trip, at a job site, during an outdoor movie night, or at home when the power goes out. And if you've been considering one for any of those situations, the Power 2000 is currently down to $749.99 from its original $1,299 price, taking nearly $550 off what would otherwise be a fairly expensive investment.

It's about the size of a carry-on suitcase and weighs close to 50 pounds, so it's not something you'd strap to your back, but it fits easily in a car trunk. The battery itself is built to last, rated for 4,000 charges before it starts losing any noticeable capacity. Performance-wise, DJI says the 2,048Wh capacity can keep a refrigerator running for up to 40 hours during a home power outage, charge a laptop 18 times, or power a projector for 18 hours. Those numbers line up with what you’d expect from a unit this size, and they make it useful for both emergencies and planned outdoor use.

You also get a solid mix of ports—there are three AC outlets, a 30-amp port for heavier appliances or RV setups, multiple USB-C ports (including a 140W option for laptops), and DJI’s own SDC ports for direct drone charging. If you use DJI gear, that alone makes life easier in the field, notes this Mashable review. Recharging is also fast for a battery this size. Plugged into a wall outlet, it can go from empty to full in about 90 minutes. You can also top it up with solar panels or from your car, which makes it workable for longer trips. Rounding out its features is its companion app, which lets you check its battery level from your phone without having to walk over to it, a small thing that turns out to be pretty convenient. Note that this unit has no built-in light, which is something many competing power stations include.

#3506. Bass X Machina Season 2: Renewal Status & Everything We Know

Faith Roswell is a Senior Writer on Screen Rant's Classic TV team. Since earning her degree in Creative Writing over a decade ago, Faith has written articles on film and TV from a variety of different angles. Faith now combines her knowledge of psychology with her love of monster movies to give more insight into what makes the best ones.  You may have read her Screen Rant lists and features covering horror, sci-fi, and fantasy, or read her Amazon Top 10 book, "Movie Monsters of the Deep." Faith has had an extensive career as a writer, appearing on BBC live radio, researching true crime for Rotten Mango podcast, and writing for publications including Mental Floss, Atlas Obscura, and The Daily Jaws before beginning here at Screen Rant.

Great space Western TV shows are surprisingly few and far between, given the cult success of Firefly and the enduring appeal of Cowboy Bebop, so when a new series arrives to the level of critical acclaim that Bass X Machina has seen, it is hardly surprising that fans of the genre are paying attention. Bass X Machina puts an entirely new spin on the story of the real-life Bass Reeves, a formerly-enslaved man who became a legendary deputy US Marshal. His story has already been told in Lawmen: Bass Reeves, but Netflix's space Western combines Taylor Sheridan and Arcane.

Bass X Machina takes a significant amount of creative license, turning its titular character and one of Western TV's greatest lawmen into a modified steampunk hero with a cybernetic arm, a job as a bounty hunter, and a very different family situation to the real Reeves. The show is a historical reimagining in the same vein as Quentin Tarantino's Inglourious Basterds, so fans of historically accurate dramas may not be impressed. However, the series has been groundbreaking, resulting in fans and critics alike wondering if its success will result in a second season.

Netflix has become the home of excellent miniseries, and Bass X Machina looks set to join them, having been presented and marketed as a limited series. Still, many successful miniseries have been unexpectedly renewed, and as Netflix has historically kept plans quiet despite fan speculation, it is not out of the question that a second season of Bass X Machina will be announced. That said, the six-episode series only premiered on November 3, so waiting to see if the show's momentum continues is a reasonable course of action.

Bass X Machina has six episodes, lasting between 29 and 40 minutes each.

Even so, the signs look promising, with Bass X Machina fitting in perfectly with some of Netflix's best animated TV shows. Animation has previously been seen as a creative style aimed at children, but shows like Arcane, Love, Death & Robots, and Cyberpunk: Edgerunners prove that this is far from the case. Bass X Machina is gritty, violent, and yet beautifully animated, impressing both critics and audiences.

Bass X Machina already has a 100% positive Rotten Tomatoes rating from critics, who have praised its theme, tackling the injustices of the West through the eyes of Black and Native American characters, with Roger Ebert highlighting the series for the way it "brings Black justice to the steampunk old West." ScreenRant's review of Bass X Machina described the series as "engrossing as much as it is exciting," highlighting the way the series has enough substance to carry the story, with enough style to make it one of the best looking Western TV shows in years.

Rotten Tomatoes might not yet have enough audience reviews to give the show an official rating, but the signs have been optimistic, with the series' unflinching depiction of both good and bad American history through a steampunk lens impressing viewers. The trailer and first looks were already exciting, with the show's stacked cast and detailed animation attracting interest, but this momentum has grown, with Metacritic rating Bass X Machina 82 out of 100, and fans raising the possibility of a second season.

Bass X Machina has an extremely clever ending, setting the iconic character in the position that most are familiar with by revealing that the series was a stealth origin story. Having shown mercy to Lighthorse, Reeves ends the series as the lawman we know, but positioned for much more. There are now endless options for a second season to develop him as a character, exploring what kind of lawman he intends to be while giving him more intense conflicts to deal with.

As ScreenRant's review highlighted, the one criticism of the series is an issue with pacing. Bass X Machina is a Western TV show that can be binged in a weekend, but it could easily have benefited from another couple of episodes or saving some of its many ideas and themes for use in a second season. Bass X Machina is already a perfect limited series, but the door is open for more, and with such a skilled voice cast and creative team, it would be exciting to see what they do next.

Bass x Machina, released in 2026, is set in a lawless Steampunk West where a father navigates a landscape infested with outlaws, machines, and supernatural terrors. He becomes judge, jury, and executioner to protect his family, though each act of justice threatens to take away those he loves.
