#3492. Will Brill Won a Tony and Got His First Leading Film Role, but That’s Not How He Measures Success

It’s all glamorous — chatting Tony wins and snagging leading roles in movies and sterling New York Times reviews — until your cat needs something. Fortunately, actor Will Brill knows a thing or two about balance, and managed to both a) charmingly answer our many varied queries about his wide-ranging career and b) attend to his yowling tabby’s needs while doing so.

Brill is one of those actors you know, even if you don’t know him by name. One of the “oh, I love that guy!” kind of performers. The kind of performer who shows up and instantly makes things better, or brighter, or somehow richer. His credits are wide and deep — movies like “Caught Stealing” and “Test Pattern,” shows like “The OA” and “The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel,” theater like “Oklahoma” and “Stereophonic” — and things are only picking up for him. Related Stories ‘Cherry & Virgin’ Review: A Fantastic Indie Anime Blends Different Art Styles and a Slew of Pop Culture References into an Innovative Modern Rom-Com Alan Cumming Says ‘Tip Toe’ Was His Greatest Role Ever — but He Never Wants to Think About It Again

In 2024, Brill won his first Tony for the beloved rock musical “Stereophonic,” snagging Best Featured Actor in a Play in a field that included two of his own co-stars. In 2025, he got his first leading role in the film, care of Giselle Bonilla’s darkly hilarious “The Musical.” Not too shabby, right? It gets better.

When Brill spoke with IndieWire, reviews were just hitting for the limited run of “Kramer/Fauci” at St. Ann’s Warehouse. Daniel Fish’s lauded play previously ran at the Skirball earlier this year and, this fall, Brill reprised his role as, yes, that Dr. Anthony Fauci. The creative, thrilling play dramatizes a 1993 C-SPAN call-in show, during which Fauci (then the director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases) and Larry Kramer (the famously outspoken playwright and activist) went at each other over the plans for a new government task force on H.I.V. and AIDS.

“I’m one of those weirdos who will read [reviews],” Brill said with a laugh when asked if he’d been keeping up with the glowing criticism for the show. “I read every single review. I’ve read every review of ‘The Musical’ on Letterboxd. Some would say I’m a glutton for punishment.”

Helen Shaw’s review in the New York Times, he agreed, was not punishment. “I felt auspicious because I knew that Helen Shaw had seen it at Skirball and really enjoyed it,” he said. “But, even so, to say, ‘The most beautiful play I’ve seen all year and I would happily see it 10 more times’ is crazy. I mean, it’s so cool.”

Brill has been doing live theater as long as he’s been acting, getting his start in children’s theater when he was still just a kid in the Bay Area. Process is compelling to him, and he lights up when asked about something as workaday as what he does during the hours between demanding shows.

“It depends on the show a lot, the difference between this show and ‘Stereophonic,’ for instance, is that Stereophonic was a three-hour, 15-minute show where I was screaming and crying most of the times that I was on stage, and this show is an hour long and I never have to raise my voice,” Brill said. “I get to lie down for part of it! Also, for ‘Stereophonic,’ we were in Midtown Manhattan, and for this, I’m in Dumbo, so I get to go outside and sit by the river and read my book, which is dreamy. And then during ‘Stereophonic,’—”

That’s when Curtis the tabby really gets going. “Sorry, my cat is really going through it. Can you hear him?,” Brill said, before darting off-screen to retrieve and present a gorgeous and giant striped feline. “This is Curtis. What is it, baby? He’s screaming. He’s been walking around screaming his head off. Oh, I wonder … I have a robot litter box now and it looks like it is… Sorry, this is such a chaotic morning for me. I think it just needs a reset. Maybe that’s what’s going on with him.”

Yowling cats will keep anyone grounded. In a weird way, so will Tony wins. I asked Brill what changed — or didn’t — after he won his first.

“I think less changed than I sort of expected it would,” he said. “There’s all kinds of legends about what people go through, what changes for people. Oh, my gosh, people love to say, ‘Oh, I thought my entire career was going to change and then I didn’t work for three years.’ And that was certainly not the case for me, but I did have to make a pretty difficult choice about whether or not I was going to go do the show again in London, which I ultimately decided not to do. I had a year where I made less money than I would have, but I did some really rewarding and very challenging things. I starred in a movie for the first time. I had never done that before, so that was really exciting and new and different.”

Bonilla’s feature debut “The Musical” debuted at this year’s Sundance Film Festival and was recently released in theaters and on VOD. It’s a tricky film to explain — it has a twist, sort of, but really just a devilish sense of humor — and Brill loved that. He stars as middle school drama teacher Doug Leibowitz, recently dumped his girlfriend, consumed by his failures as a playwright, and perhaps in the exact right mental headspace to put on an, ahem, shocking new musical.

“I wish I could remember when exactly it dawned on me in the script, because definitely it took me by surprise and it was at that moment where I thought, ‘Oh, I have to do this. There’s no question about this. This is my role,’” he said when asked about the moment he realized what the film was doing with its central musical conceit. “Because it was so exciting and so unlike anything else that I had read. Giselle and I would sneak in to screenings to hear the audience realize what’s happening and listen to them respond to it, and it’s always terribly gratifying.”

We won’t spoil the film here, but suffice to say, Doug and his merry band of middle schoolers put on a show that is based on perhaps the last event you’d ever expect to inspire a musical. The first time Brill saw the film with an audience who had no idea what they were in for, he realized going in cold might be the move.

“I realized that really the best way to experience the movie is with other people not knowing what is coming, because the shock is so crazy,” he said. “And something about the way that it has been finagled is that you are pulled in so many directions, between wanting Doug to fail, but also wanting the children to succeed. It’s such a torrent of things happening that it’s really sort of best to experience with a bunch of other people at the same time.”

The role might have been Brill’s first leading one on the big screen, but he’s no stranger to tough material — or the weight of it. In 2019, he starred alongside Brittany S. Hall in Shatara Michelle Ford’s staggering debut feature, “Test Pattern.” The film follows couple Renesha (Hall) and Evan (Brill) as they navigate a horrific sexual assault and a system not at all equipped to handling survivors with grace.

“They share more DNA than you would think,” he said of Bonilla’s film and Ford’s. “‘Test Pattern’ was the biggest emotional undertaking that I’d ever taken on film before. I was being trusted with a lot by Shatara. They were also a first-time filmmaker, so there was a lot of trust that we were giving to each other, and that was very palpable from the first time we met each other, that we were embarking on something that was pretty untrod territory for both of us and maybe in the landscape of cinema. We both felt tremendous responsibility. We both took it very, very seriously and were asking a lot of ourselves and each other.”

Ford’s film was made “on a shoestring budget” with “absolutely no amenities of any kind,” the actor added. “But that said, it was really rewarding, and everybody showed up really desperate to do well every day,” he said. “Similarly, on ‘The Musical,’ I’m on camera in almost every scene of the movie, so I felt a lot of pressure at the time. I knew that a lot of the success of the thing relied on me, and usually, at least in my career, that’s not been the case. I’ve played a lot of supporting roles, and I know that I can show up for a scene and deliver something special and ultimately get to walk away and say, ‘This thing does not live or die on my performance alone.’ I couldn’t write that off with either of the two movies.”

Brill has also dipped into studio features, including a small but memorable role in Darren Aronofsky’s 2025 crime dramedy “Caught Stealing,” in which he plays a homeless man who offers a surprising key to a complicated story.

“Those experiences are wild, because you walk onyo the set and it’s you and Austin Butler and Zoe Kravitz and Darren Aronofsky,” he said. “And you’re just sort of like, ‘OK…’ It’s a lot of pressure, and it’s a lot of excitement. ‘Test Pattern’ had a crew of 20 people on any given day, and then there were 100 or more people on the set of ‘Caught Stealing’ every time I was there. We were shutting down blocks of New York City traffic for hours in the middle of the night. It was really wild.”

The role might have been firmly supporting, but the experience really stuck with him. “I had two very big votes of confidence while I was working on that movie that I felt really cool about,” the actor said. “One was that when pedestrians got hustled by. on more than one occasion, people were like, ‘Why aren’t they moving this homeless man who’s on the street?’ People had to be like ‘He’s an actor.’ So that felt really good. I got sort of nervous that I was going to be there in the presence of this auteur who was going to be self-serious and formidable and difficult, and Darren was everything you want a director to be. He was so game, he was so fun. He was appreciating the magic of every moment, and he was so supportive of his actors. Every time I did a take, he was like, ‘Oh my God, this is so much fun. I wish we had you for longer.’ It’s very cool to show up to the big game and have it be as cool as you want it to be.”

Brill will round out this year with another supporting turn in a big film. In Sian Heder’s crowd-pleasing biopic “Being Heumann,” he plays Gene Eidenberg, a real-life political adviser who kind of takes the heat when Mark Ruffalo’s Joseph A. Califano Jr. (the U.S. Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare) won’t give much leeway to disability rights activist Judy Heumann and her compatriots during a historic sit-in.

“Sian’s take on the world is so cool, because she has such a good heart and is so funny and fun. The way she sees the world is so filled with light and joy, even when she’s taking on pretty heavy topics,” he said. “I don’t know that I have laughed that much on a set. I can’t remember the last time I did. Sian is so funny and fun, and so is Mark, and so is Dylan [O’Brien]. It was such a joy.”

Heder’s film is remarkable for the way it built actual access into its story about the need for more equitable access for all. Even as an able-bodied actor playing an able-bodied role, Brill felt the power of that.

“I think when the culture is about ‘let’s take care of people and meet needs,’ the work can thrive more,” he said. “I think the camaraderie amongst actors becomes very different. It becomes a lot tighter. There were these group green rooms and dressing rooms that you sort of never get. We had these lounges where we were hanging out and we were able to dissect the day, and that was really lovely. I mean, as with any movie, I think it was still really difficult at times and there are these monumental learning curves, but that’s part of the joy of filmmaking too, is that every single project is a new project. You never stop learning how to make a movie.”

And Brill knows about all kinds of projects. This is the kind of actor who pops up everywhere. A quick glance at his IMDb page is filled with delights — like the year 2017, when he appeared in not only an episode of “Law & Order: SVU,” but also “NCIS: New Orleans.” He laughed when I mentioned that double whammy.

“What was really cool was that I couldn’t have played more different characters,” he said. “I was like a coke dealer who lived in Soho in ‘SVU,’ and in ‘NCIS,’ I was a spirit medium who thought that he was a con artist, but then started actually communing with spirits. ‘NCIS: New Orleans,’ I filmed four days and was in New Orleans for three weeks, so I just had all this free time to explore New Orleans for the first time. It was incredible.”

Brill, it seems, finds value — of all kinds — in every project and part. So, is there some sort of magic balance he wants to strike with his choices? Is there a way to plot this kind of trajectory?

“It’s really tough to say, because there’s no continuity, it always changes,” Brill said. “But I have been lucky enough to really find a family in theater in New York, and so I do feel like it is there for me on some level. There are definitely things that I really want to do. There are challenges that I want to give myself, and I would say that the most open plane for that right now is television. I really want to find out what it’s like to play a character who lives and changes over a decade. I’m desperate for that experience.”

He’d like to be able to do that and still do theater. He added, “I see my friends who are on television shows and are navigating doing theater in their off time. Michael Urie is a huge inspiration in that because he’s such a theater creature, but he’s always been on TV too. So that’s a thing that I think about a lot, is the balance.”

But what he ultimately wants is something a bit harder to pin down, a balance that goes beyond designations like “film” or “TV show” or “theater,” the kind of spot that values experience in all its shapes. And, yes, probably the kind of space in which spending time with his cat is just as rewarding as a varied resume and making stuff with friends.

“I feel like life is long and I’m here for the challenge, and I’m going to get to do all of it. I’m just biding my time,” Brill said. “I feel like nowhere more than in this industry does the aphorism apply of ‘if you want to make God laugh, make plans.’ I’m down to ride the wave and let things come as they come. The most rewarded and fulfilled I’ve ever felt in this industry are the projects that are born out of tight-knit groups of friends or where tight-knit friendships are made, because what we do is storytelling, and storytelling is about creating and solidifying community. I think the thing that I will always keep wanting to do is telling stories with close friends, whatever the medium is. That’s the thing I want to do most.”

Apple will release “Being Heumann” in select theaters on Friday, November 6 and on Apple TV on Friday, November 13. A Blue Harbor Entertainment and Variance Films release, “The Musical” is currently available to rent or buy digitally on major streaming and VOD storefronts.

#3491. ‘Being Heumann’ Review: Siân Heder’s ‘CODA’ Follow-Up Is an Essential Biopic That’s Not Afraid to Have Some Fun

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 10, 2026 during the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Apple will release the film in select theaters on Friday, November 6 and on Apple TV on Friday, November 13.]

When Siân Heder’s “CODA” premiered at Sundance in 2021 (during the festival’s online-only “pandemic year” and months and months before the film would go on to win Best Picture), it became an early favorite of mine. Mostly, I wrote in my review, though the “drama is marked by familiar beats, its characters bring new dimension to a staid genre.” The same can be said about Heder’s follow-up feature, “Being Heumann,” which brings real life back to the biopic, not only through innumerable compelling characters, but the smart choice to tightly focus this story on one essential moment in the life of the activist Judy Heumann. Related Stories Will Brill Won a Tony and Got His First Leading Film Role, but That’s Not How He Measures Success ‘Cherry & Virgin’ Review: A Fantastic Indie Anime Blends Different Art Styles and a Slew of Pop Culture References into an Innovative Modern Rom-Com

When we first meet Judy (Ruth Madeley in a true star turn), she’s zipping along a busy New York City street in 1972. That might sound fun, but for Judy, it’s just the way things are; a wheelchair user since she was just a toddler (thanks to an early bout with polio), the world is not made for people like Judy, and she makes her way through it however she can. Often, that means doing things like, oh, zipping down city streets, because there are no curb cuts to assist her in smoothly moving from sidewalk to sidewalk. As Judy goes barreling down the street, people stare, drivers yell, and the brassy Brooklynite throws up a finger.

That Judy has natural presence is a given, but the central question of Heder’s film — which she adapted from Heumann’s autobiography alongside co-writer Rebekah Taussig — is how she will use all that verve to truly enact change. It’s the sort of concern that has always impacted great leaders, and suffice it to say, Heumann was indeed a great leader. But while Heumann’s long, storied life had many incredible chapters (she passed away in 2023, two years after she started working with Heder on the film), the filmmakers smartly zero in one on seminal slice of life to craft “Being Heumann.” Cradle to the grave this is not, but the film still succeeds mightily when contextualizing Heumann’s role in the disability rights movement and her singularity as a true American original.

That’s not to say that the period of time covered by the film — which soon jumps ahead five years — isn’t complicated and dense. The film opens in 1972, because that’s when Judy and eighty other activists staged a sit-in on Madison Avenue to protest the vetoing of Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, which we’re told was one of the very first pieces of federal legislation meant to guarantee certain rights to people with disabilities (from accessibility to education). The act was eventually signed in 1973, but when the film picks back up in 1978, it has not been implemented. It needed one last step: a signature from newly-installed Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare Joseph Califano (Mark Ruffalo). And he wasn’t signing.

Heder and Taussig’s script distills the legal wrangling down well: this piece of legislation will help bring about massive positive change for the disabled community, but it will cost a lot of money, and Califano has already been asked to slash the budget. These are excellent stakes.

Judy doesn’t care about the cost to the government — why should she? — but she does care about the cost to her community. A seasoned and dogged activist, most of the people in Judy’s life are disabled in some way, and it’s her mission to a) wrangle them into action and b) be pretty pushy about it. Heder and her casting directors Bernard Telsey and Adam Caldwell have assembled a wonderful, winning cast around Madeley (herself a wheelchair user), including a number of disabled performers, cast here as icons in their own right. Standouts include Madeline Delp as Kitty Cone (the honey to Judy’s vinegar), Andrew Pilkington as Hale Zukas, Antwan Tolliver as Brad Lomax, “CODA” star Daniel Durant as Steve McCleeland, Roberta Colindrez as Joni Breves, and instant star Charlie Rush-Reese as Dennis Billups.

That Heder would cast actually disabled people in these roles should seem obvious (this is the filmmaker behind “CODA,” after all), but there’s no question that it totally pays off all the same. The wide array of performers on offer here is thrilling, and it’s a treat to see them all settling in so well to this period world, rendered tactile and realistic by smart costuming choices by Danny Glicker and unfussy production design by John P. Goldsmith.

Enraged over the lack of movement on the signing of 504, Judy and her compatriots launch a series of protests around the country, focused on federal buildings that house HEW offices. Califano, stuck back in DC, can only hear about these events as they unfold, utterly stymied but what to do, paralyzed by fear for his job, and intent on reminding people he’s one of the good guys (he supported the Selma marches!). But the world has changed. When Judy somewhat impulsively leads a pack of protesters inside the SF federal building, what follows will only spark further change.

Despite the historical implications that follow — the SF sit-in became one of the country’s largest — Heder doesn’t noodle on the cultural vegetable aspect of this story. Instead, “Being Heumann” becomes something unexpectedly frisky and fun. The sit-in comes with plenty of challenges (beyond the myriad needs of the disabled community, there’s in-fighting to spare, government pressures galore, and deep worries about how it might actually pan out), but there’s also a streak of joy that runs through it. It’s thrilling to see people doing literally whatever they can for their well-being, and having a good time in the process (yes, you’ll get acquainted with their “sex tents” soon enough). There are almost too many colorful characters here, a sprawling ensemble in which everyone deserves their own film, though we occasionally lose some threads along the way.

That isn’t always easy for Judy, though, who remains set in her ways even as she sees real change happening around her. Madeley captures the real Judy Heumann’s energy beautifully; she’s funny and flinty and spiky and smarter than anyone else around her and totally driven by her sense of justice and equality. But that’s not always enough, a lesson that “Being Heumann” is not shy about. Fighting for what’s right involves just that, fighting. Sometimes, that even means fighting your own instincts.

A film like ”Being Heumann” is destined to be called rousing — a call to action that’s every bit as entertaining as it is inspiring. It’s a film about tough choices and even tougher circumstances, but it’s also about the tangible good that can come from people working together. What could be more joyous than that? More biopics could learn from this formula, and from this feeling. Be more like Judy: be tough, but never be afraid of joy.

“Being Heumann” premiered at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Apple will release it in select theaters on Friday, November 6 and on Apple TV on Friday, November 13.

#3490. ‘Club Kid’ Review: Jordan Firstman’s Brazen, Funny, and Surprisingly Earnest Directing Debut Is a Wild Party Movie with Heart

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on May 15, 2026 during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. A24 will release “Club Kid” in theaters on Friday, November 6.]

Ask any gay man with a social media account, and they likely have an opinion about Jordan Firstman. The backlash-courting queer actor/comedian, controversial most recently because of an online flare-up over querying the sexual realism of “Heated Rivalry,” is labeled either candid or confrontational. He also has a record of taking on sexually explicit projects like Sebastian Silva’s suicide-ideating, ketamine-fueled dark comedy “Rotting in the Sun.” His status as a self-aware, hyper-online provocateur may not seem to suggest the makings of a bona fide filmmaker, but just wait. Related Stories ‘Being Heumann’ Review: Siân Heder’s ‘CODA’ Follow-Up Is an Essential Biopic That’s Not Afraid to Have Some Fun Will Brill Won a Tony and Got His First Leading Film Role, but That’s Not How He Measures Success

While that reputation might have Firstman on guard as he debuts his feature writing/directing debut “Club Kid,” as it will certain circumspect corners of the audience, this terrific movie should put any of those nervous feelings to rest. Even his haters won’t be able to resist what’s announced here as a major filmmaking talent with a sensitive side that belies his brash, internet-based persona.

He also stars as the protagonist of his hugely crowd-pleasing, excruciatingly funny, and poignant first film — one that plays to all sides of the room despite being brazenly, unapologetically queer — which will prime Firstman-savvy viewers to immediately interpret “Club Kid” as autobiographical. That’s because it is.

He plays party promoter Peter, now in his thirties after a decade-plus of MDMA-addled revelry, the kind where all the days blur and blot into one long and sweaty night with a coming horizon in the shape of regret. Firstman may not be playing himself this time, but he is playing a version of that self, having, as he says, spent enough years in Berlin to be labeled “the angel of Berghain” by his new friends, but now ready to put the days-that-became-years of GHB, MDMA, and other letters of the alphabet behind him.

“Club Kid” is exactly about what happens when the lights go up on the party, the shameover of the morning after that becomes a way of being, and the need to do it all over again to stave off last night’s aching after effects. But it’s also about — earnesty alert! — family lost and found, not only because of the queer community formed around the now-orphaned Peter, who lives in the rent-controlled Manhattan his mother left him after she died, but because he wakes up one day to find a child he fathered and never knew about, literally on his doorstep.

“Club Kid” was shot on 35mm on location in New York City with a team of backers including “Anora” Oscar-winning producer Alex Coco and nepo filmmaker Olmo Schnabel, and a millennial cast of queer comedians. So it’s hard not to leave the movie thinking all that’s needed here is an A24 logo slapped onto the opening credits, and it’s ready for the world. But no matter; while Firstman’s aesthetic is loudly in A24’s register, it turns out to be an asset rather than a limitation.

Beginning inside a sensually lit, drug-soaked party and ending as one rages on without you from afar, “Club Kid” drops us into Brooklyn 2016. Peter, sing-screaming Rihanna’s “Sex with Me” in a clown car of an Uber ride with his friends, is headed into yet another bender to remember (but also eventually forget). At a club of the sort that now dominates night culture in Bushwick, rising party promoter Peter ends up hooking up — and then really hooking up — with a couple of hyperactive “innit, babes?” British women in the back room. It’s all inconspicuously taking a turn for the sexual when the movie smash cuts to “a decade or so later,” when the proverbial party is still dying down, but Peter is still living in it — albeit more sweaty and tragic 10 years on.

He’s now made a career out of his drug use with his best friend and business partner Sophie (a marvelous, perpetually coked-out Cara Delevingne, who’s two inches from a breakdown at all times). A few days before the one that’s about to change his life, they have an important sit-down coming up with FiDi investors to help expand their New York party empire. But alas, as he couldn’t help himself once again the night before, Peter wakes up drugged to the gills, rushing to the meeting only to nod off at the table, still in a GHB-spiked stupor. (His reaction to a dropper of hot sauce that looks curiously similar to the one he used last night to get high is one of the film’s many brilliantly funny little pratfalls.)

All of that’s to say Peter’s life is still totally a mess, and his arrested development from a decade of partying has now washed him out to the point where sobriety is maybe never part of his day. (A weekend spent dissipated, hungover, jerking off to internet porn and eating Popeye’s in bed rings painfully true.)

Party’s certainly over, though, when one of those British “innit babes” from 10 years ago, Edison (Kirby Howell-Baptiste), shows up from London at his apartment (where Peter lives with an “Azerbaijanian aspiring queer philosopher” who doesn’t pay rent) with an eight-year-old boy. “You’ve got a kid! ‘Yay!,’” she tells him while delivering the news that Arlo (preternaturally gifted young breakout actor Reggie Absalom) is in fact Peter’s child with one of the other women from that opening-scene heterosexual encounter, who’s just died. The first and only time Peter fucked a woman, and now he’s fucked himself into having to finish raising a small boy.

Cue the manic panic, more drug use, and resignation to the idea that there’s no sending this kid back to the U.K.

While it’s a bit sudden how fast the switch flips from Peter feeling wildly ill-equipped for parenting to becoming a nurturing caretaker, he and Arlo turn out to have more in common than not. Arlo, for one, has the music taste of someone who grew up on Pitchfork, eagerly taking to the $300 Elliott Smith record Peter buys for him in a later scene. (The soundtrack on this thing, by the way, rules, from Arthur Russell during the film’s melancholy final act to “The White Lotus” composer Cristobal Tapia de Veer’s deeply felt original score.) Their relationship, however quickly, becomes the film’s so-far unexpected sweet center, as Peter starts to really appreciate and eventually love Arlo, who has traumas of his own.

A lot of the success of “Club Kid” rides not only on Firstman’s shoulders, but also on the collaborators he’s working with, including cinematographer Adam Newport-Berra who captures a certain lost-era grit in New York as well as in the chaos-packed nightclub sequences. “Club Kid” also takes advantage of New York City as not just a backdrop but a central character in the storytelling, using the city in a way that feels rare onscreen these days.

“Club Kid” freewheels and unwinds like a head rush of a zippy party movie until Arlo’s introduction brings the comedown. It turns out he feels more at home among Peter’s “found family” of queer revelers, discovering his own DJ skills in the process, than he ever did in London. Could Peter really warm to fatherhood? Real emotional stakes start to heighten as he begins recognizing the unexpected realities of his new arrangement, like getting Arlo into school, or keeping the boy shielded from the drug use of his friends while Peter’s own finally starts to diminish. A nervous, tentative romance comes into view with child psychologist Oscar (Diego Calva), and on a date where a namecheck of Gregg Araki’s “Mysterious Skin” becomes not just a tender confession, but a turn-on.

“Club Kid” takes a sharp dramatic turn, in which the nature of Arlo’s living situation becomes even more dire and probably illegal, that almost shouldn’t work in a comedy like this — but it’s a turn that feels inevitable given how “Club Kid” is structured like the rise and fall of a drug experience, a high that crashes down into despair. The emotional arc bends toward “Kramer vs. Kramer” territory with a cathartic (and well-played by Firstman) courtroom oner. Peter may be insecure about his own place in a world where only parts of it have room for him, but as a storyteller with an eye, Firstman is anything but.

Firstman is by now an established comedic voice, but his work on all sides of the camera here leaves pretty of room for revelation, for him to become a genuine discovery beyond an audience of gay, internet-addled millennials. “Club Kid” has real potential to break out bigger than its seemingly niche scope would suggest, with Firstman finally shirking the ironic pose he’s taken online for years to emerge as a sincere storyteller with heart as much as humor.

“Club Kid” premiered at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. It is currently seeking U.S. distribution.

#3489. These Are the Best Arc Browser Alternatives, Now That It's Shutting Down

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

Well, it happened: The Browser Company has finally announced that it will be sunsetting the Arc browser before the end of 2026. The writing has been on the wall for well over a year now: Arc had already been put on ice, receiving only maintenance updates after the Browser Company switched its focus to Dia, an AI browser that shares Arc’s framework but lacks the wonderful interface features that made Arc such a joy to use.

This is sad news for the Arc faithful. If you're one of them, or if you’re looking for an alternative to the regular browsers like Safari and Chrome, all hope is not lost. Export your Arc data, and try out one of these Arc-like alternatives.

Zen has become the de facto option for all users looking to find something that looks and works like Arc. In some ways, it’s better than Arc; in some ways it falls short.

I’ve been using Zen for months, and I’m quite happy with it. The only downside I can see is the Firefox web engine; while Gecko has come a long way, it can still sometimes fall short of Chromium, mostly because Google Chrome is such a popular browser, most websites are designed to run best on it. When I run into an issue with a website, I tend to switch to Chrome for a while. Zen can also sometimes be a memory hog, but once I got better at tab hygiene (automatically closing older tabs and being vigilant about workspace management), the experience got quite a bit better.

And yes, there is extension support: Anything that runs on Firefox will run here too. Firefox has most of the important extensions covered, and it’s the only major browser that still supports the full-scale uBlock Origin ad blocker (which works like a treat in Zen, too).

Alternatively, you can go to the opposite end of the spectrum and try out a maximalist browsing approac:. For a while, Microsoft Edge was the cleaner, faster, better version of Chrome, but now, that title goes to Vivaldi. Under the hood, Vivaldi uses the same Chromium engine that powers Google Chrome, so all your websites will work as expected, and all the extensions will be familiar. But Vivaldi is an extremely customizable browser, and for a certain kind of user, it might be the perfect fit.

There are tons of built-in features. It comes with an ad blocker and integrates with ProtonVPN for free, limited VPN access. You can add a free reader, email accounts, note-taking, and a calendar to the sidebar. Using the Web Panels feature, you can dock any website to the sidebar as well (this works well for media and messaging sites).

Vivaldi also has robust tab management features: You can use two websites in split screen (like with Zen and Arc), and you can organize tabs in workspaces. You can also group related tabs in Tab Stacks, Vivaldi’s unique two-level tab management system. One thing Vivaldi lacks by default is a vertical sidebar, which even Firefox and Chrome now support, though it can be added using a mod.

If you want to keep to a Chromium-based browser, but one that offers all the customization features you can think of, go for Vivaldi. At its core is a powerful, fast, and reliable browser that you can slowly remake to be your own.

Helium: Think of it as a minimalist version of Google Chrome. Same Chromium engine, but no Google tracker, no popups, ads, or extra features.

Dia: If you really want to use something that’s built by the same team as Arc, and don’t mind the AI features, you can try the Dia browser as well. It’s not an exact replacement, but Dia now has an option to use a vertical sidebar and pinned apps.

Quiche: If you were using Arc on iPhone or iPad, try using the Quiche browser, which is our favorite browser for the iPhone. It’s a tastefully designed independent browser, with a fully customizable layout.

#3488. All bottle locations in Ocarina of Time

Store all of your valuables... like this bug!

Bottles are one of the many items that Link carries around in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake.

Bottles are extremely valuable, as they allow you to store things like potions, fairies, bugs, and Lon Lon Milk. You can use your stored items at any time you wish, meaning you can drink your red potion or Lon Lon milk if you're just about to die. However, bottles can be hard to come by, as you'll need to go a bit out of your way to find them.

Here's where to find every bottle in Ocarina of Time remake.

In Ocarina of Time remake, you can have up to five bottles at once, which is one more than in the original game.

You can find a bottle in the following locations:

For more information on how to get every bottle, check out the sections below.

You can get the first bottle at the Potion Shop in Hyrule Castle Town. On your first visit to the shop, the Potion Shopkeeper will be panicking about a bug that escaped. They'll give you an empty bottle to catch the bug skittering around. Press R and swap to the empty bottle. Then, walk over to the bug on the floor and press ZR to scoop it up. As a reward, he'll give you a red potion. If you drink the potion, it'll just turn into an empty bottle, which you can use to store other things like another bug.

After you wake up Talon outside of Hyrule Castle, he'll run back home to Lon Lon Ranch. Go to his house during the day, and you'll find him asleep on the floor. Talk to him and he'll ask if you want to play his cucco-findin' game, where you have to find three super Cuccos within 30 seconds.

Before you start, look at the three Cuccos behind Talon, which are the three super Cuccos. They'll periodically lift their wings into the air and let out a cuckoo. To find the super Cuccos during the game, you'll need to quickly look around the room to find the three Cuccos that do the same action, and pick them up.

When you're ready to start, pay Talon 10 rupees, and watch the super Cuccos fly away behind him. The direction they go is indicative of where they are in the room. To make things easier, each super Cucco flies farther than every other Cucco, so you'll find them in their respective corners of the house. Quickly look to the southwest corner, northwest corner, and northeast corner, spot the Cucco that lifts their wings, and pick up them. Additionally, after the super Cuccos fly away, they'll always start off facing the wall.

If you complete the challenge, you'll earn a bottle full of Lon Lon Milk. If you fail, you can immediately retry for five rupees, but if you leave and come back, you'll need to pay full price.

For those who have played the original, you unfortunately cannot throw the Cuccos away before the game starts, so you'll need to find them the hard way.

The third bottle is given to you by the Cucco Lady in Kakariko Village. After you talk to her, you'll learn that she's missing all seven of her Cuccos, and it's up to you to return them to their pen. Every Cucco can be found in Kakariko Village, but some of them are a bit trickier to retrieve.

In the map above, we've marked the locations of every missing Cucco, but the Cuccos do like to roam around a bit. Well, except for Cucco #2 as they're trapped in a box. For Cucco #5, 6, and 7, you'll need to use another Cucco to reach them. After you return every Cucco to the pen, the Cucco Lady will give you an empty bottle.

The fourth bottle is found in Lake Hylia. First, progress through the story until you unlock the Silver Scale at the Zora Domain. Then, dive into the shortcut that takes you from the Zora Domain to Lake Hylia. If you look underwater in front of you, you'll see a bottle that has a bunch of air bubbles coming out of it. Dive into the water and grab it to find Ruto's Letter, but more importantly, a bottle!

The fifth bottle is the hardest to get out of all the bottles. To get this one, you'll need to hunt down five Big Poes as adult Link. Look out for the lanterns scattered around Hyrule Field and jump over them with Epona. You can find the lantern and Big Poe locations in the map above.

A Big Poe will spawn, and you need to hunt them down. You can either hit them with two arrows or one Light Arrow, and they'll turn into a yellow ghost orb. Bottle them up, and take them to the Poe Collector, who has made the old guard room in Hyrule Castle Town his storefront.

As soon as you enter Hyrule Castle Town, turn right, and you'll find the entrance to his shop. Sell five Big Poes to him for 30 rupees each, and he'll give you 500 points and an empty bottle. If you turn in all 10 Big Poes, they'll reward you with a gold rupee, which is worth 200 rupees!

#3487. 34 Years After Aladdin Hit Cinemas, Disney Confirms Bizarre New Lore

Aladdin has always been one of Disney’s most beloved classic films and continues to draw in both new and returning fans, even decades after its release. However, what many viewers may not know is that there’s a new comic book installment that continues the series while expanding the universe in unexpected ways.

Published by Dynamite Entertainment on November 4, 2026, Aladdin #4 shares a bizarre development that fans likely didn’t see coming. For just a short moment, it takes the iconic Genie somewhere he has never been before, crossing paths with unlikely characters that are far removed from Agrabah, and it’s not only entertaining, but also undeniably fitting for Genie.

The Aladdin comics currently have four issues, all of which are written by James III and illustrated by Agnese Eterno. The fourth and most recent issue follows the people of Agrabah after the city is trapped inside a glass bottle. With panic spreading among citizens, Princess Jasmine steps up to take charge while Aladdin and Genie search for a way to save their home from the outside.

While the central conflict centers on the city’s predicament, the issue also includes a quick, unexpected development involving Genie that reveals the universe Aladdin takes placein is far bigger than anyone expected. One page early in the issue follows Genie as he finds himself careening through the cosmos, where he comes into contact with extraterrestrial life in a spaceship as he passes by.

The moment is a quick, humorous detour that doesn’t have a major impact on the issue’s central plot, but it does establish that the universe is much larger than anyone imagined. Until now, Aladdin has only been known for magic, grand kingdoms, and fantastical adventures rather than anything sci-fi-related.

That said, the development is also extremely fitting for Genie, given that he has always existed beyond the bounds of the ordinary. After Aladdin’s wish to set him free, it’s only natural that Genie would have unexpected adventures and encounters, even if those take place somewhere out in the cosmos. In fact, this small moment arguably encapsulates Genie’s legacy in the franchise as limitless and full of possibility.

Even before being freed from the lamp, Genie had always existed somewhere beyond traditional limitations, making him an extraordinary character, even in a world filled with sorcerers and magic flying carpets. Even his personality adds to how boundless he truly feels, and this subversive portrayal reflects Disney’s history as well, because Genie defied the conventions of his time.

Genie stood out from other Disney characters for a variety of reasons. Brought to life by the legendary Robin Williams, Genie constantly incorporated contemporary references and celebrity impressions, along with plenty of fourth-wall breaks and improvised performances. At the time, Disney was still known for classic fairy tales and a more traditional storytelling approach, making Genie’s character completely revolutionary.

One of Disney's most beloved movies gets a five-chapter prequel spinoff that expands a villain's backstory right before the events of the film.

Beyond that, he was far from just a simple comic-relief character. Genie had a deeply meaningful arc surrounding his desire for freedom, driving him to enter a transactional agreement with Aladdin that ultimately led to the film’s emotional climax when Genie’s cuffs were finally gone, allowing him to live as he wished.

This journey makes Genie feel truly larger-than-life, and his experiences after the film continue to mirror that. While Genie’s brief encounter with alien life might be little more than a passing moment in the latest comic, it truly does capture his character’s lasting appeal and seemingly limitless reach within the story. Even decades after he was introduced in Disney’s Aladdin, Genie continues to defy expectations and push the boundaries of every story he’s in.

#3486. Ben Affleck’s New 106-Minute Thriller Clings to Streaming Crown

He has covered everything from Marvel to the Oscars, and Marvel at the Oscars. He also writes obsessively about the box office, charting the many hits and misses that are released weekly, and how their commercial performance shapes public perception. In his time at Collider, he has also helped drive diversity by writing stories about the multiple Indian film industries, with a goal of introducing audiences to a whole new world of cinema.

Despite having received the worst reviews of his filmmaking career, Ben Affleck's new political thriller has emerged as a bona fide hit for Netflix. The streamer is currently undergoing a major change-up behind-the-scenes, but Affleck's film marks a culmination of a new strategy to pivot away from mega-budget tentpoles and focus on mid-budget genre titles.

Over the course of 2026, Netflix has released a string of smaller-scale hits, several of which have hit the coveted 100 million views mark. After having topped the streamer's viewership charts for four weeks in a row, Affleck's new movie is on its way to hitting the milestone as well, despite some less-than-flattering reviews.

The movie in question follows a Los Angeles mayoral candidate who finds himself in a moral dilemma when his son is kidnapped. The film shares the same premise as Akira Kurosawa's classic drama High and Low, which inspired a Hollywood remake only a few months ago. This time last year, director Spike Lee reunited with Denzel Washington on the Apple TV film Highest 2 Lowest, which received more positive reviews than Affleck's version.

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your life would be like.

You do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he. What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the plan.

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she. Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with yourselves.

You have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this list.

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

We're talking, of course, about Animals. The movie appears to have settled at a 29% score on the aggregator website Rotten Tomatoes, where the consensus reads, "Despite all the makings of an enticing story, including a compelling Kerry Washington, Animals’ weak writing prevents it from reaching its full potential." By comparison, Lee's Highest 2 Lowest holds a "Certified Fresh" 83% score on the aggregator. Despite the mediocre reviews, Animals added 4.7 million views in the week of October 26 to November 1.

In its previous three weeks of release, the movie generated 23.8 million views, 30.8 million views, and 10.7 million views. This takes the film's total viewership to 70 million in four weeks. This year, Netflix has released a string of genre movies that have passed 100 million views; this list includes War Machine, Thrash, and Apex, with The Last House having generated more than 90 million views and The Whisper Man sitting at more than 80 million views. Netflix calculates total viewership based on a title's performance in the first three months of its release, meaning that Animals has two more months to go before the counting stops.

Animals is streaming now on Netflix. Stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

#3485. The Newest Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition Is Finally Worth the Extra Money

I love e-readers, but I'd be the first to admit that as far as the general public is concerned, they are just about the least exciting tech devices around—and that goes double for the Amazon Kindle. Any attention the space has gotten over the past couple of years has involved obscure players like Boox and weird concepts like the phone-shaped Palma or the tiny Boox Picco. But the clear leader in terms of market share is still Amazon, and despite some minor innovations over the years, the device hasn't received an essential upgrade in around a decade: A Kindle is a Kindle is a Kindle.

I'd still say this holds true in 2026, even after the company unveiled a complete redesign of the Kindle lineup (this, a few months after significantly raising prices across all of the devices). While the new flush-front display is nice-looking (and Amazon is quite proud of the new process it has developed to add colored bezels by painting them directly onto the outer glass screen), competitors have offered similar designs for years, and it's hard to get too excited about "innovations" like an $80 case that adds back the physical buttons that used to be built in or finally opening up the firmware to allow for the use of a Bluetooth page-turn remote.

But one thing has changed about the 2026 Kindle lineup: I think the $50 premium Amazon charges for the top-of-the-line Signature Editions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft is finally truly justified.

Amazon introduced the first "Signature Edition" of the Kindle Paperwhite back in 2021, and while the 25% price increase didn't get you nothing, the features it did add weren't too exciting: At 32GB, it had three times the storage versus the standard Paperwhite, but how important is a ton of storage when most e-book files are tiny? (That's still enough room for more than 6,000 texts, well more than even true bookworms will read in an entire lifetime.) Other bonuses, like wireless charging and an auto-adjusting front light, won't matter at all to a huge subset of readers, and it's hard to think of "no ads on the lock screen" as an extra perk.

But the latest Signature Editions of the Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft actually give you more for the price premium, and for the first time, I would recommend shelling out the extra cash. While the important specs are still the same as the standard model:

7-inch, 300ppi flush-front display (with color content on the Colorsoft maxing out at 150ppi)

USB-C charging with battery life "up to 12 weeks on a single charge," per Amazon

Bluetooth support for wireless headphones

...the Signature Editions give you quite a bit more this time around, including, most noticeably, a totally new design with an all-metal rear panel that gives the devices a much sleeker look and feel without adding much in the way of weight (the standard plastic models weigh around 7.2 ounces, while the Signature Editions weigh 8.1 ounces). The new design makes the Signature Editions feel truly premium.

But that's not the only meaningful addition. Once again, alongside wireless charging and automatically adjusting lighting, the Signature Editions have a boosted 32GB of storage, which is still probably overkill, but worthwhile if you like to load your device with a bunch of audiobooks or (in the case of the Colorsoft) color comics.

You also get an accelerometer, which means the display will auto-rotate if you flip it upside down, giving you more flexibility in how you hold it (especially if you're springing for the new Page-Turn Cover, which brings back physical buttons à la the beloved, discontinued Kindle Oasis). Moreover, there's a new ability to turn pages by double-tapping on the bottom sides or back of the device rather than touching the screen (though it only works for moving forward in your book).

Speaking of which, you'll need to go for the Signature Editions if you want to use accessories like the Page-Turn Cover or the also-new Charging Stand (not yet available for pre-order), as only the Signature Editions include the built-in magnetic pogo pins you'll need to connect them. (If you're interested in the Kindle Click page-turn remote, it at least works with any Kindle from 2024 or later.)

Finally, if you care about your Kindle looking pretty, it's worth noting that only the Signature Editions are available in Seaglass Green (for the Paperwhite) and the reddish-purple Plum (for the Colorsoft).

Outside of those extras, the 2026 Kindles don't feel much different than the 2024 models. According to Amazon, they are the fastest Kindles ever, but that's mostly hype—any recent Kindle will turn pages quickly enough that you'll barely notice the speed difference, if you notice it at all. They all still run on the same firmware, which is both a good thing (Amazon makes it extremely easy to browse for and buy books and audiobooks directly on the device; there are a ton of options to search through and sort your library; and quality-of-life features like being able to sideload books via email using the "Send to Kindle" feature are a godsend) and a bad thing (I hope you like being locked into the Amazon ecosystem).

One change to the entire 2026 Kindle lineup is already proving divisive: Judging by reactions on the Kindle Reddit, not everyone is in love with the new flush-front design, which eliminates the raised bezels around the screen that were present on the 2024 model, but at the cost of adding a thin layer of glass over the e-ink display.Depending on how picky you are, you may find fault with this setup, as the additional layer of glass slightly reduces text clarity by putting more distance and another barrier between your eyes and the text or images in your book. Is this something I noticed myself? No—I don't have an older Kindle to make a direct comparison, and the text is still much, much sharper (and the front lighting more even) than what I see on competing e-readers like the Boox Go 6 or the Xteink X4 Pro. But there is a contingent of readers already lamenting the change, so take that for what you will.

The question to consider whenever a new device model rolls around is simple: Is this worth the upgrade? If you have a working Kindle from any time after the introduction of temperature-adjustable lighting, I would say no—the 2026 models are nicer, but they still don't do anything to make them worth it, especially at the new higher price points. That said, if you are in the market for a new Kindle, I'd suggest opting for the Paperwhite over the entry-level model, which has a smaller screen and lacks the warm light option—and if you're getting a Paperwhite or Colorsoft, you might as well pay the premium for the Signature Edition, because it's finally worth the extra money.

#3484. ‘Wildwood’ Director Travis Knight on How Live-Action Filmmaking Shaped His Stop-Motion Animated Adventure

Many scenes in “Wildwood” are designed to look spectacular. Even if each frame weren’t already rendered with the meticulous detail and artistry of stop-motion animation, the Laika Studios film is full of complex, chaotic battle sequences, a forest writhing with eldritch magic, and giant eagles soaring through the sky.

But some of the most technically challenging scenes, according to director Travis Knight, aren’t the ones that look the most majestic. They are — true to the spirit of the film and the lesson learned by its stubborn, caring protagonist Prue (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) — the simple magic of everyday life. Related Stories ‘Club Kid’ Review: Jordan Firstman’s Brazen, Funny, and Surprisingly Earnest Directing Debut Is a Wild Party Movie with Heart ‘Being Heumann’ Review: Siân Heder’s ‘CODA’ Follow-Up Is an Essential Biopic That’s Not Afraid to Have Some Fun

In fact, Knight told IndieWire on an episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit podcast that one of the most challenging sequences in “Wildwood” was simply getting its hero from one end of her bedroom to the other. Laika prefers Canon cameras mounted on large motion-control rigs, which offer the flexibility needed to capture puppet movements adjusted one frame at a time. But when the camera moves, it also has to do so one painstaking frame at a time.

Knight, who’s now directed live-action features “Bumblebee” and “Masters of the Universe” in addition to his Laika work on “Kubo and the Two Strings,” wanted “Wildwood” to have the same camera language as a live-action film. He wanted the intimacy and wordless visual storytelling of a camera tracking Prue as she huffs across her bedroom, where the camera movement helps us see the decor shift from the artifacts of a carefree kid to those of a more disaffected teen.

“I still wanted it to feel like it was shot like a live-action film, with that kind of intimacy with the camera. But a camera on a motion-control rig is the size of a Ford F-150 in our [puppet-scale] world. It’s huge. And so if a camera is moving, you have to create space for the camera on set,” Knight said.

This is on top of creating space for the animator, who is roughly the size of a Kaiju in comparison to the fifth-scale the humans on either side of the Impassable Wood live at. The Prue puppet is roughly 10 inches tall. Being able to move that puppet and a camera at least as large as her bedroom that the puppet is moving through? That is a particularly gnarly feat of physics.

“We essentially had to deconstruct the set,” Knight said. “It was almost like it was a clamshell. It would open to make room for the camera, and then it would close up again. It was such a complicated engineering feat, when all it is [for] is a camera panning across a room. Those are the kinds of challenges that the team has to figure out, which is stupid, but it’s what it requires if you’re trying to tell a story like this.”

There is much to be said, and rightly, about the awe-inducing moments of spectacle in “Wildwood.” The Laika team had to figure out how to make giant puppets out of fabric and feathers instead of standard-issue silicone to simulate flight compellingly, accurately, and tactilely. Combat sequences required enormous attention to detail. But when Knight watches the film, he’s just as struck by the invisible work that makes “Wildwood” feel like a live-action epic — the thankless but involving work that viewers aren’t ever meant to see.

“I learned a great many things about what to do, what not to do [working in live-action]. It fundamentally changed my relationship with the camera, which is one of the reasons why ‘Wildwood’ looks so different. It’s because I wanted it to feel as if it were without the inherent limitations you would typically find in stop-motion cinematography,” Knight said. “When I see this movie, I am seeing all these little miraculous moments of engineering and artistry and human creativity at play on the big screen, and that’s one of the reasons it moves me so much.”

#3483. ‘The Ballad of Lieutenant Dan,’ Documentary About Gary Sinise’s Work with Veterans, Acquired by Freestyle Digital Media

Freestyle Digital Media, the digital film distribution division of Byron Allen’s company Allen Media Group, has acquired VOD rights to the documentary feature “The Ballad of Lieutenant Dan.”

The documentary follows Oscar-nominated and Emmy-winning actor Gary Sinise‘s decades-long mission to honor America’s fighting men and women, support injured veterans, and stand beside Gold Star families. It’s a calling that was inspired by Sinise’s work playing a Vietnam vet in “Forrest Gump.”

“The Ballad of Lieutenant Dan” will be available on North American digital HD internet, DVD, cable, and satellite platforms starting on November 10, 2026. It features interviews with Sinise, as well as Jay Leno, Tim Allen, Joe Mantegna, Chip Foose, and Mykelti Williamson. Sinise is also known for his work in films such as “Ransom” and “Apollo 13,” as well as the TV series “CSI: NY.” He starred in “George Wallace,” winning an Emmy. Related Stories ‘Wildwood’ Director Travis Knight on How Live-Action Filmmaking Shaped His Stop-Motion Animated Adventure ‘Club Kid’ Review: Jordan Firstman’s Brazen, Funny, and Surprisingly Earnest Directing Debut Is a Wild Party Movie with Heart

The film also follows Sinise as he grapples with personal tragedy after his son, Mac, dies of cancer at the age of 33. The documentary looks at how Sinise is motivated by the credo: “We can always do a little more.” “The Ballad of Lieutentant Dan” was directed by Steve Mitchell Beebe and produced by Bud Brutsman.

“’The Ballad of Lieutenant Dan’ looks into the world of actor and humanitarian, Gary Sinise, and explores how his commitment to veterans and first responders created a community that supported him through a difficult period in his life,” said Beebe. “This is a story about selfless kindness and, I hope, will inspire all of us to do what we each can to uplift our friends, neighbors and communities.”

Freestyle Digital Media negotiated a deal to acquire the documentary directly with the filmmakers.

#3482. 10 Greatest Opening Lines In Sci-Fi Movie History, Ranked

Without a doubt, science-fiction movies can have some of the greatest and most visually stunning opening sequences in cinematic history. However, sometimes what makes these openings so memorable can be what is heard and/or read just as much as what is shown on screen. Additionally, some of the best lines in a sci-fi movie can be the ones we get right off the bat.

Typically used to introduce a universe, overarching concepts, themes, or most important ideas, the opening lines in a sci-fi movie can be some of its most important and/or memorable. Frequently, the first lines we get are written and shown as introductory text rather than spoken aloud (though sometimes it's both). These can be warnings about dark futures, explanations for major cosmic concepts, the time and setting, chosen figures, and even crucial dreams.

Keeping that in mind, here's a ranking of 10 of the greatest opening lines in sci-fi movie history, ranked from great to the absolute greatest of all time.

Ridley Scott's Blade Runner (1982) immediately establishes its setting and dystopian future via critical opening text that immediately gets audiences oriented to this world and current status quo. Explaining the creation of replicants by the Tyrell Corporation, the introduction is incredibly efficient as we're brought into the movie's primary conflict before we even meet Harrison Ford's Rick Deckard. The audience can quickly understand that this is a world where replicants are being hunted and considered illegal on Earth.

Kicking off the first-ever live-action Transformers franchise, Michael Bay's 2007 movie opens with the introduction of the AllSpark, the mysterious object that created all life on Cybertron (and the movie's major MacGuffin responsible for the conflict between the Autobots and Decepticons on Earth).

However, what makes this opening so memorable is that the nature and history of the AllSpark is narrated by Optimus Prime himself, who's voiced by the late, great Peter Cullen. As such, there's something inherently special about hearing Prime's first-ever lines of live-action dialogue from the same actor who first brought him to life in the original 80s animated series.

James Cameron's first Avatar movie opens with Sam Worthington's Jake Sully narrating his dreams. Well before he even sets foot on Pandora and takes control of his late brother's Na'vi avatar, Jake was dreaming of flying over jungles and embracing the feeling of freedom before inevitably waking up to a much harsher reality.

Ultimately, the line is even better in retrospect once the full movie is watched, seeing as how Jake very much turns those dreams into a reality that both includes and stretches well beyond those dreams he had back on Earth. It's a simple opening, yet one that carries great meaning as both the franchise and Jake's journey continue to expand in the Avatar franchise.

Continuing with more James Cameron, his first Terminator movie wastes no time establishing the horrifying future awaiting humanity with some grim opening text detailing the eventual rise of the machines under Skynet following the brutal aftermath of nuclear war. Like with the previous examples, the opening text is brilliantly efficient yet compelling as the movie's overall time-traveling premise is set up, kicking off one of the most popular sci-fi franchises of all time.

Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) takes a very unconventional yet brilliant approach to its opening, which is likely why it's still considered one of the greatest sci-fi movies of all time today.

Following the film's iconic overture and visuals showing the sun, Earth, and moon in alignment, we get the simple opening title card that reads "Dawn of Man", which is all that's needed to establish the movie's initial prehistoric setting. Focusing on a group of ape-like hominids and their encounter with the alien black monolith, the movie's opening suggests that it was this otherworldly experience that influenced and sparked the evolution of humanity itself before jumping millions of years forward to the movie's present.

Before audiences fully understand the rules and world featured in The Matrix (1999), the movie opens with a recorded telephone conversation between Trinity and Cypher, confirming that their leader, Morpheus, believes a man named Neo is "The One." It's a fascinating way to kick off the movie by setting up its destined "Chosen One" before anything else, one that sets up major questions and mysteries that eventually get answered as Neo himself learns more about the true nature of the false reality he lives in and his true role and destiny within it.

Denis Villeneuve's first Dune movie opens with an anonymous Sardaukar priest speaking in the low bass tones of his own language, with the on-screen translation reading: "Dreams are messages from the deep," immediately establishing the importance of Paul Atreides' prophetic dreams and destiny as the Kwisatz Haderach, taking the mantle of the Fremen messiah Lisan al-Gaib, and becoming the galaxy's next emperor of the Imperium. Followed by Chani's narration introducing the crucially central world of Arrakis and its beauty, audiences are immediately drawn into the movie and its core themes.

Celebrating its 20th anniversary this year, Christopher Nolan's The Prestige begins as a psychological mystery thriller that gradually unveils its major sci-fi elements as the movie progresses. However, its opening line is unequivocally the movie's best, encouraging viewers to examine the movie and pieces of the puzzle as closely as they can, while also highlighting the movie's major themes of deception, perception, and the nature of illusion itself.

The Prestige challenges audiences to distinguish between what they're seeing and what's actually happening, with the full trick and major misdirects not being revealed at the very end. Thanks to its brilliantly unique and intentional narrative construction, the opening line is certainly one of the greatest of all time.

Few opening narrations are as recognizable or as memorable as the classic Star Trek monologue declaring space as the final frontier and the mission of the USS Enterprise. While it's most closely associated with the opening themes of the television series, the narration (and variants of it) have appeared in movies as well, including 2009's Star Trek reboot and its sequels starring Chris Pine, Zoe Saldaña, and Zachary Quinto.

Setting the perfect tone and themes of galactic exploration, discovery, and adventure, these opening words have come to represent decades of excellent sci-fi storytelling across shows and movies alike, making it one of the most timeless and iconic opening lines in all of sci-fi (except for one).

It's difficult to imagine any sci-fi movie opening greater or more iconic than Star Wars' opening text: "a long time ago, in a galaxy far, far away." Before the opening crawl even begins, George Lucas establishes that audiences are about to experience something resembling a modern cosmic fairy tale rather than an outright sci-fi epic.

This memorable text is so brilliant in that it separates Star Wars from traditional science fiction. Despite all of its spaceships, robots, lightsabers, and futuristic technology, the franchise is fundamentally a fantasy epic with its peak hero and villain archetypes, supernatural powers, and overarching themes of destiny, good vs. evil, oppression, rebellion, and more. The opening line communicates that distinction immediately, inviting audiences into a universe that feels both futuristic and timeless (and it's a huge part of what has given Star Wars its enduring appeal for generations).

Nearly 50 years later, the key Star Wars phrase remains instantly recognizable, so much so that it's arguably the greatest invitation into any sci-fi movie world ever.

#3481. Watch ‘The Greatest’ Team Discuss How They Made the Impossible ‘Possible’ on Muhammad Ali Series

As tall an order as it was to make a series about the greatest boxer of all time, “The Greatest” creator Ben Watkins had faith he assembled the right team for the job and the unique assurance of making it with the blessing of Muhammed Ali’s family. At IndieWire’s recent Consider This event at Pacific Design Center, presented in partnership with Prime Video, he broke down the process that brought the series to life.

“One of the things I want to do is humanize Muhammad Ali because everybody sort of pictures him as a fully formed icon and legend. And I want to disconnect people from that and introduce them to a kid who just had a dream. But that means I got to show all of him. I got to show flaws and fears and vulnerabilities and tell the truth like that. And it’s sometimes messy,” Watkins said, recalling his pitch to the boxer’s widow Lonnie Ali . “Her response was, ‘That’s what I want too,’ because that will make him more relatable. And as we introduce him to a younger generation and reintroduce him to the people who already love him, that is what will make this story fresh.” Related Stories Alan Cumming Says ‘Tip Toe’ Was His Greatest Role Ever — but He Never Wants to Think About It Again ‘The Greatest’ Review: Amazon’s Handsome Muhammed Ali Biopic Connects in Spite of Itself

Boxing is an individual sport, but making “The Greatest” was a team effort. Watkins was joined on the panel by many of his crafts team members, including editor Steve Lang, costume designer Marci Rodgers, production designer Elisa Suavé, composer Stanley A. Smith, music editor Jordan Wiggins, and music supervisor Robin Urdang.

One of the aspects that made the eight-episode limited series tracking the protagonist’s rise from Olympian gold medalist Cassius Clay to heavyweight champion Muhammad Ali feel fresh was the use of contemporary music, but that also came with its own challenges for the post production team.

“Going contemporary in an Olympic boxing match with so many things going on between commentary, the fight itself, the reactions, and then we also have a song playing. I think we went through about 120 songs,” said Lang, telling the story of how they landed on a key piece of music for the series opener.

“I usually come on pre-production, [but] I came on during post, and one of the first things was ‘We want an original song here and we need it now,’” Urdang added. “I said, ‘We can’t get it until we create the sound of the show because there’s no sound of the show right now.’”

That first music cue became the last song they used for the show, an original track from Grammy winner Wyclef Jean titled “Gladiator.” “There was a poem that [Ali] hears about a gladiator talking about his time in the Colosseum. Ben mentions that to Wyclef, who then takes those lyrics and turns them into the song that you hear during that fight,” said Lang.

“It ended up in two spots in episode one, and then it also became the main title [music],” said Wiggins. “It was a lot of cutting that Jordan did for us,” said Urdang.

The Colosseum also happened to be the setting for one of costume designer Marci Rodgers’ greatest challenges working on “The Greatest.” “I was put on the spot in Rome where I had to do a quick change on camera, which is actually the first scene [as well]” she said. “So we’re in the Colosseum and it’s Marci’s time. And so I reached out to one of my mentors, Paul Tazewell, who walked me through a process in which we see essentially his suit removed as the camera is moving around.”

“Those are the things that they said would not be possible. Then the first production meeting I said, ‘Hey, I want to do a shot where he’s in a suit and as we’re circling, it all goes away,’” said Watkins. First it was a challenge to even shoot on location, but “We ended up [as] the first television show to ever shoot in the Colosseum,” he said. Then it was getting confirmation that they could also shoot more around Rome. And finally, it was shooting the aforementioned pivotal scene. “At that point I said, ‘We’ll never get that shot off.’ And then Marci says, ‘No, we’re going to figure out a way to build a suit, to do it in a way to get the shot off.’ And then Elisa and her team figured out a way for us to not just be able to shoot in the Colosseum, but they recreated a 60s-level Italian neighborhood because, ‘Hey, we’re in Rome now, so let’s get the most out of it.’ And they got us all of that, all things they said they couldn’t get.”

For her part, Suavé said “When you look at the world in the ’50s and the ’60s, there was no digital anything. Every single sign, every single thing you think was made by our scenic artists by hand, not with projections that they were copying. We did it all by hand. We made all the molds for all the parking meters. We made the molds and we created the gold medals.” She added, “There was not one world that we didn’t touch or create.”

Composer Stanley A. Smith also chimed in on how the series kept things analog, saying “We use all live musicians in this score.” “No AI,” added Urdang.

“Ben was really great about going to bat for getting the budget to do that. And we used live string players.” said Smith. “Just because of the nature of the tone we wanted, we used predominantly people of color for our strings — not always — but because we wanted that feel. And actually, I’m going to go one step further. It was 60 to 40 percent female.”

Ending the panel, Watkins said “That’s the big testament to everybody up here. We took what I would say is a modest television budget and we made a high budget film.”

“The Greatest” is now streaming on Prime Video. Watch the complete panel with the showrunner and artisans who worked on the limited series in the video above.
