#3480. 5 Sci-Fi Books You Can Finish in a Weekend

Sci-fi can be a lot to take in, and that's understandable. Luckily, some of the best sci-fi books can be finished in two days or less. From time travel and alternate universes to human-made dystopias, the genre explores familiar and unfamiliar concepts, imagining worlds where technology seems to have no bounds and human intelligence has reached unimaginable heights.

But progress comes with consequences, no matter how logical a decision might seem. Science cannot exist without the humans who practice it, and ultimately, their morals determine whether it is used for good or bad. That's some pretty heavy philosophical stuff, but certain writers know how to tackle these ideas in shorter books or through plots that are a breeze to read. From an absurdly ridiculous take on alien encounters to a survival thriller set on Mars, here are sci-fi books you can finish in a weekend.

Winner of the 2020 Hugo Award for Best Novella, Amal El-Mohtar and Max Gladstone's This Is How You Lose the Time War follows Blue and Red, two rival agents working for opposing organizations across different timelines and universes in a post-apocalyptic future. Both women are tasked with manipulating events in the past to secure the future their respective factions desire. Although they've crossed paths countless times during their missions, they've never exchanged a word — that is, until Blue breaks the routine (and the rules) by sending Red a letter. What begins as a simple exchange soon blossoms into a companionship that puts their reputations, loyalties, and duties at risk.

At approximately 200 pages, This Is How You Lose the Time War is told in an epistolary format, which makes sense given that Blue and Red's main form of communication is through letters. This also makes the novel an easily digestible read that you can finish in two days. However, its shorter length doesn't take away from the ambitious scope of the story, especially when concepts like branching timelines and alternate universes are often reserved for longer novels with extensive worldbuilding. But this novel is more than just sci-fi. It's also about a forbidden love with consequences that extend beyond the two people involved. Their relationship could potentially threaten the fragile nature of the universes themselves, showing how something as personal as love can have far-reaching scientific implications that put humanity at risk.

At around 200 pages, Douglas Adams' The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy stuffs an entire universe of ridiculous adventures into a surprisingly quick read. It all starts when Earth is demolished by the Vogons to make room for a hyperspace bypass, leaving ordinary Englishman Arthur Dent scrambling to survive. He escapes with Ford Prefect, an alien friend who takes him across the galaxy alongside a bizarre group of companions: the two-headed president Zaphod Beeblebrox, the chronically depressed robot Marvin, and Trillian, another human survivor. Their journey eventually brings Arthur closer to discovering Earth's actual purpose, which, naturally, involves a supercomputer.

Adams wastes little time making it clear that this isn't your typical sci-fi adventure. The universe operates on its own ridiculous logic, whether that means destroying an entire planet for a space shortcut or electing a two-headed president. The jokes come so frequently that readers barely have time to question the absurdity before the next one arrives. Beneath all that humor, the novel also takes a swipe at humanity's obsession with finding meaning in everything. People spend their lives searching for the ultimate answer to existence, only for the universe to offer very little in return. And when the supercomputer finally delivers its answer, the result is so hilariously underwhelming that it makes the whole search even funnier.

At just 84 to 176 pages, depending on the edition, H. G. Wells' The Time Machine is a Victorian-era predecessor to Back to the Future. The novella follows an eccentric English scientist known only as the Time Traveller, who builds a machine capable of traveling through time. Curious about humanity's future, he journeys to the year 802,701, where he encounters the Eloi, a seemingly carefree society living among the remnants of an advanced civilization. However, the world he discovers is far more complicated than it first appears, forcing him to reconsider what humanity’s future might look like.

Released during the Second Industrial Revolution, The Time Machine explores how technology shapes humanity and its relationship with nature. While these forces continue to intersect in the 21st century, seeing them through a late 19th-century perspective offers a fascinating glimpse into Victorian anxieties about progress. During this period, technological advancement was often seen as the key to Britain's continued dominance, reflecting the belief that humanity would only grow smarter, stronger, and more powerful. However, the Time Traveller's journey challenges that assumption. The book shows that human evolution has no guaranteed endpoint, and reaching what seems like the pinnacle of progress doesn't mean humanity's future will be any brighter.

Four ships, four completely different reasons to be up there at all. Here is the one that has your seat, what flying with them would cost you, and what it would give back.

You belong on the fastest piece of junk in the galaxy, with a crew that took the job for the payday and then quietly stopped caring about the payday. Nothing on the Falcon has ever gone according to plan, and everybody aboard prefers it that way.

You belong with the crew that turned a tiny cell of misfits into an actual rebellion. The Ghost is a home before it is a ship, and everybody who boards it arrived with something broken that the rest of them decided to look after.

You belong with the four kids who found a buried ship, launched it by accident and are now extremely lost in a galaxy that eats people like them. Nobody here knows what they are doing, and that turns out to be the fun of it.

You belong in the quietest ship in the galaxy, with one small passenger and a code you have never explained to anybody. You told yourself this was a job, and then it stopped being a job somewhere around the second week.

At roughly 370 pages, Andy Weir's The Martian is longer than some entries on this list, but its brisk pace—and the light, conversational tone from the lead character himself—makes it easy to keep turning pages. Mark Watney is on NASA's Ares 3 mission when a dust storm forces the crew to abandon Mars. An accident leaves him injured and separated from the others, who assume he is dead and head home. When Mark wakes up, he finds himself alone, with limited supplies, a damaged spacesuit, and no way to contact Earth. His only chance is to use his scientific knowledge to solve problems and find a way back.

The setup may sound like a straightforward survival thriller, but Weir gives the story an emotional purpose. Mark's resourcefulness keeps him alive, while the rescue effort shows how far people will go for someone they refuse to abandon. Back on Earth, NASA must decide whether another mission and its crew should be put at risk to bring him home. That dilemma gives the novel its heart. For all its science and engineering, The Martian comes down to one moral lesson: one person's life matters, even when saving it demands sacrifice. It's a reminder that survival is less of a solo achievement and more about people refusing to give up on you.

Reading is a crime in Ray Bradbury's Fahrenheit 451—arguably treated as more serious than murder. Anyone caught hiding, distributing, or even reading a book risks imprisonment. Firemen have an unusual job in this society: instead of putting out fires, they set books alight. Guy Montag has never questioned this arrangement until he meets Clarisse, a young neighbor whose curiosity about life challenges everything he has accepted as normal. His doubts deepen after he witnesses a woman choose to die with her books rather than surrender them. The encounter forces him to reconsider his job and the society he has served.

Depending on the edition, Fahrenheit 451 runs between 156 and 256 pages, but Bradbury packs a chillingly prophetic vision into that length. Published in the 1950s, the novel imagines a society that feels uncomfortably familiar today, from attempts to ban books deemed "controversial" to people spending hours glued to their phone screens. It also raises concerns about political forces seeking to silence criticism and discourage independent thought. Bradbury's warning is not simply that technology can distract people from the world. In the wrong hands, it can also become a tool for enforcing conformity, keeping the public occupied while those in power avoid scrutiny. Anyone who challenges that system risks consequences.

#3479. Cinematography Legend Robert Richardson Answered a Film Student’s Email — Their Conversation Became ‘The White Devil’

Robert Richardson has spent decades answering questions about how he makes movies look the way they do. The legendary cinematographer is a regular collaborator of Martin Scorsese, Oliver Stone, and Quentin Tarantino, with three Oscars to his name — for “JFK,” “The Aviator,” and “Hugo.” But something caught his attention when a film student from the Czech Republic emailed him in 2016: Jana Hojdová wanted to know about everything else.

“I get a number of requests for this kind of work and I am not really interested,” Richardson told IndieWire. “There wasn’t one that was technical. It was who are you? Where do you come from? What’s your life like?” Related Stories ‘The Ballad of Lieutenant Dan,’ Documentary About Gary Sinise’s Work with Veterans, Acquired by Freestyle Digital Media ‘Wildwood’ Director Travis Knight on How Live-Action Filmmaking Shaped His Stop-Motion Animated Adventure

Richardson started writing Hojdová back, and a decade later, their correspondence has grown into a friendship and Hojdová’s feature directorial debut, “Robert Richardson: The White Devil.” They’ve also got an ongoing book project, which aims to organize and share even more of the film’s underlying research: an intellectual arsenal backed by the vast archives from Richardson’s house in Massachusetts.

“350 pages and we are not done,” Hojdová said, sitting next to Richardson for a Q&A after a private screening of her film at Soho House West Hollywood on October 29. “This is our homework in Los Angeles,” she said. “That we need to finish our book.” Richardson smiled.

“No is not in her vocabulary. It’s a lifetime achievement here.”

Hojdová originally approached Richardson in support of her master’s thesis at Prague’s FAMU film school. The daughter of a director and cinematographer herself, she told IndieWire she also grew up watching Richardson’s films with her family in the Czech Republic. Richardson’s first response felt “life-changing” for Hojdová and, by the time she traveled to New Zealand to meet him in 2017 on the production of Baltasar Kormákur’s “Adrift,” she said she thought she really knew the man behind the movies. In person, it became apparent just how much Hojdová still had to ask.

“I started to capture everything that he’s doing,” she said. “He’s driving [his] car to the set, his eating, everything.” Watching Richardson work and go about his daily life felt like an obvious film to Hojdová, but Richardson was less convinced. “My life is not interesting,” she recalled him saying.

Still, Hojdová kept shooting, and after six months of discussion, Richardson agreed to the project on the condition that its director would be shown, too. At first, that presented a problem for the young filmmaker who, like Richardson, greatly prefers the other side of the camera.

“I don’t like my voice, I don’t like watching myself,” she said. “It was like, ‘OK, I will say yes, but maybe I will not really be in there.’” Then, the pandemic brought her and Richardson even closer.

In 2020, what began as a short visit to look through photos and records at Richardson’s place in Cape Cod expanded as Hojdová realized just how much material the artist had kept in his basement — and lockdown forced her to extend her stay. The two ultimately wound up living together for months.

“If we didn’t have COVID, it wouldn’t be a movie,” Richardson said. “It wouldn’t be the same movie in any way at all.”

Four years after first contacting her hero, Hojdová said she knew many of Richardson’s personal stories but had previously lacked the material to put them on-screen. Suddenly, she was surrounded by countless scenes that could go with his memories, and observing Richardson, effectively in captivity, for weeks on end gave Hojdová even more to ask.

“I said to Bob that he has to be happy because we are filming at his house and he doesn’t need to go somewhere to shoot,” Hojdová said. “We are there.”

“It was really hell,” Richardson joked. “I mean seriously, you were ready to shoot every day. I had an assignment every day.” Later in the conversation, he offered another description: “She’s a spy. She convinced me that it was cool to do this, bit by bit.”

Eventually, Hojdová faced 650 hours of footage and the overwhelming task of finding the feature documentary inside it. Shaping all that material meant deciding how much of her own relationship with Richardson actually belonged on screen. It wasn’t until Hojdová reached the editing room that she fully appreciated her subject’s original condition. Viewers needed someone to accompany them into Richardson’s world — and the curious cinematographer trying to understand him? She was the way in.

“I had to fight for me being in the film, which was very hard for me because I don’t like it,” Hojdová said. “But I realized it was a great choice because I think people can connect more with me than with Bob.”

The filmmaker’s plan to bring Richardson’s personal life into conversation with the all-timer movies he helped create presented another challenge for Hojdová in post. Working extensively with executive producer Matej Chlupácek, she had to secure legal permission to use dozens of iconic images. Finishing “The White Devil” edit meant beginning an extensive licensing process, with roughly 390 entries to clear.

“It was really a nightmare, but we did it,” she said.

Of course, Richardson — whom Hojdová warmly described as “impatient” — wanted to see results as soon as possible. Still, she said he trusted the process and, more importantly, his director’s judgment.

“She was very smart,” Richardson said. “Her choices were good. She was persistent and I thought working with her was a pleasure.” Really watching the film he was asking about? That’s another matter.

Sprawled out in the front row of Soho House’s plush private theater, Richardson said the October 29 evening in L.A. felt like his first real viewing. “The White Devil” had its world premiere at the Czech Republic’s Karlovy Vary International Film Festival on July 5 and will make its North American premiere at DOC NYC on November 14. But at Karlovy Vary, where Richardson also received an award, he said he was too overwhelmed to absorb the portrait.

“I was not in body — because, then, you’re sitting in front of 1500 people and they’re playing this film,” he said. “I don’t remember half of it.”

A thrilling and sensitive consideration of cinematic genius, “The White Devil” explores Richardson’s sometimes contentious relationships with crews, his evolving collaborations with elite directors, a deeply troubled personal life, and even his experiences with psychedelic drugs. But the difficulty of living with such beautiful and raw honesty became apparent during a sweet exchange between Richardson and Hojdová in front of the Soho House audience.

Asked about watching the film, Richardson said, “When I was sitting here watching it, I was like, ‘Oh, this isn’t bad. This isn’t so bad. We could cut that down a little bit.’”

“But how was it for you to see?” Hojdová pressed in response. Richardson paused.

“I don’t like watching this movie because it’s a very transparent approach to who I am,” he said. “Most times you would think the documentary wouldn’t necessarily have as much of the shadow side.” Hojdová reminded him that exposure was part of the understanding they’d reached together: “You told me that if this film can tell someone something, it needs to be transparent.”

Speaking to the audience, Richardson turned to the subject of his five children and, as he does in “The White Devil,” took responsibility for the personal connections he sees as damaged by his deep commitment to a demanding artistic career.

“Looking back on that, it’s very hard,” he said. “I haven’t been able to fall back into a good relationship with the first two. The third has become very close.” He also reflected: “I’m trying. It’s a long time when you’re addicted to one form of drug or another. You’ve got to wean yourself off that particular methodology.”

Richardson’s youngest gave him something lighter to discuss: “I’m pretty close to the three year old, but he’s a monster,” he joked. “He is worse than I was as a child. He needs to be sent away to school now.”

Hojdová herself has a three-year-old daughter, and the adult friends’ children were born only a month apart. Still, “The White Devil” director sometimes played the parent steering Richardson onstage.

“Did you learn something?” Hojdová asked.

“I learned pain and I learned that now I should try to work harder, try to make the family work better,” Richardson said. After 10 years, a student’s shot-in-the-dark inquiry had become a genuine discovery on both sides — with each artist maturing and educating the other along the way.

“She started in her 20s in this film. Now she’s in her 30s. It’s a long time that you grow together,” Richardson said of Hojdová. “She’s seen all the worst sides of me anybody could see. She’s probably been the second longest relationship with a female in my life.”

“Robert Richardson: The White Devil” screens at DOC NYC on November 14 and 16 at IFC Center. The film is also streaming in the U.S. through November 29 with the purchase of an online screening ticket.

#3478. Dungeon Crawler Carl: Point Mongo Is Blowing Up Ahead Of Franchise's Official Return

Dungeon Crawler Carl has already taken the literary world by storm, and Matt Dinniman's wildly popular LitRPG series is now preparing to conquer tabletops with its highly anticipated role-playing game. Developed by Renegade Game Studios, the Dungeon Crawler Carl RPG promises to let fans experience the chaos of the World Dungeon firsthand, creating their own adventures in Carl and Princess Donut's dangerous universe.

Following an enormously successful crowdfunding campaign, thousands of backers have already begun receiving their orders, with more than 25% of U.S. orders fulfilled by the end of October. Fortunately, whether you're among the lucky backers who've already received their copies or you're planning to pick up the RPG later this month, there's something else you should have on your radar: Point Mongo, which could become an invaluable part of your next adventure.

With the official Dungeon Crawler Carl RPG preparing for its wider retail launch, fans have already created an incredible resource that could make their adventures through the World Dungeon way easier. Point Mongo is a completely free, community-driven website dedicated to homebrew content for Renegade Game Studios' upcoming tabletop RPG, offering players and game masters an expanding collection of tools, ideas, and original creations.

The name itself is a reference to Point Mongo, a town featured on the sixth floor of the World Dungeon in The Butcher's Masquerade (Book 5). Princess Donut takes control of the settlement, which becomes an important location during Carl and Donut's adventures through the Hunting Grounds.

The website is equally ambitious, having already surpassed 1,000 entries across 30 categories, with contributions from approximately 150 community members. Its enormous library covers practically everything players might need to expand their campaigns, including custom races, classes, magical items, monsters, bosses, spells, pets, quests, and even entire dungeon environments.

Beyond its extensive collection of user-created content, Point Mongo offers several useful features:

Point Mongo is also entirely community-supported, with users encouraged to submit original creations and help complete missing statistics for existing entries. Everything is freely accessible without requiring an account or subscription, and the project is unofficial and unaffiliated with Renegade Game Studios.

The website has already received an enthusiastic reception among RPG fans on Reddit. User gameryamen praised the community's efforts, noting that reaching 1,000 entries before most physical copies have arrived is an encouraging sign for the game's future. The commenter added that the resource "will make my campaigns so much easier to plan."

Meanwhile, contributor DeaDPaN79 encouraged players to participate in the site's ongoing item-creation challenges, demonstrating how actively the community continues expanding the site.

With new content being added regularly, Point Mongo could quickly become one of the most valuable free resources for Dungeon Crawler Carl RPG players, particularly those hoping to create their own unforgettable stories within Matt Dinniman's universe.

#3477. Pixar Promotes Jonathan Garson to President, Taking Reins from Retiring Executive Jim Morris

Jonathan Garson has been promoted to the role of president at Pixar Animation Studios, while standing executive Jim Morris moves into the role of president emeritus as he prepares for retirement. The Walt Disney Company, which owns Pixar, announced the leadership transition Wednesday afternoon.

Garson, who has notched 30 years at Disney and most recently served as Pixar’s general manager after leading its marketing and franchise team, will become president on January 4. The role will see him oversee production and operations at the animation giant, partnering with chief creative officer Pete Docter.

Disney states that Morris, who has been with Pixar for 21 years and served as president for the past 12, will remain involved with Pixar through an executive producer role on “Incredibles 3” (due out in June 2028), along with talent development, mentorship and technology initiatives. Both Garson and Morris will report to Alan Bergman, chairman of Disney Entertainment and Studios for The Walt Disney Company. Related Stories IndieWire and Disney to Celebrate Emmy Rossum and the Cast of ‘Furious’ at Special Pass the Remote Screening After ‘Avengers Endgame: Encore,’ Infinity Vision Might Turn Out to Be a Thing

“Having worked closely with Jim Morris for more than 20 years, I have enormous respect for his leadership and unwavering commitment to Pixar and its people,” Bergman wrote in a statement leading the press release on the leadership changes. “He’s not only a tremendous partner in business but a great friend. As we prepare for his eventual retirement, this transition will ensure a smooth succession for the team.”

Bergman continues, “With a deep background at both Pixar and Disney, Jonathan Garson has proven to be an exceptional leader with a strong sense of what makes Pixar unique and how its storytelling comes to life in so many ways for fans, and Pete Docter and I are excited for him to step into this role. In addition, Jonas Rivera brings a wealth of creative expertise that will serve the team well as he works even more closely with Pete.”

Morris’ statement follows: “Leading Pixar has been the privilege of a lifetime, and I’m honored to have been a steward of its legacy alongside extraordinary artists, storytellers, and technologists who keep redefining what animation can do and expanding the art of cinema. After 52 years in the business, and almost 40 at Lucasfilm and Pixar, I’ll be stepping back from the day-to-day, but I’m thrilled to move into handling a number of special projects, working alongside my friends Pete, Jonathan, and Jonas at Pixar, and of course Alan Bergman, who has been such a supporter of Pixar throughout the years. Looking ahead, I can’t think of anyone better than Jonathan to carry the legacy of this beloved studio forward. He’s a Pixar person through and through, a fierce champion of our films, our people, and our culture. Pixar is in very good hands.”

Garson then writes, “I still remember seeing ‘Toy Story’ for the first time – never imagining I’d one day work at Pixar, let alone step into a leadership role such as this. Every day I walk in the door here, I’m reminded just how special this place is and how lucky I am to be a part of it. Jim has shown me what it looks like to safeguard this culture of quality, innovation, and creative ambition, and I’m extremely grateful to both him and Alan for their trust and support. It’s a humbling opportunity, and I look forward to working with Pete, Jonas, the production leadership team led by Katherine Sarafian and Lindsey Collins, and all of the extraordinary talent here at Pixar as we continue to push boundaries and lead our studio into the future.”

Along with Garson, Pixar will also bump Jonas Rivera to executive vice president of creative, overseeing directors, creative vice presidents, development, casting, and content advisement departments, in partnership with Docter. The two will serve as executive producers on all Pixar films.“Ever since I walked through these doors as Pixar’s first production intern, this place, its people, and its stories have been my life’s work,” said Rivera. “I am deeply honored to step into this new role alongside Pete, partnering with him and Jonathan to support our incredible filmmakers and artists. Jim has been an extraordinary mentor and leader, and I intend to build on the lessons I learned from him as we look toward our next chapter.”

Pixar is coming off of a sequel success in “Toy Story 5,” which earned over $1.1 billion at the global box office to rank as the 10th-highest-grossing animated feature of all time. Up next are two original features — “Gatto” in March and “Ghost Market” in March 2028 — followed by “Incredibles 3.”

#3476. Five Hacks Every Wordle Player Should Know

Wordle’s biggest draw is its simplicity: Anybody can look at five blank spaces and think of a five-letter word. But when it comes to playing Wordle well, and enjoying the game over time, you might do better with a few tips. I have a nearly 100% win rate in Wordle—more about win rates below—so here are some of mine.

If I could only give one strategy tip, it would be this: Your first guess, and even your second and third, shouldn’t be attempts to solve the puzzle. Instead, you should be gathering information about possible solutions.

This means that if you guessed a word ending in “ER” and those letters turned green, you should not try another word ending in ER as your next guess. If you guess a completely different five-letter word, say BENCH, you can find out whether B, N, C, and H are in the solution, while also getting information about whether there’s an E in the second position (which helps you know whether words like LEVER and METER might be in play).

There is a toggle in the game interface that requires every word to use green squares from your previous guesses. It’s called “hard mode.” If you ask me, this should be called “luck mode,” because it takes away one of the game’s best strategies for smart solvers, as guessing letters you already know is just wasting guesses.

I wrote more about this strategy here, and included more examples. Use this tip, and you’ll avoid the trap of losing after guessing FOUND, ROUND, POUND, MOUND, SOUND, and WOUND when you could have used MARSH as your second guess and instantly figured out the answer (HOUND).

There are competing schools of thought on choosing the best starting word for Wordle, an issue I have considered in depth. But to summarize the best advice: Choose a word with five different letters (no repeats) that includes at least two or three of the English language’s most common consonants.

Those most common consonants include T, N, S, H, R, D, L, and C. That means TRASH is a great starter, and so are CRANE and STEAL and STARE. For best results, use E and/or A as your vowels, since these are some of the most common vowels in English.

A starting word needs to give you information about what might be in the solution, but you don’t gain a ton of information with just five letters. So I recommend having another starting word that doesn’t overlap with the first, but expands the amount of information you can collect to 10 total data points.

After all these years, my trusty pair is still ARISE and TOUCH. That gives me all five vowels and a good sampling of the most common consonants, as discussed above. (Only N is notably missing, but I can always play that in a later guess.)

Feel free to come up with your own pair, where the second guess fills in gaps left by the first. If you like to start with a vowel-heavy word like ADIEU, use more consonants in your second move: perhaps THORN. Or if you start with TRASH, perhaps follow it with OUNCE.

I pride myself on my 100% Wordle win rate, but the truth is, I’m actually at 99% right now. The NYT’s “About Wordle” page says that “Win % counts the percentage of total puzzles played that you have won,”  but that doesn’t seem to be entirely correct. It also does not say how the app handles rounding. I believe I’ve lost three times over the 1,368 games I’ve played, which is actually a 99.8% win rate. But after every loss, the count has eventually gotten back up to 100%.

What I’ve figured out is this: As soon as you lose a game, your 100% win rate drops to 99%.But if you win (I am pretty sure!) another 200 in a row, you can earn that last percentage point back. I haven’t kept a perfect count since my last loss, but I’m pretty sure I’ve played more than 100. And despite losing a few games over the years, I’ve usually managed to keep a 100% win score.

For its first few years, Wordle never repeated a solution. If you could remember ever seeing a certain word as a solution, it was guaranteed not to be that day's answer. But that changed in February of 2026, when the New York Times officially announced that previous solutions may be reused.

Not the day you're after? Here's the solution to today's Wordle.

#3475. You Can Preorder XReal's First Wired XR Glasses

The VR headset may be becoming a thing of the past. At Google's Android Developer Summit this morning, XReal officially debuted XReal Aura XR glasses, smart glasses with full XR capability. They're powered by Android XR and run on a Snapdragon Reality Elite-powered puck, with Xreal's X1S Chip in the glasses themselves. The result: Aura packs a 70° field of view in a pair of glasses that weigh less than 95 grams.

Customers in the United States, Canada, Japan, and South Korea can order XReal Aura on XReal's site starting today, and they're expected to begin shipping in mid-November. The limited-time launch price is $1,099 for the 12GB + 256GB configuration and $1,299 for the 16GB + 512GB configuration, $180 and $200 less, respectively, than XReal announced earlier this month. The lower prices will be available until the end of the year.

If the claim of mixed reality in a pair of sunglasses seems dubious, I tried them out a few months ago, and they are exactly that.

Instead of an enclosed headset, XReal Aura projects digital content on transparent lenses so you can be present in the real world while also in the digital world. Unlike "traditional" virtual reality headsets, the Aura's batteries and main compute are in a wired puck/controller you can slip into your pocket. That keeps the weight down and makes them comfortable enough to wear for longer periods. Because it's built on Android XR, users will have access to millions of 2D and 3D Android apps right out of the box.

If you want to go beyond Android, you can plug a USB-C-compatible computer or gaming console into Aura, and use that device in the same virtual space as native Android XR apps.

XReal Aura is launching with a library of over 150 "made for XR" apps as well, including games like Nevatars, designed by Andy Serkis, Fallout: Factions, a dice-based head-to-head game in the Fallout universe, and Landing Party, "the world's first outdoor roleplaying video game." There will also be companion apps for the NBA, NASCAR, and the San Francisco Ballet Company’s The Nutcracker. In terms of productivity, ShapexXR, a platform for software developer collaboration, is making its debut on Android XR, and you'll be able to use apps like Frontline.io for job training and assistance, and Plynk Spatial for stock research and trading.

If you want to get down to the nitty-gritty, here are the Aura's specs:

Split-compute architecture with compact compute puck

Wired Mirroring for laptops and compatible handheld gaming devices

USB-C connectivity using a standard connection

Electrochromic dimming for more immersive viewing

Support for voice, hand, keyboard, trackpad, and game controller input

#3474. Denzel Washington's Sci-Fi Crime Thriller 'Déjà Vu' Is 'Minority Report' Meets 'Looper'

If you’re in the mood for a fast-paced action thriller that goes in a surprising speculative direction, then you need to jump over to Tubi for one of Denzel Washington's greatest on-screen exploits. Currently free to stream on the platform is Déjà Vu, a post-9/11, post-Hurricane Katrina thriller that speaks to nationwide fears at the time, infusing them with a sci-fi twist that elevates the film to be more than just your average action flick. If it's been a few years, now is the perfect time to revisit the picture, as November marks the 20th anniversary of this Tony Scott-directed classic.

Like most of his features, Déjà Vu boasts Scott's signature style of kinetic energy and hyper-focused characters, as ATF agent Doug Carlin (Washington) struggles to catch a domestic terrorist, Carroll Oerstadt (Jim Caviezel), a self-appointed "patriot" who bombed a New Orleans ferry containing U.S. Navy sailors and their families. Soon after the attack, FBI agent Paul Pryzwarra (Val Kilmer) brings Carlin aboard his specialized task force centered around a secret government project that may help catch the killer. As it turns out, scientists have accidentally created a window in time—a window that offers Carlin the chance to stop the tragedy before it occurs. The only problem is that they can only look back just over four days, and those days pass by in real time with no ability to rewind. With little else to do but study the life of victim Claire Kuchever (Paula Patton), Carlin comes to recognize both the killer and his role in stopping him.

Déjà Vu is one of those action-thrillers that has you on the edge of your seat the entire time. Although the worst of it has already happened, the film treads in reverse as it attempts to put all the pieces together, intelligently weaving a narrative where the past and present intersect. This, naturally, leads to some interesting philosophical, as well as theological, conundrums, as Carlin and the team debate the ethics of such government surveillance (after the conspiratorial Enemy of the State, but before The Dark Knight did the same) and the moral uncertainty that arises from operating a window into the past: If God allows such a window to exist, is it not so that Carlin and company can then use it to not just solve a murder, but perhaps prevent one? These are the questions that anchor Déjà Vu, presenting the audience with some complex choices as time rapidly slips through the hourglass and the window into the recent past moves closer to the present tragedy.

Second watches are for catching everything you were too stressed to notice the first time.

Of all five collaborations between Washington and Scott, Déjà Vu is perhaps the most creatively engaging. (Yes, that's even considering the truly remarkable Man on Fire.) The 2006 thriller uses Scott's distinct visual style to go beyond the simple action thriller, bending genre and making way-out speculative concepts palatable for standard action audiences. At the same time, Washington toes the line between romance and duty as he begins to fall for the woman who, in his timeline, is already dead. It's a brilliant concept with impeccable execution that goes beyond the pair's usual brand of grounded, fast-paced thrillers.

As such, Déjà Vu offers the viewer plenty of thrills, chills, and philosophical pondering, and pits them against a ticking clock that screams "already, but not yet." It's an exceptional film that perfectly encapsulates the anxieties of early 2000s America while not grounding itself in them so deeply that it feels outdated or outpaced. Indeed, it's the type of film that they don't seem to make anymore—a mid-budget thriller with a stacked cast and great thematic potential—and that's a real shame. Tony Scott was a visionary filmmaker who never let genre (or anything, really) constrain his vision, and with Denzel Washington in the leading role, Déjà Vu is still just as great today as it was 20 years ago.

Déjà Vu is available for streaming on Tubi.

#3473. Your Discord Messages Will Soon Be Discoverable on Google Search, but You Can Opt Out

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you are a member of a large public Discord, your posts may soon be visible in Google Search—even to those without a Discord account. Starting in November, Discord's Discoverable Servers will have server web pages that show up in web search results, including summaries and messages from public channels. While messages won't be tied to your username or avatar, you may still want to opt out.

This change applies to Discoverable Servers on Discord, which are public spaces that have at least 1,000 members. There's no invite link, so anyone can find and join them as long as they have a Discord account. (Other servers on Discord are either invite-only Community Servers for larger groups or Friend Servers, which are small, private spaces.)

On Nov. 16, Discord is launching server web pages for Discoverable Servers, which will display discussion summaries from public channels as well as some individual messages. By mid-December, these pages may appear in search results. While these servers have always been fairly easy to access since they are public, this removes the requirement to sign up for Discord and join servers in order to view them.

In its announcement detailing the change, Discord notes that private servers and DMs will remain private. Plus, server admins can choose which channels are included in web search or opt them out entirely.

Messages you send before mid-December won't be included in search regardless of your setting preferences. However, if you leave this enabled and decide to turn it off later, anything you send between mid-December and disabling the setting will stay up unless you delete the message from Discord entirely.

#3471. Taylor Sheridan Crime Thriller’s Andrew Garfield Villain Pitch Revealed By Star

Sylvester Stallone has a vision for Andrew Garfield joining Tulsa King.

The crime thriller series was created by Taylor Sheridan, with Stallone playing Mafia capo Dwight "the General" Manfredi, who builds his own criminal empire in Tulsa, Oklahoma. The series is now in its fourth season and has been a major hit for Paramount+, leading to the upcoming spinoff series Frisco King that will follow hitman Russell Lee Washington Jr. (Samuel L. Jackson) now pursuing a criminal empire in Frisco, Texas.

In an exclusive interview with Marina Hyde on The Rest is Entertainment podcast, Stallone revealed that after spending time with Garfield, he wants the Academy Award nominee to play a villain in a future season of Tulsa King. Stallone pitched the idea of The Social Network actor playing a more "thoughtful" antagonist that Dwight would "have no idea how to stop," along with creating "a whole different dynamic" for the show. Check out his comments below:

I was with Andrew Garfield last night. I never thought we would hit it off, ever. And I thought, boy, I'd love to have him as a villain in Tulsa King because it would create a whole different dynamic. Instead of this big, lumbering, you know, villain, maybe it's, you know, it's thoughtful. Maybe it's AI-driven. Maybe it's something that I have no idea how to stop.

Paramount+ has renewed Tulsa King for season 5, but it is already in production, so it is likely too late to make Garfield a villain for the upcoming season. That being said, if the show's success continues and the creative team wants to continue it, a sixth season could happen that makes Stallone's pitch a reality. Along with playing the protagonist, Stallone is an executive producer and has co-written select episodes, while Terence Winter and Dave Erickson are the showrunners.

Mentioning that Garfield's potential villain could be part of an "AI-driven" threat is timely not only because of the growing prominence of AI, but with the actor playing Sam Altman, co-founder and CEO of the company OpenAI that created ChatGPT, in Artificial. The first reactions to Garfield's new movie were overwhelmingly positive, with many critics hailing it as the best performance of his career and cementing him as a frontrunner for the upcoming Academy Awards. It also has a 95% Tomatometer score based on 40 reviews ahead of releasing in theaters on December 25.

#3470. If You Loved 'East of Eden,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

One of the best things about truly great stories is how they can be endlessly adapted and reinterpreted. John Steinbeck published “East of Eden” in 1952, and each time it’s adapted to a screen, it looks a little different. Netflix’s try at this huge, complex story offers up some searing performances, especially from Florence Pugh as the notorious Cathy Ames. Ames is one of the best characters ever crafted in American literature, but her sociopathic nature has sometimes made her into a simple villain—but the series, and Pugh's performances, adds depth to the charcter. If the limited series has you wanting more complex female characters from classic novels, your next move is obvious: Vanity Fair, starring Reese Witherspoon as Becky Sharp.

First published in the mid-19th century, “Vanity Fair” by William Makepeace Thackeray is an enduring classic of American literature, satirizing the artificial manners and pretensions of Victorian society. At the center of the story is Becky Sharp, whose moral ambiguity and self-serving actions were surprising and unexpected at the time—and have made her a kind of antihero in the modern age. Sharp is a complicated character who, like Cathy Ames, can easily be flattened into a villain, a social climber who uses people.

The 2004 adaptation leans into the more modern take on Sharp’s character, giving her more justification for her actions and humanizing her more than the novel. Sharp is orphaned at a young age, but is almost feral in her determination to secure a position in society—which, at the time, meant securing an advantageous marriage. The story doesn’t have the same sweep as East of Eden, chronicling a relatively short period of time—but that period is the Napoleonic Wars, so there’s a lot going on. This gives the film a similarly epic feel even as it focuses on Sharp’s constant scheming and endless flirtations with people who she thinks can help her out.

In many ways, Sharp is simply playing by the rules imposed on her by men, and if that was scandalous in 1848, it’s almost heroic by today’s standards, and Reese Witherspoon imbues her Sharp with a bit of grace to reflect that. But she’s still someone who does what she must to survive and thrive, and that prickly edge will appeal to fans of Pugh in East of Eden. Rent Vanity Fair on Prime Video.

Need more historical epics with fascinating, complex characters? Luckily, the movies tend to specialize in that—here are a few more movies that fans of East of Eden will love.

If you thought the best thing about East of Eden was Florence Pugh, you’re going to love Lady Macbeth. Pugh plays Katherine, a young woman pushed into an arranged marriage with wealthy landowner Alexander Lester (Paul Hilton) in England in 1865. The marriage is solely intended to produce an heir, and Katherine is initially imprisoned in the house. When Alexander and his father leave Katherine alone for some time, she walks the estate and begins a brazen affair with a worker, setting off a chain of violent events that gets bleaker with each scene. Pugh’s portrayal of another dark, determined woman is mesmerizing. Stream Lady Macbeth on Kanopy or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you want more sprawling family drama in a historical setting, look no further than Legends of the Fall. Set in the early 20th century, it follows Colonel William Ludlow (Anthony Hopkins) and his sons Tristan (Brad Pitt), Alfred (Aidan Quinn), and Samuel (Henry Thomas) as they navigate life choices and deal with the emotional wounds they inflict on each other. From World War I to Prohibition, the Ludlows fall in love (sometimes with each other’s wives), suffer crushing loss, and remain connected to their ranch and the natural beauty of Montana through it all. Anchored by a star turn by Brad Pitt, this movie will scratch the itch left behind by East of Eden. Rent Legends of the Fall on Prime Video.

If you want to see a different take on the novel, check out the 1955 adaptation directed by Elia Kazan (grandfather of Zoe Kazan, who co-wrote and directed the 2026 series). Starring James Dean (who would die a few months after its release), it’s an old-school Hollywood epic that only covers the final third of the book. That makes it a very different narrative experience from the series, which has more room to explore the novel’s complexities—but the film looks amazing, Dean’s performance is terrific, and Kazan directs the heck out of it. Rent East of Eden on Prime Video.

Another choice for epic family drama, Giant was James Dean’s last film, and offers family drama in heaps. Like East of Eden, it follows a family over the course of decades as patriarch Jordan “Bick” Benedict, Jr. (Rock Hudson) tries to maintain his family’s ranching legacy in the face of changing times and a flood of oil money, while his former ranch hand Jett Rink (Dean) pines for Bick’s wife, Leslie (Elizabeth Taylor), and strikes it rich with oil. As money’s corrosive effect takes its toll on Jett, the Benedict family grows and changes, with plenty of drama to spare along the way. Rent Giant on Prime Video.

If East of Eden makes you curious about other adaptations of Steinbeck’s work, your next stop should be John Ford’s 1940 version of The Grapes of Wrath. Set during the Great Depression, it follows Tom Joad (Henry Fonda) after his release from prison for manslaughter. He finds his family has been forced off their land, and joins them in a desperate migration to California in hopes of finding work and security. Along the way, Joad kills again and undergoes what can only be described as radicalization, dedicating his life to organizing labor and fighting back against the predations of capitalist society. It’s a remarkable film pulsing with emotional heft and deep family drama, and if its story and setting are very different from East of Eden, the impact will be similar. Stream The Grapes of Wrath on Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3468. 10 Fun and Quirky iPhone Duo Apps Worth Checking Out

The launch of the iPhone Duo marks the first time that Apple has fundamentally changed the form factor of the iPhone. This is an exciting development because, among other reasons, it allows app developers to get even more creative. If you have an iPhone Duo, plan to get one, or if you're just interested in creative app interfaces, then you should take a look at these apps.

With Tiny Computers ($4), when you use the Duo half-open, it turns the bottom display into a keyboard, and the screen goes up top. The app features computers inspired by Commodore 64, Windows 95, iMac G3, Macintosh, IBM PC, Amiga 500, ThinkPad, iBook G3, Powerbook G4, and Windows XP. The attention to detail is great, but early App Store reviews mention that the app can be buggy.

I miss the tactile nature of playing music on my cassette player at home, and my old Sony Walkman clone. Deck-Man ($5) is an app that brings the Walkman's interface, complete with all the clicks and clacks, to your iPhone Duo. Each time you play an album, Deck-Man lets you "insert" the cassette in the player before it starts playing. The app links to your Apple Music account and it also supports playing local music files.

Foldissimo (free, $10 to unlock all songs) simulates the sound of airflow in an accordion as you fold and unfold your iPhone Duo. It has some songs pre-loaded, and you can pay $10 to unlock all songs. Foldissimo also supports a few other instruments (accordion organ, panpipes, and theremin), but you'll need to pay an additional $10 to unlock those.

With Flipcorder ($5), while the viewfinder and the retro interface are visible to you when you have the Duo in tablet mode, your subjects can also see the frame via the outer display. When you fold the Duo, the app saves the clip, and allows you to record up to 30 minutes of video per day, each of which is saved in a virtual "tape."

Orisuji ($5) is a puzzle game where you solve mazes by folding your iPhone Duo. It has 69 levels, and you'll be solving most of these by folding or unfolding the device to shift the position of the maze to make your characters move, unlock doors, or to find keys to get past locked doors.

Toastie ($3) is a game where you, well, make sandwiches: It has 10 recipes for you to master, with a time limit of 15 seconds per step as your in-game customers wait for you to serve them. You fold the phone to "cook" the sandwich; leave it folded for too long and you'll end up with burnt toast.

Marbles Unhinged (Free, $3/each to unlock all levels in a world) is a puzzle game where you guide a marble towards the exit in each level. When you fold your iPhone, it turns the top half of the level into a ramp, and alters the speed of the marble. You can keep the phone at different angles to change the nature of the stage, which will lead you to the solution.

ChompDuo (Free, $1 to unlock all monsters) uses the Duo's folding mechanics to make monsters "chomp" down, and you'll feel each bite via haptic vibrations. When you close the Duo, the monster's eyes stare at you from the outer display. It's a silly app that you or your kids could enjoy playing around with.

Unfold Your City (Free, $5 to unlock all cities) simulates pop-up books to guide you through the highlights of different cities. It reminds me of Robert Sabuda's beautiful pop-up books, especially when you use the app on iPhone Duo. It slowly pops up the artwork for each city as you unfold the device, and displays the cover when you close the "book."

In the Pokémon anime, the Pokédex is an encyclopedia that catalogs information about your friendly neighborhood pocket monsters. Dex Fold (Free, $3 to unlock optional features) simulates the device from the anime, which means that you can only use the app when you unfold the iPhone Duo.

#3467. Ridley Scott's Apple TV Crime Thriller Is a 10/10 Binge-Watch

A crime series needs certain qualities to work. Of course, there have to be twisty plots, plenty of exciting and suspenseful moments, and characters that you become instantly drawn to. Recent shows like True Detective, Task, and MobLand have all introduced viewers to thrilling episodes that provide an inside look at dark, mysterious criminal underworlds. One series in particular flew under the radar when it was released, but remains every bit as worthy of a binge-watch as the other shows in this genre.

The Ridley Scott-produced drama Dope Thief premiered on Apple TV in March 2025. Over a succinct eight episodes, the Peter Craig-created series never shies away from creating an intense and brutally violent yet completely captivating story. The series was adapted from a 2009 novel by Dennis Tafoya, and follows two best friends named Manny Carvalho (Wagner Moura) and Ray Driscoll (Brian Tyree Henry), who are trying to survive on the rough streets of Philadelphia. They've created a small-time robbery scheme where they pose as DEA agents and steal from local drug dealers.

After you watch 'Dope Thief,' go back and watch these shows!

Their con works pretty well until they take on a job that brings their whole lives crashing down. Even though there are plenty of red flags from the start, Ray and Manny rob a drug operation that is actually already being surveilled by real DEA officers. From there, the two men fall deeper and deeper into a massive criminal enterprise that puts them in danger at every turn. Can Manny and Ray outrun their fates, and will their friendship survive the danger that's coming for them? Each episode is fast-paced and drama-packed, but Dope Thief also manages to infuse its story with a wry humor that makes all the bloodshed a tiny bit easier to stomach.

Dope Thief stands apart from other crime shows because of its impressive blend of genres. One moment, you'll be covering your eyes at the violence, while a moment later, you'll be chuckling at the silly antics Manny and Ray are forced to perform to escape danger. Despite the humor and levity, Dope Thief never shies away from emphasizing the story's high-stakes circumstances. The series also impressively emphasizes the importance of found family. The bonds between many characters are compelling and authentic, and although most aren't related by blood, their connections are just as powerful. Dope Thief also successfully portrays the long-lasting effects of trauma and the heartbreak of knowing someone struggling with addiction, weaving these elements to make each episode better than the last.

Much of Dope Thief's success is tied to Wagner and Henry's performances. Their chemistry is both electric and effortless, and each actor proves why they're considered among the best in the industry right now. It's no surprise that Henry was nominated for an Emmy for his work as Ray. Marin Ireland is also incredible as Mina, a beautifully broken undercover agent who becomes entangled in Ray and Manny's lives. We'd be remiss if we didn't mention the stellar performances of Kate Mulgrew as Ray's tough-as-nails adoptive mother and Ving Rhames as Ray's gruff, embattled father.

For more than a year, fans wondered if there would be future episodes of Dope Thief. However, a few weeks ago, it was announced that Apple TV wouldn't be moving forward with the series. Although it's a shame that there'll be no Season 2, you should still check out this exceptional show. With an impressive 86% Rotten Tomatoes score and edge-of-your-seat storytelling, Dope Thief is the perfect addition to the crime thriller genre.

#3466. Apple confirms iOS 27.3 beta is coming next week with Apple Intelligence in China

Apple today took the unusual step of confirming when its next iOS developer beta is expected to arrive, as part of an announcement detailing the upcoming launch of Apple Intelligence in China. Here are the details.

In mid-July, Reuters reported that, following a lengthy back-and-forth with Chinese regulators and multiple delays, Apple Intelligence had finally cleared a major regulatory hurdle ahead of its long-awaited launch in the country.

Then, a couple of weeks ago, Bloomberg reported that Apple was planning to launch Apple Intelligence in China in December as part of iOS 27.3, although without Siri AI and other newer features.

The following day, China’s state-backed media outlet The Paper reported that Tim Cook had confirmed regulatory approval for the platform, with a test version expected before the end of October.

Then, just last Monday, Apple released iOS 27.2 and its counterparts, expanding Siri AI support to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. On the same day, the company announced that four more languages, including Traditional Chinese, would be supported by the end of the year.

However, while that announcement confirmed additional language support for Siri AI, it offered no updates on the rollout of Apple Intelligence in China, where Siri AI itself will remain unavailable for the time being.

While Apple typically releases the first beta of its next software update shortly after the previous version becomes available, iOS 27.3 has yet to materialize.

Now, as spotted by MacRumors, a press release published on Apple’s Chinese Newsroom website confirms that testing of Apple Intelligence in China will begin on November 4, as part of the next iOS developer beta.

Importantly, Apple has only confirmed November 4 as the start of Apple Intelligence testing in China, not necessarily the release date of iOS 27.3 beta 1 itself.

In the press release, Apple confirms that users in China will get an improved Siri experience, including Type to Siri and the ability to access Alibaba’s Qwen for certain requests, but not Siri AI itself.

The Qwen integration will also extend to Writing Tools and Visual Intelligence. According to Apple, users will be able to ask questions about photos and documents, including PDFs and presentations, as well as generate original content from scratch through Writing Tools. Users will be able to access Qwen by signing into their accounts or using Sign in with Apple.

Other features included in the initial rollout are Live Translation in Messages, FaceTime, and Phone, Writing Tools, Genmoji, Clean Up in Photos, natural-language photo searches, priority notifications, notification summaries, and Smart Reply, among others.

Apple also noted that the initial rollout will be exclusive to the iPhone, with support for other platforms coming only after the necessary regulatory approvals have been obtained.

The features will be available on the iPhone 15 Pro and Pro Max, iPhone 16 and later, iPhone Air, and iPhone Duo, with both Siri and the device language required to be set to either English or Simplified Chinese.

The company also confirmed that the features will become publicly available in December, with the official release of iOS 27.3.

#3465. Five Hacks Every Suunto Race 3S User Should Know

Suunto's new Race 3S is a lightweight, premium racing watch—but at a retail price of $599, it's a steep climb from the Race S, which is regularly on sale for $299. Still, there are certainly some major upgrades: The battery holds 46% more than the Race S's, and it's good for up to 38 hours of dual-band GPS; storage is double the Race S's, at 64GB. And as always, with the SuuntoPlus store, you can download apps and integrations so your watch can do more than just the default features. After all, the best way to justify the price is to really make use of everything the watch can do. Here are five ways to get more out of your Suunto Race 3S.

(Suunto Race 3S users should also check out these Suunto Run hacks).

There are several ways you can explore new hikes, straight from your watch or app, and all from the comfort of your home. First up, make sure you download offline maps at home. The Race 3S offers free worldwide offline maps with contour lines and place names, and you pay no subscription. Download your regions over wifi before you leave, so you aren't relying on a phone signal at the trailhead. The 64GB of storage leaves room for several regions, so grab the places you actually run, plus anywhere you're traveling. Menu paths can shift with firmware updates, so check the Suunto app if the layout has changed.

From there, build a library of points of interest. A POI is any spot worth returning to, such as a trailhead, water source, campsite, or viewpoint—and with Suunto specifically, you get a broad definition of “POI,” including spots for hunting, fishing, foraging, or wildlife watching. There are built-in POI types for noting where a deer seemed to have rubbed its antlers, where you've seen marine mammals, or where you've spotted mushrooms. And with the Race 3S, you can store up to 250 of them on the watch.

You can create them on the map in the Suunto app without even being there in person, or when you do stumble upon one, you can save your current location from the watch mid-run. You just have to plug in the POI as a Navigation Target under the options for your trail run or other activity. There's also a navigation app, accessible from the bottom of the widget list (select All Apps), and you can navigate without having an activity running. Organize them by area before a hiking trip, and you can navigate to a trailhead or a spring with a few taps, with the map showing the terrain around you.

For all the hikers out there, you can use Climb Guidance to preview the climbs. When you load a route, Climb Guidance splits it into flat, uphill, downhill, climb and descent sections, and shows remaining ascent. Use it to decide where to push and where to hold back. It doesn't set your pace for you, but it lets you pace by terrain.

Suunto’s Race line includes a storm alarm that watches for rapid pressure drops, a warning sign that weather is turning. It only helps if the barometer reading is trustworthy, so set your altitude to a known reference (a trailhead sign or a verified elevation) before you head up. To turn on storm alerts, go into Settings > System notifications > Alerts > Storm. (This is also where you can set up sunrise and sunset notifications.)

Just remember to recalibrate your barometer every time you start from a new elevation. Also under the Settings menu, you can select Alti & Baro, and then you have the option to either Set altitude or Auto adjust altitude. The auto-adjustment uses a GPS reading to make sure the altimeter is calibrated. But if you know your current altitude from a map, you can set it manually.

Training by heart rate is a great idea, but the default zones on your watch are based on broad formulas and guesses. With the SuuntoPlus app store, you can select Anaerobic Threshold and follow the instructions to find the heart rate where effort turns hard, so your zones reflect your body.

Be prepared: A threshold test is a tough workout. After a warm-up, you’ll be asked to run as fast as you can for 30 minutes. At the end, the app will tell you the heart rate that seems to correspond with your lactate threshold.

Now here’s the cool part: On your watch, go into Settings, then Training, then Intensity zones. Choose either the Default HR zones for all sports (what I’d recommend if you aren’t sure) or choose a sport under the advanced setting. Here, you can set the boundaries between your zones. The boundary at the bottom of zone 5 (and thus the top of zone 4) should be set to the number you got from the threshold test. If you’d like to tweak the other zones, Suunto has more information on how to calculate numbers for the other zone boundaries.

And for any threshold test, where precision matters most, I recommend pairing with a chest strap.

SuuntoPlus apps run on the watch and show extra data during activities, and these two are worth setting up during your training:

Cadence Coach shows live cadence and stride length so you can work on running form and, in Suunto's words, avoid injuries. Run a few easy sessions with it, find the cadence that feels smooth, and use it as a target.

Sprint automatically records your strides and sprints, using wrist acceleration. Instead of tapping laps during strides or hill sprints, just run, and review the efforts afterward.

Activate both in the Suunto app's SuuntoPlus store before starting an exercise, and watch your running economy start to improve.

My favorite time-saving shortcut is to pin the timer widget. Widgets are reachable from the watch face by swiping up or turning the crown, and you can choose which ones to show and in what order in the Suunto app. Move the timer to the top, and pin it so a crown press opens it. Then the upper button starts and stops the stopwatch, and the lower button resets it. It's ideal for intervals, cooking, and race-day warm-ups, and you never have to start a full workout for a quick timing job. The timer remembers whether you last used the stopwatch or the countdown.

Finally, I’m keeping my eye on the launch of the Race Planner feature. It's meant to build a pacing plan from your route, weather, and goal time, and then guide your pace on race day. Suunto hasn't announced a date yet, so I wouldn’t exactly buy the watch for it.

#3463. Steam Makes Brand-New RPG Free To Keep Forever

Steam is always getting free games, but the quality of those free titles can sometimes be hit or miss. While countless games have gotten free demos or free early access periods, the window is a bit smaller when it comes to games that are 100% free to keep forever. Thankfully, there's a brand-new RPG that's on Steam now, and not only is it free to keep, it's actually pretty solid, currently sitting with "Positive" reviews after being available for only the last 24 hours.

Arguably, most free RPGs on Steam are actually free-to-play and gacha games that will entice players with a purchase or two along the way. That's thankfully not the case here. Instead, you're being offered a completely free RPG that requires nothing but your time. It's admittedly pretty short (most people can beat it in around 2 hours), but for an RPG that's being offered up at no cost, it's a pretty sweet deal.

WendyQuest: Legend of the Four Corner Stones is a brand-new RPG on Steam that pays homage to the classic JRPGs. It has classic pixel-art, giving it a SNES look that should remind fans of games from that era like Final Fantasy 6, Chrono Trigger, and Secret of Mana. You'll also need to solve puzzles, giving it some serious The Legend of Zelda vibes, and fight off against mech bosses.

As you might expect, you'll play as Wendy herself, but there are a number of party members joining you along the way. With enemies like Golden Archers and Hot Sludge Sundaes, the Dragon Quest-like puns should keep you smiling the whole way through. Yes, this is all just a clever and shameless marketing scheme to get us all to buy food from Wendy's, but at least it's a GOOD marketing scheme.

WendyQuest: Legend of the Four Corner Stones is available to play on Steam Deck as well, so you can chip away while on the go (maybe even while waiting in a drive-thru). The RPG is also 100% free on Steam, and it's yours to keep. So, even if you're just morbidly curious to see what a fast food-themed JRPG would be like, you can check it out at zero risk and zero cost. The game currently sits with "Positive" review scores on Steam.

Wendy's has been on an absolute tear lately when it comes to clever marketing. Songs to Listen to in a Wendy's Parking Lot, a 6-track emo EP, came out a month ago. It was surprisingly catchy and well-done, and anyone who grew up in the early 2000s should instantly feel nostalgic. Now, that's being followed up with the RPG, WendyQuest: Legend of the Four Corner Stones. At this point, I'm just excited to see what the company comes up with next.

It's no secret the fast food chain has been suffering when it comes to sales lately, but this kind of clever marketing is surely a way to keep Wendy's at the front of people's minds. Be sure to check out WendyQuest: Legend of the Four Corner Stones on Steam. In terms of free RPGs, it's actually a lot of fun.

#3462. The Kindle Click Is the One Accessory Readers Have Been Waiting For

The Kindle is the world's most ubiquitous e-reader, but that's not the same as being the best. Don't get me wrong: Amazon deserves a large share of the credit for bringing e-books into the mainstream, and over the years, the Kindle has consistently offered a top-tier user experience, thanks to both generally good hardware and its integration into the retailer's ecosystem (for better or worse). But the company also rarely innovates in the space, waiting until other players like Barnes & Noble and Boox have tested out new features (like temperature-adjustable lighting and color screens, respectively) before adopting them itself. It's also not shy about dictating to customers what they can and can't do with their Kindles, from removing the ability to directly download copies of their e-books to limiting support for third-party accessories.

One such accessory has been maddeningly absent from the Kindle for years, despite the device having the technology in place to support it: a Bluetooth remote control (all Kindles released since 2018 support Bluetooth for connecting wireless headphones, but only wireless headphones).

A few years ago, third-party e-reader remotes became a big thing on BookTok, prompting competitors like Kobo and Boox to release their own versions of the peripherals. But with the Kindle's Bluetooth protocol locked down, Kindle owners were mostly out of luck; their only option a third-party clip-on accessory that attaches to the side of the device and manually taps the display at the press of a remote button—far from ideal, as they can only turn pages in one direction and block a portion of the screen.But finally, Amazon has seen the light and made its own Bluetooth remote, which it has dubbed the Kindle Click. More importantly, it has opened up the Bluetooth protocol within the Kindle firmware so it can connect to the accessory in the first place—though it will only work on Kindles from 2024 or later. (It pairs well with the new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, no pun intended.)

If you've never used one before, it can be a bit confusing to consider why someone would want a remote for their Kindle—why bother fussing with an extra device when you can just tap the screen or press a button? But for certain scenarios, it really does make sense.

Most practically, a remote can allow you to turn pages in circumstances where holding the e-reader itself is less than convenient, as when you're exercising: Holding a Kindle in your hands is tough when you're on an elliptical, and the words can bounce around too much if you're trying to use a spin bike while gulping down a few chapters of Yesteryear. But if you can prop the e-reader onto the machine's handlebars or a nearby surface, you can turn pages easily without missing a step.

Then there's the coziness factor: Reading under a big blanket in winter is one of the coziest activities I can imagine, but if you have to keep your arms outside of the blanket to turn pages on your Kindle, well, that's going to have an impact on how cozy you feel. (This is a real problem!) But what if you could comfortably arrange the device within your line of sight and turn pages while keeping your hands ensconced within your weighted throw? Some readers are willing to spend multiple tens of dollars to achieve this level of coziness.

How many dollars? In the case of the Kindle Click, around 35 of them (plus tax). Though that may seem like kind of a lot for a simple little remote with two basic functions and four buttons, it's just $5 more than the admittedly much cuter Boox Tappy. Speaking of which, while the new firmware update will also allow the Kindle to support cheaper third-party alternatives, there's no guarantee they will work as well.

So how does the Kindle Click work? Pretty seamlessly: You press and hold one button on the remote to put it in pairing mode. You open up the Settings menu on your 2024 or later Kindle and tap Accessories (you may need to perform a software update, if you aren't seeing that option). You tap Kindle Click in the resulting list to pair it. Once paired, the remote seems to connect to the Kindle automatically if the two devices are nearby and both powered up, provided you keep the latter's Bluetooth functionality turned on; you don't have to manually pair them every time.

That's pretty much it: Once you've opened a book, you can now turn pages with a button press (you can map which of the big grey buttons moves pages forward or back to suit your preferences). The volume-like buttons on the side can be used to adjust the brightness of the front light. You can't use the remote to navigate around the device or open a different book, so choose your reading material carefully before you enter your cocoon.

While the Click definitely works as advertised, Amazon could have been a bit more creative with its functionality. The Boox Tappy, for example, can switch between modes so it can be used to jump backward and forward between tracks in an audiobook or scroll pages in a web browser. While the Kindle can't display websites, it definitely supports audiobooks, but you can't use the Click to jump between chapters or adjust the volume while listening to an Audible book; these both seem like no-brainers to me.And while being able to turn the brightness up or down is nice, why not let the remote control the warmth settings as well, either through enabling different modes (like the Tappy) or via a combination of button presses? I'm not an engineer, so I don't know how complicated it would be to get that to work, but Amazon employs a lot of them, and I bet they could figure it out.

#3461. WhatsApp announces four new features to make group chats easier to manage

In a blog post this week, WhatsApp confirmed that it is rolling out four new features designed to make it easier to manage group chats and keep track of what’s going on in each one. Here are the details.

WhatsApp this week announced that the filter drawer, which appears when users swipe down on the conversations list, will now include a “Mentions and replies” button alongside other filter options such as Groups, Favorites, Unread and custom filters.

Once tapped, the chat list will show only “unread group conversation[s] where you were either mentioned or received a direct reply, including @all messages,” says WhatsApp.

Additionally, WhatsApp will now let users pin messages indefinitely in group chats, rather than choosing between 24 hours, 7 days, or 30 days.

Another in-chat feature coming to groups is the ability to “send someone recent messages retroactively after they’ve joined a group just by tapping their name in the chat.” Previously, this was only possible when adding someone to a group, rather than after they had joined.

Finally, WhatsApp is rolling out group status sharing, which lets users post updates visible only to members of a specific group. Other members can view, react to, and add their own statuses, which disappear after 24 hours.

As is often the case with WhatsApp updates, it may take some time for all four features to become available to everyone. To check out the full announcement, follow this link.
